# Tools, skills, and MCP

Source: https://tracon.dev/concepts/tools/

An agent gains capability in a few ways. They differ in where the code lives and who
is allowed to add it.

| | What it is | Where the code runs |
|---|---|---|
| **Tools** | Methods in your codebase | Your process |
| **Client-side tools** | A declaration in your codebase, no server-side body | The caller's process (typically a browser) |
| **Skills** | Markdown instructions plus resources | Nowhere — they are text |
| **MCP tools** | Tools published by a remote MCP server | Someone else's process |

## Tools

A tool is a method you wrote, registered at startup. See
[adding a tool](/getting-started/tools/) for the mechanics.

The rule that governs the whole design: **tools are defined in code only**. The
console lets a user *select* from registered tools; it never defines one. If it could,
anyone who reached the console could execute code on your server.

Wrapping for approval happens in the **registry**, not at the call site. The registry
is the single place where "an agent may only point at a registered tool" is enforced,
so no other code path can skip the wrapper.

### Who owns what

Six concerns belong to the registry and its pipeline, never to a tool body:

| Concern | Owned by |
|---|---|
| Authorization (can this caller call this tool at all) | `IToolAuthorizationHandler` in the pipeline |
| Approval (does a person need to say yes this time) | The registry's approval wrapper |
| Timeout | The registry's timeout wrapper |
| Output truncation | The registry's truncation wrapper |
| Tenant scoping | `TraconRunContext.Current` |
| Audit (what ran, with what result) | Run recording, driven from the registry |

A tool body reads `TraconRunContext.Current` when it needs the tenant, run, or
session — it never re-implements any of the other five; they already ran before the
body was ever invoked.

### Lifecycle and concurrency

The registry is a **startup snapshot**. It is built once, from every `AddTool*` call
made during startup, and never mutates afterward — there is no runtime `AddTool`. MCP
tools are the one deliberate exception: they are discovered from a remote server and
can appear or disappear as that server's own catalog changes, which is why MCP has its
own, separate dynamic model instead of sharing the code registry's snapshot guarantee.

Every tool instance is a **singleton**, shared by every tenant, every run, and every
thread that happens to call it. Keep no per-call state in an instance field — read
[the empty service provider rule](/getting-started/tools/#the-rule-that-trips-people-up)
for the related mistake of resolving a scoped dependency the same way. When a
dependency genuinely has to be fresh per call, register the tool with `AddScopedTool`
instead of `AddTool` — see
[scoped dependencies](/guides/write-your-own-tool/#scoped-dependencies).

Because a tool is shared, the same tool can already run **concurrently across
different runs** today, whether or not `ToolLoop.AllowConcurrentToolCalls` is set —
that setting only governs whether one run's own turn calls its several tools
one after another or at the same time. A tool body that keeps no mutable
instance state handles both cases for free.

### Authorization, validation, and timeout

Three more wrappers apply next to approval, in a fixed order: **authorization**
(outermost), **validation**, **timeout**, then **approval** (innermost), then the real
method. The same order applies whether the tool is code-defined or MCP-sourced — one
composition point builds both.

Authorization asks a different question than approval. Approval asks "is this call okay
this time" and stops to wait for a person. Authorization asks "can this caller call this
tool at all" and answers instantly from your own policy — implement
`IToolAuthorizationHandler` and register it; the default allows every call, so an
application that registers nothing keeps today's behavior exactly.

```csharp
public sealed class MyAuthorizationHandler : IToolAuthorizationHandler
{
    public ValueTask<ToolAuthorizationResult> AuthorizeAsync(
        ToolAuthorizationRequest request, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
        => request.RequiredPermission is "orders.cancel" && !CallerHasPermission(request)
            ? ValueTask.FromResult(ToolAuthorizationResult.Deny("You cannot cancel orders."))
            : ValueTask.FromResult(ToolAuthorizationResult.Allow());
}

services.AddSingleton<IToolAuthorizationHandler, MyAuthorizationHandler>();
```

A denied call does not fail the run: the model receives the reason text as an ordinary
tool result and continues its turn — the same way a search that finds nothing is not an
error. If your handler throws, the call is denied (fail-closed), never allowed.

The authorization layer asks two gates, in this order, and a call needs both. First the
tenant's [tool policy](/concepts/tools/#per-tenant-tool-policy), which an administrator
writes as data (which tool names and permissions the tenant holds); then your handler, which is
your code. A call the policy refuses never reaches your handler. A tenant with no policy passes
the first gate, so a host that saves none behaves as before.

The chain does not stop at tools you register. The `file_access_*` tools of a session workspace
and the two search tools Tracon adds itself, `search_knowledge` and the on-demand
`search_conversation_memory`, run through it too, so the handler, the validator, the timeout and
the budget check apply to them. The searches have the effect `External`, because the text of the
query leaves the process. [Which tools reach the handler](/guides/embedding/#which-tools-reach-the-tool-authorization-handler)
lists what is covered and what is not.

Validation asks a narrower question, right after authorization: "are these specific
arguments acceptable". Binding already rejects a type mismatch or a missing `required`
field — including a required member of a generated tool's **object** parameter
(a public record or class with a single public constructor, see [Write your own
tool](/guides/write-your-own-tool/)) — and register `IToolArgumentsValidator` for
anything binding does not catch: an extra field the schema does not declare, for
example, or a generated `minimum`/`maximum`/length/`pattern` constraint, which the
schema carries but binding never enforces on its own; a validator that wants to
enforce one reads `tool.JsonSchema`.
Unlike a denial, a **rejected** call is recorded as `ToolFailed`, not as an ordinary
result — see [argument validation](/guides/write-your-own-tool/#argument-validation)
for the full mechanism, including the fail-closed behavior on a throwing validator.

`[TraconTool]` also carries an effect class and a per-tool timeout:

```csharp
[TraconTool(
    "cancel_order",
    "Cancels an order.",
    RequiresApproval = true,
    Effect = ToolEffect.Destructive,
    RequiredPermission = "orders.cancel",
    TimeoutSeconds = 30)]
public static string CancelOrder(string orderId) => ...;
```

`Effect` (`Read`/`Write`/`Destructive`/`External`) is information, not a gate — the
console shows it as a badge, and the audit trail records it. By default the approval
card an operator sees carries only this raw call; register
[`IToolApprovalPresenter`](/concepts/governance/#approvals) to show a resolved entity
name instead. A call that outlives its
timeout does not fail the run either: the model sees a tool error and continues, the same
as a denial.

When the timeout elapses the body is handed a **cancelled token** — a token linked to the
caller's own, which this layer cancels. Cancellation is cooperative, so what happens next
depends on the body:

- **A body that reads its token** stops there and spends nothing more. Accept a
  `CancellationToken` parameter and pass it down to every call you make.
- **A body that never reads it** is not forcibly stopped and keeps running to completion,
  possibly with a real side effect, after the model has already moved on.

A call in that second group is still accounted for. When it finally settles successfully,
its result, its real duration and anything it reported through `TraconToolUsage.Report`
are written onto **that same call's record** — `lateCompletedAt` on the
`ToolInvocationRecord` says when, `timedOut` and `error` stay as they were because they
record what the *model* was told. This matters for a tool that spends money: image
generation that needs 35 seconds against a 30 second limit has produced and been billed
for a real image, and without this the charge would appear in no cost report at all. The
amount also reaches the tenant's quota counter, once, in `Tracon:Pricing:Currency` (the
run's own recorded total is not changed). No second record is written, so per-tool totals
still count one call.

The timeout applies to execution only, never to a pending approval, which can wait
indefinitely.

A tool body can also run **more than once for the same logical call**, on two different
timelines that are easy to conflate:

- **Within one turn:** Microsoft Agent Framework retries a throwing tool call up to
  `MaximumConsecutiveErrorsPerRequest` (3 by default) times before giving up and
  re-throwing to the caller. A tool that is not safe to call twice in a row needs its
  own idempotency guard, regardless of any Tracon setting.
- **Across an interrupted run:** `SafeToRepeat` (only read for `Destructive`/`External`
  tools) tells Tracon whether resuming a run that was cut off mid-call may repeat
  that call. It says nothing about the in-turn retries above.

The one case that does **not** repeat a completed call is a provider fallback: if a call
already finished before the primary provider failed, the fallback model asking the same
question again is answered from that result instead of running the tool's body a second
time — see [Fall back to a secondary provider](/guides/reliability/#fall-back-to-a-secondary-provider).

### Per-tenant tool policy

`IToolAuthorizationHandler` is your code: one rule for every tenant, changed by a
deployment. When each tenant should run a different set of tools, and an administrator
should change that without a deployment, save a **tool policy** for the tenant. The
policy is two closed lists:

- `allowedTools`: the tool names the tenant may run;
- `grantedPermissions`: the permissions the tenant holds. A tool that declares a
  `RequiredPermission` passes when that permission is listed.

A call passes when its tool name is in `allowedTools` **or** its permission is in
`grantedPermissions`. A tool that declares no permission and is not named is refused,
and two empty lists refuse every tool: an empty policy is not the same as having none.
Names and permissions are compared exactly, with letter case.

The policy is a gate **in front of** your handler, not a replacement for it. A call needs both
to allow it, and a call the policy refuses never reaches your handler. A refusal is not
a failure: the model reads `This tool is not enabled for this tenant.` as the tool's
result and the run goes on, and the call is recorded with `authorizationDenied`. The
policy covers exactly the tools your handler is
[asked about](/guides/embedding/#which-tools-reach-the-tool-authorization-handler): tools
registered in code, MCP tools, the `file_access_*` tools of a session workspace,
`search_knowledge` and `search_conversation_memory`. Hosted tools, agents called as tools,
skill tools, the file memory, todo and harness tools are not covered. An MCP tool declares no
permission, so only its name can allow it: list it as `{server}_{tool}`, the name `GET /api/tools`
does not show. A name the server renames drops out of the list and the tool is refused, never
allowed by accident.

A tenant with no saved policy is unrestricted by the policy, so a host that never saves one
behaves as before. A multi-tenant deployment can close that gap with
`Tracon:Tools:RequireTenantPolicy` (default `false`): turned on, a tenant with no policy runs
**no** tool, and the default tenant needs a policy row like any other. Saving a policy is never
blocked by the switch. The switch is read when the host starts. It is one of the two answers to
the `UncheckedToolCalls` decision of
[`RequireProductionProfile()`](/guides/embedding/#make-a-production-decision-required); the
other is a handler of your own.

The policy is read from the store on every tool call and kept in no cache, so a saved
policy applies to the next call, even of an agent that is already running. The cost is one
store read per call; a store that cannot be read refuses the call and logs an error, because
a gate that read a failure as "no policy" would open exactly when the store is down.

The policy is managed under `/api/tenants/{tenantId}/tools` (`GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE`), guarded
by the `SecurityAdmin` API key scope; a tenant other than the caller's own also requires
platform authority, as for [egress](/concepts/governance/#per-tenant-provider-credentials-and-egress). Every save and
delete lands in the audit trail as `tenant_tool_policy.save` and `tenant_tool_policy.delete`
with both lists. The console shows the policy under the egress policy in the tenant panel of
the settings screen.

### Result representation and persistence

Whatever a tool returns, Tracon turns it into one **canonical text form** before
anything else — a content guard, the output limit — inspects it. `null`, `string`, and
`JsonElement` each have one stable text form; a primitive, `Guid`, or date value is
serialized the same, culture-independent way every time. A collection, record, or class
result is only canonicalized when the tool's generated declaration carries a consumer
`JsonSerializerContext` for it — code-defined tools using the `[TraconTool]`
attribute (see [Write your own tool](/guides/write-your-own-tool/)) require one for
any result type beyond a plain string or primitive. That context, not reflection, is
what turns it into JSON, which is also what keeps the guard AOT-safe. A raw CLR object
returned directly from a hand-written `AIFunction` with no such context attached is
**not** serialized by guessing: it is
treated as an unsupported result and replaced with a generic, secret-free failure text
rather than passed through unguarded or serialized with reflection. This closes a real
gap: inspecting a type name or a placeholder instead of the actual data would let a
guard approve content it never really looked at, and silently trusting an unknown
object would let it bypass the guard and the output limit entirely.

That same canonical text is what gets **persisted**: a tool's arguments and result are
written into the run's permanent record and streamed to the console over SSE. Neither
one is written into a telemetry span. A tool that would otherwise return a secret —
a connection string, an access token — must redact it before returning, because both
of those surfaces keep it in full. A tool exception is treated more carefully: only
Tracon's own exception types keep their message; everything else is replaced with
a generic `Tool failed with <ExceptionType>.` before it reaches the record or the
stream, and the original message goes only to your log.

### Output size limit

A tool's result is unbounded by default and goes straight into the model's context. Set
a byte limit — per tool, or once for every tool that does not set its own — and a
result over it is trimmed before the model ever sees it. The limit is measured against
the same canonical text form described above, for every result type it applies to —
a large complex object is bounded exactly like a large string, not skipped because it
is not one. A tool that answers with `AIContent` blocks rather than text — every MCP
tool does — is measured the same way, by the text its provider adapter sends. A result
that fits reaches the model with its blocks intact; one that does not is replaced by
the same envelope any other oversized result gets.

```csharp
services.AddSingleton(new TraconToolRegistration(
    AIFunctionFactory.Create(GetReport, "get_report", "Fetches a report."))
{
    MaxOutputBytes = 4096,
});

services.Configure<TraconOptions>(o => o.Tools.DefaultMaxOutputBytes = 4096);
```

No change is required to keep today's behavior: the default is unlimited, and a tool
that never sets a limit is never touched.

Bounding a tool's output inside its own body is always better — the tool knows its
data, this only counts bytes. Treat the limit as the last line of defense for the day
that bound is forgotten, not a substitute for it: a single runaway tool can otherwise
spend a tenant's whole token budget on one call.

A result over the limit is trimmed and wrapped in an envelope, so the trimmed text can
never break the JSON the model reads:

```json
{"truncated": true, "omittedBytes": 1830, "content": "..."}
```

`truncated` and `omittedBytes` are always present on a trimmed result — a silently
shortened answer would lead the model to a confident, wrong conclusion. A result that
already fits is returned exactly as the tool produced it, never wrapped.

### Concurrent tool calls

By default, when a model turn calls several independent tools at once, Tracon
runs them one after another. Set `ModelBinding.ToolLoop.AllowConcurrentToolCalls` to run them
at the same time instead — each call still gets its own authorization decision, its
own recorded result, and its own entry in the tool-usage metrics; none of that mixes
up between calls that happen to overlap.

Off by default: with no change, tool calls run one at a time exactly as they do
today. Turn it on only for tools whose bodies are safe to run concurrently with
themselves — a tool that shares mutable state across calls without its own
synchronization should not opt in. See
[Model providers](/guides/model-providers/#tool-call-loop) for where this
setting lives on `ModelBinding`, and for the other settings of the loop.

### Built-in image generation

When `Tracon:Images:Enabled` is true and a supported image provider is
registered, Tracon adds `generate_image` as an `External` tool. It accepts a
prompt and returns attachment ids, never base64 image data. Generation can spend money
and sends a prompt to an external provider, so the normal authorization, timeout, run
recording, and continuation rules apply. In particular, an interrupted run does not
automatically repeat an image-generation call.

See [Multimodal input and generated images](/guides/multimodal/) for registration,
storage, and price configuration.

### Report what a tool spent beyond tokens

A tool billed by something other than a token — speech by the character, a transcript by
the second, an image by the piece — reports that from its own body:

```csharp
_ = TraconToolUsage.Report(new ToolCallUsage
{
    Unit = ToolUsageUnits.Characters,
    Quantity = characters,
    Cost = price,
    Currency = "USD",
    Provider = "elevenlabs",
    Model = "eleven_multilingual_v2",
});
```

- **The measurement belongs to the call.** It is written onto the call's record
  (`GET /api/runs/{runId}/tools`) with its unit, quantity, amount, currency, whether the
  quantity was estimated, and the provider and model that did the work. A tool that
  reports twice in one call replaces its first report, so report the total at the end. The
  call returns `false` and does not throw when recording is off or the code is not inside a
  tool call; a call that reported and then never settled keeps what it reported. It also
  returns `false`, and attaches nothing, for a measurement the record cannot hold: an empty
  unit or one longer than 64 characters, a currency longer than 16, a provider longer than
  100, a model longer than 200, a quantity outside 0 to 9,999,999,999 or an amount outside
  0 to 1,000,000,000. These are the limits a function node's items have.
- **It also joins the run's non-token total, the moment the tool reports it.** The same
  rule as a [workflow function node's items](/concepts/workflow-function-nodes/#report-what-a-node-spent-beyond-tokens)
  applies: amounts in `Tracon:Pricing:Currency` add, a quantity is never added across units,
  and a call with no amount is listed and counted as not added — unknown, not free. The
  call-tree budget, the tenant's cost quota and the `run.completed` webhook therefore count a
  `speak` call the way they count a function node that spoke. A measurement that arrives
  after the run closed, from a call that outlived its timeout, stays on the call's record
  and does not change the run's total, but it is added to the tenant's quota counter once,
  because that money was spent.
- **It stops the next tool call.** Once the call tree's budget is spent, a tool call that has not
  started does not start: its result says why, and a streaming run records the call as failed. The call that
  crosses the ceiling runs to its end, so report the amount as soon as you know it. See [A spent
  budget stops a tool call from starting](/guides/reliability/#a-spent-budget-stops-a-tool-call-from-starting).
- **The built-in tools report it already.** `speak`, `transcribe` and `generate_image`
  fill `Provider` and `Model` as well as the measurement. Prices come from
  `Tracon:Pricing`; with none configured the amount stays unknown. `search_knowledge` reports
  the input tokens of its query embedding in the unit `tokens` with no amount: an embedding has
  no price in Tracon yet, so the call is listed and counted as not added.

## Hosted tools

`AddHostedTool(name, kind, factory)` registers a tool that the model provider runs inside the model call:
a web search, a code interpreter, or a file search. The registration is code, like every tool, and a
definition selects it by name in `ToolNames`. Tracon calls nothing, so no approval, permission, timeout, or
output limit applies; the data goes to the provider the model call already uses. The provider's API surface
decides which kinds run, each call is priced from configuration, and each call is a tool event under the
registered name. See [Hosted tools](/guides/hosted-tools/) for the registration rules, the provider table, and
the limits.

## Client-side tools

`AddClientTool(name, description, jsonSchema)` registers a tool the SAME way — the
declaration lives in code — but with no body at all. The model can still call it; the
server returns the pending call to the caller instead of running anything, and the
caller answers it on the next request. See
[Client-side tools and the embeddable widget](/guides/client-side-tools/)
for the full mechanism and the chat widget built on it.

## Skills

A skill is markdown with frontmatter, optionally carrying resources — reference text
the agent can pull in. Skills are tenant-scoped and editable from the console, because
they are *instructions*, not code.

A skill can also be registered in code with `AddSkill`. The code skill wins its name,
as a code-defined agent does: the console opens it read only, and the API refuses to
save a stored skill under that name (`409`), because such a copy would never run.

A skill can also live on disk, as a `SKILL.md` directory under a skill root
(`UseSkillScripts`, `SkillRoots`). An agent names it like any other skill. A name is
looked up in code first, then in the tenant's store, then under the skill roots, so a
disk skill is installation-wide like a code skill: whoever deploys the application
writes it, and every tenant may name it; a tenant's stored skill under the same name
shadows it for that tenant. An edit to its `SKILL.md`, or a script or resource added
or removed, reaches the next run of an agent that names it. The console's skill list
shows stored skills only, so name a disk skill through the API.

An agent lists skills by name. Deleting a skill an agent still names is a real break:
compiling that agent then fails with "the skill was not found" until the reference is
removed or the skill is recreated. Check which agents use a skill before deleting it.

### Approval of the skill tools

An agent that names skills gets three tools from Microsoft Agent Framework: `load_skill`,
`read_skill_resource` and `run_skill_script`. All three ask for approval by default. That is
a problem where nobody can answer: an agent exposed over A2A or MCP, a run with no `sessionId`,
a scheduled run. Its first `load_skill` call closes the run `Failed` with the error type
`approval_unanswerable`.

A definition can turn the approval off for the two tools that only read text:

```csharp
new AgentDefinition
{
    Name = "support",
    Model = new ModelBinding { Provider = "openai", Model = "gpt-5.4-mini" },
    SkillNames = ["house-style"],
    Skills = new SkillSettings { DisableReadApproval = true },
}
```

The same setting in the HTTP body of `POST /api/agents` and `PUT /api/agents/{name}`, and
in the console's skills section, is `"skills": { "disableReadApproval": true }`. A request is
the whole definition: a `PUT` that leaves `skills` out turns the approval on again.

| Tool | Default | With `DisableReadApproval` |
|---|---|---|
| `load_skill` | Asks | Runs |
| `read_skill_resource` | Asks | Runs |
| `run_skill_script` | Asks | **Asks** |

`run_skill_script` keeps its approval. It runs code, so the definition has no setting for it. A
standing approval rule that an administrator writes for `run_skill_script` can still approve the
call; a definition cannot. Where nobody can answer and no such rule exists, a model that calls it
ends the run at the call.

Skill text reaches the model as instructions. When the approval is off, no person reads that
text before the model does. Turn it off only for skills that a tenant administrator writes.
A workflow step treats a skill tool like any other tool: with the approval on, the step stops
and waits for a person to answer ([a tool that asks for
approval](/concepts/workflows/#a-tool-that-asks-for-approval)).

### Skill scripts — the strict exception

A skill may also carry **scripts**, and this is the second deliberate exception to the
code-only rule. Unlike MCP, the process runs **on this machine** by default; a host
that registers an `ISkillScriptExecutor` runs it where that executor runs it — see
[Write your own script executor](/guides/write-your-own-script-executor/).

It is off by default and can only be turned on in code, with a mandatory
acknowledgement flag, an interpreter allowlist that starts empty, and skill roots
given in code.

Every execution passes five gates in order, and if any is closed the executor is
never called. After the fifth gate the call waits for a free slot under the
concurrency quota; the quota delays a script, it never refuses one. The slot is held
until the executor returns, or until the timeout plus five seconds has passed:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Skill script security gates
    accDescr: A skill script runs only after the enabled flag, a tenant grant pinned to its content, the interpreter allowlist, the argument, name and size checks, and the audit write all pass in order; it then waits for a free slot under the concurrency quota and goes to the registered executor.
    G1["1. enabled"] --> G2["2. valid grant<br/>pinned to this content"]
    G2 --> G3["3. extension on the<br/>interpreter allowlist"]
    G3 --> G4["4. argument size and schema ·<br/>plain stored name ·<br/>file within the size limit"]
    G4 --> G5["5. written to<br/>the audit trail"]
    G5 --> Q["waits for a slot<br/>(concurrency quota)"]
    Q --> RUN["executor — built-in: separate process<br/>allow-listed environment · same OS user<br/>stdin args · timeout · output limit"]
```

A script file under a skill root passes the same `MaxScriptContentLength` as a
stored script. An empty file, a file larger than the limit, and anything that is not
a regular file — a FIFO, a link to a device — is refused from its metadata, before it
is opened.

:::danger[Gate five is an exception to an exception]
Everywhere else in Tracon an audit-trail write failure is swallowed, because
observability must not break function. Here it is not: a script execution that cannot
be written to the audit trail would be remote code execution with no record of it, so
the run is refused.
:::

Grants are visible and revocable at `GET /api/skill-script-grants`. A grant without a
script name covers every script in a skill; one with a name covers only that script.
Grants can expire.

A grant for a stored or code-defined skill **pins the content** it was given for. Read
`scripts[].contentHash` (one script) or `scriptSetHash` (every script) from
`GET /api/skills/{name}`, review what will run, and send the value as
`expectedContentHash`. A skill-wide grant pins the whole script set: adding, removing,
or changing any script stops every script in the skill until it is granted again. A
hash that no longer matches returns `409` — read the skill again. In a multi-tenant
host, granting a stored script also needs platform authority: a key with
`PlatformAdmin`, the static token, or the `Tracon.PlatformAdmin` policy. A script read
from disk is not pinned, so keep its directory read-only.

:::caution[Tracon does not sandbox]
It provides **no** filesystem jail, network restriction, memory or CPU quota, or
privilege dropping. With the built-in executor the process runs under the same
operating-system user as Tracon and can read what that user can read — on Linux, the
environment Tracon started with too, through `/proc`. In a multi-tenant host a granted
script can therefore reach every tenant's data; the [threat model](/reference/threat-model/)
lists this as an accepted risk. Isolation belongs to the hosting environment — a
container, cgroups, and an unprivileged user — or to an executor that runs scripts
somewhere else; Tracon cannot verify either. The acknowledgement flag exists so the
feature cannot be enabled without seeing this: with execution on and the flag off,
the application fails at **startup**, whichever executor is registered.
:::

## MCP servers

Registering a remote MCP server means accepting tool definitions from outside, which
is the first deliberate exception to the code-only rule. The process runs elsewhere;
Tracon is only a client. Five guards:

1. **`http` and `https` only — there is no stdio transport.** Starting a local process
   would break the rule outright.
2. **`RequiresApproval` defaults to true** for tools discovered this way. Switching it
   off waives approval for every tool of the server, which is the decision a standing
   approval rule makes for one tool. Called with an API key, the save then needs the
   `SecurityAdmin` scope as well as `AgentsAdmin`: for a new server, for a server that
   required approval, and for a server whose endpoint changes while approval stays off.
   A standing rule for one of these tools is bound to the server's endpoint the same way
   ([approval rules](/concepts/governance/)).
3. **A remote tool whose name collides with a code-registered tool is ignored.** Your
   code always wins; a remote server cannot shadow a local tool.
4. **The registration stores no credential.** It stores the *name* of the
   configuration key the value is read from at call time — for the `Authorization`
   header and for any other credential header alike, in `headerConfigurationKeys`.
5. **Every call is recorded** with the source server's name.

Prompts fetched from an MCP server are a **snapshot** an administrator copies into the
console — an agent never pulls one live. Resource access is limited to the URI set the
server itself advertises; accepting arbitrary URIs would be an SSRF tool.

OAuth tokens are held in memory per tenant and server and are **never written to the
database**.

### A server asks the user for input

An MCP server can stop a tool call to ask the user for something: a value the tool
lacks, or a confirmation. The protocol calls it *elicitation*. Tracon tells every
server it connects to that it can answer, with form fields only: it never opens an
address for a server. What the server gets depends on who can answer:

| The call runs in | What the server gets |
|---|---|
| A run you start with `POST /api/agents/{name}/run` and a `sessionId`, or over the [AG-UI endpoint](/guides/ag-ui/#approvals-and-requests-for-input) | The run stops and asks you. Your answer is the input of the next request |
| A run without a `sessionId` | `decline`: an answer has nowhere to go |
| An OpenAI-compatible call, an A2A task, an MCP tool call, a queued run | `decline`: these surfaces have no way to carry the answer |
| An agent called by another agent | `decline`: a sub-agent cannot wait in the middle of its parent's tree, the same rule as for [approvals](/concepts/governance/#approvals) |
| A request to open an address (`url` mode) | `decline` |

`decline` is a complete answer. The server decides what the tool does next, and
nothing is dropped without a word: a decline inside a run writes a
`tracon.tool.input.declined` run event that names the server, the tool and the reason.
A request that reaches the connection outside any run (an older server sends one that
way) has no run to hold an event; the application log records it instead.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    accTitle: A tool call suspended for user input
    accDescr: The caller starts a run, the MCP server asks for input and the run stops. The caller sends the answer as the next request of the session, and the tool call runs again from its start with the answer.
    participant Caller
    participant Tracon
    participant Server as MCP server

    Caller->>Tracon: POST /run (sessionId)
    Tracon->>Server: tools/call
    Server-->>Tracon: input required: "What is your name?"
    Tracon-->>Caller: inputs frame · run is AwaitingInput
    Caller->>Tracon: POST /run (sessionId, inputResponses)
    Tracon->>Server: tools/call, from its start
    Server-->>Tracon: input required: "What is your name?"
    Tracon->>Server: tools/call with the answer
    Server-->>Tracon: result
    Tracon-->>Caller: the model goes on with the result
```

The streaming response sends an `inputs` event right before `done`; a response with
`Idempotency-Key` carries the same list as `inputs` in its body. One entry per request:

```json
[{
  "requestId": "01a16896-7da7-74c9-93a1-3b404320e32c",
  "toolName": "crm_ask_name",
  "serverName": "crm",
  "message": "What is your name?",
  "requestedSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "name": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 } },
    "required": ["name"]
  }
}]
```

`requestedSchema` is flat on purpose: text, numbers, integers, booleans, and single or
multiple choices. The run closes `AwaitingInput`. Answer in the next request of the
same session, by `requestId`:

```bash
curl -X POST https://your-host/tracon/api/agents/support/run \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sessionId": "s-123",
    "inputResponses": [
      { "requestId": "01a16896-7da7-74c9-93a1-3b404320e32c", "action": "Accept", "content": { "name": "Ada" } }
    ]
  }'
```

`action` is `Accept`, `Decline` or `Cancel`. Only `Accept` carries `content`. The
playground in the console shows the form and sends the answer for you.

Rules that follow from the mechanism:

- **The tool call runs again from its start.** Tracon cannot keep a call open while a
  person thinks, so the answer comes with a second call of the same tool and the
  same arguments. A server that asks first and acts after is safe. A server that acts
  before it asks repeats that action.
- **The replay asks no second approval.** The call was approved, or exempt, when it
  first ran.
- **An answer belongs to its question.** If the server asks something else the second
  time, it gets `decline`, not your old answer. A tool call stops for input at most
  once: a server that needs a second answer gets `decline` for it.
- **A wrong answer is refused before the run starts.** An unknown or repeated
  `requestId`, a field the server did not ask for, a required field left out, or a
  value of the wrong type answers `400`. A request that was already answered answers
  `409`. A request without a `sessionId` answers `400`. A run in a session that
  belongs to another user answers `403`, as every run does.
- **The values go to the server and nowhere else.** Tracon does not keep them in the
  session. The audit entry `tool_input.answer` names the request, the server, the
  tool, the action and the *names* of the fields, never a value. It is written before
  the call runs again; if it cannot be written, the answer is not applied
  ([what is guaranteed to be written](/concepts/governance/#what-is-guaranteed-to-be-written)).
- **An older server asks the older way.** A server that speaks only the earlier
  protocol sends a request of its own while the call runs. It cannot be suspended, so
  it gets `decline`.

## Knowledge

Separate from tools: documents are chunked, embedded, and searched by vector distance.
This needs PostgreSQL — the other providers answer `501` on those endpoints.

`POST /api/knowledge/{collection}/search` runs the same retrieval an agent performs,
which makes it the way to separate a retrieval problem from a prompt problem. If the
right chunk does not come back there, the agent was never going to see it.

## Read next

- [Governance](/concepts/governance/) — approvals, audit, and limits
- [Workflows](/concepts/workflows/) — coordinate multiple agents with checkpoints and human input.

# Answering a workflow

Source: https://tracon.dev/concepts/workflow-answers/

What happens when a person answers a workflow that waits for input, and what happens when
the same request gets a second answer? This page covers the two response modes, the audit
entry and the record every answer leaves, the cases where an answer can be given again, and
the answer to an agent's tool call that waits for approval.
How a workflow asks, and how an answer resumes it, is in
[Asking a human](/concepts/workflows/#asking-a-human).

## One answer per request

By default every answer opens a new run, so a second answer to the same request opens a
second branch — a double click or a retried call runs the steps after the request twice.
A workflow that must take one decision per request sets its **response mode** to
`SingleAnswer`: `responseMode` on `PUT /api/workflows/{name}`, the *One answer per
request* switch in the console's editor, or, for a workflow defined in code, the
`AddWorkflow` overload that takes `WorkflowRegistrationOptions`:

```csharp
builder.AddWorkflow(
    "publish-approval",
    services => BuildPublishApproval(services),
    options => options.ResponseMode = WorkflowResponseMode.SingleAnswer);
```

`WorkflowRegistrationOptions.Description` carries the catalog description and
`ResponseMode` the mode. A call that passes a literal `null` as the
third argument does not compile, because it fits both the description overload and this
one; leave the argument out instead.

A waiting run is answered under the mode of the definition version it recorded, so
changing the mode while a person decides does not change how that run is answered.

| The answer | `SingleAnswer` does |
|---|---|
| The first one | Starts the run, as in the default mode |
| The same answer again | Follows the run the first one started: the same SSE frames, read from the stored run, or the same `202` with `Prefer: respond-async`. No second run starts |
| A different answer | `409 Conflict`; the body names neither the run nor the other answer |
| The same answer after its run stopped before it took the answer | Starts the work again in a new run |

Two answers are the same when their `approved`, `text` and `data` are the same; the
checkpoint and the definition version they name do not count. "Stopped before it took the
answer" means the run failed or was cancelled before the workflow received the answer, or
after it with no checkpoint written, so nothing could resume from it. A queued answer whose
job is still waiting or running is followed, because the job's recovery owns that work. A
queued answer whose job was never written — the process stopped after the answer was
recorded and before the job was queued — is finished by a repeat of the same answer: the
repeat writes the job and follows the run, and two repeats at the same time write it once.

The run an answer starts has its row opened before the answer is recorded, so a recorded
answer always names a run that exists. Two answers that arrive in the same moment can
therefore both open a run before one of them claims the request. The other one closes its
own run as `Canceled` with the error type `request_already_answered` and no events. No
webhook, metric or run event sink fires for it, but it is still a run: `GET /api/runs`
lists it and `RunStatistics.CanceledRuns` counts it, so it is part of the error rate's
denominator.

:::caution[A crash in the middle of a streamed answer locks the request]
When a process stops while a streamed `SingleAnswer` run is going, that run stays
`Running`, and a repeat of the answer follows it forever. Only run reconciliation
(`Tracon:RunReconciliation:Enabled`, off by default) closes it: reconciliation closes a
`Running` run whose heartbeat stopped, and it reads no `Queued` run. Turn it on where a
one-answer request must stay answerable after a crash.
:::

## A tool that asks for approval

An agent in a workflow can call a tool that
[needs approval](/concepts/governance/#approvals). Where the pattern hosts the agent — a
stored `Sequential`, `Concurrent`, `Handoff`, `GroupChat` or `Magentic` workflow that lists `agentNames`,
and a code graph that binds the agent with `GetWorkflowAgent` — the workflow stops instead of
failing. The step's run
closes `AwaitingApproval`, the workflow run closes `AwaitingInput`, and the request has the
form `ToolApproval`. Its `prompt` names the tool and adds what your
[approval presenter](/concepts/governance/#approvals) says about the call; the arguments
are not copied into it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: A tool approval inside a workflow
    accDescr: An agent in a workflow calls a tool that needs approval. The workflow closes as awaiting input with a ToolApproval request. The answer is audited, optionally saved as a rule, and the workflow continues on a new run that runs the tool once or hands the agent the refusal.
    CALL["agent calls a tool<br/>that needs approval"] --> WAIT["workflow closes AwaitingInput<br/>request form: ToolApproval"]
    WAIT --> ANS["POST .../respond<br/>approved, text, remember"]
    ANS --> AUD["approval.decision audited<br/>rule saved when remembered"]
    AUD --> NEW["a NEW run continues<br/>the tool runs once, or the agent reads the refusal"]
```

Answer it on the same endpoint as any other request:

```bash
curl -X POST "$TRACON/api/workflows/runs/$RUN/respond" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"requestId": "'"$REQUEST"'", "approved": true, "text": "checked with the customer", "remember": true}'
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `approved` | Required. `true` runs the tool; `false` refuses it, and the agent reads the refusal |
| `text` | Optional reason. The agent reads it |
| `remember` | Optional. With `approved: true`, also saves a rule: this agent is not asked again for this tool |

A tool approval is answered **once**, whatever the workflow's response mode: in the default mode
every other answer opens a new run, but a second "approve" would run the tool a second time. The
same decision again follows the run the first one started, and a different one is `409`.

The answer carries a decision and nothing else. It cannot name a tool call, because the
call comes from the request the workflow recorded: a `data` value is refused with `400`, and
so is `remember` together with `approved: false`, or on a request of any other form. The
request's record keeps the tool's name, the agent's name and a SHA-256 of the arguments, never
the arguments; the hash lets a remembered rule bind to the exact call. The
decision is written to the audit trail as `approval.decision` before the workflow
continues, and an entry that cannot be written refuses the answer and leaves the
workflow waiting. A rule saved with `remember` is the same rule the run-request path saves,
for the agent that asked and the tool; a request that cannot name its agent (an agent
Tracon did not wrap) cannot be remembered.

The tool runs once, in the new run the answer opens, and it runs in whatever process takes
the answer: the call is in the checkpoint, so a restart in between loses nothing. With
`Concurrent`, two agents can ask at once: each approval is a request of its own, answered on
its own, and the run that carries the first answer waits on the second. A request nobody
answers runs out like any other ([Workflow requests and time
limits](/concepts/workflow-requests/#giving-a-request-a-time-limit)); the step that waited
closes `Failed` with the workflow.

An agent that a step's agent calls as a sub-agent still cannot ask: its approval is a tool
result the step's model reads, as in [Agents calling
agents](/concepts/agents/#agents-calling-agents).

## What every answer leaves behind, in either mode

An answer that starts a run is written in three steps, in this order: the audit entry,
the row of the run it starts, and the record. A store that fails at any step refuses the
answer with `500`, and the run does not start.

- **An audit entry, written first.** Every answer that starts a run is written as
  `workflow.respond` before its run row opens. When the entry cannot be written, the answer is
  refused with `500` and nothing runs — see [What is guaranteed to be
  written](/concepts/governance/#what-is-guaranteed-to-be-written). The entry carries the
  source run, the request id, the run the answer started and a SHA-256 of the answer, never
  the answer. The hash tells two answers apart; it does not hide one. An answer with few
  possible values, such as `approved: true`, can be found by hashing each candidate.
- **A record.** `GET /api/workflows/runs/{runId}/responses` lists the answers given to a
  run's requests: who answered, when, the run each answer started and its state. A record
  that cannot be written refuses the answer with `500`, and the run opened for it is closed
  `Failed` with the error type `answer_not_recorded`. Records live in the
  `workflow_responses` table and are removed only with their source run, by a data subject
  erasure. No retention target deletes runs, so the table grows with the run history.
- **A back-link.** The run an answer starts records `workflow.response-applied` as its
  second event, right after `run.started`, naming the run it answered and the request id,
  even with `RecordToolPayloads` off.

## Read next

- [Workflows](/concepts/workflows/#asking-a-human) — how a workflow asks and how an answer resumes it.
- [Governance](/concepts/governance/#what-is-guaranteed-to-be-written) — the other operations that refuse to proceed without their audit entry.
- [Runs and recording](/concepts/runs/) — reading the run an answer started and its events.

# Workflow function nodes

Source: https://tracon.dev/concepts/workflow-function-nodes/

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    accTitle: What happens when a workflow reaches a function node
    accDescr: Before the node starts, the call-tree budget is read. A spent cost or time ceiling ends the run Failed with run_budget_exceeded, unless the node is registered to start when the budget is spent. Otherwise the registered function runs with its settings and under its timeout. A transient failure or a timeout is retried while the retry policy has attempts left; a permanent failure, or the last attempt, ends the run Failed. On success the output goes to the next node. Usage the node reports beyond tokens counts toward the budget, the tenant's cost quota and the run webhooks.
    IN["Output of the<br/>previous node"] --> GATE{"Budget spent?<br/>cost or time"}
    GATE -->|"yes"| STOP["Run Failed<br/>run_budget_exceeded"]
    GATE -->|"no, or the node<br/>starts anyway"| RUN["Function runs with its<br/>settings, under its timeout"]
    RUN -->|"transient error<br/>or timeout"| RETRY{"Retry policy has<br/>attempts left?"}
    RETRY -->|"yes"| RUN
    RETRY -->|"no"| FAIL["Run Failed"]
    RUN -->|"permanent error"| FAIL
    RUN -->|"success"| NEXT["Output to<br/>the next node"]
    RUN -.->|"ReportUsageAsync"| USAGE["Usage beyond tokens:<br/>budget, cost quota, webhooks"]
```

A real pipeline has steps that are not AI calls — a file download, a format
conversion, a database write. `AddWorkflowFunction` registers one by name:

```csharp
tracon.AddWorkflowFunction<List<ChatMessage>, List<ChatMessage>>(
    "word-count",
    services => (messages, context, cancellationToken) =>
    {
        var text = messages[^1].Text;
        return ValueTask.FromResult<List<ChatMessage>>([new(ChatRole.User, $"{text}\n\n({text.Split(' ').Length} words)")]);
    },
    "Appends a word count. Runs no model call.");
```

A `Sequential` definition's `Nodes` list can then mix that name in with catalog
agents, in order:

```csharp
new WorkflowDefinition
{
    Name = "summarize-and-count",
    Kind = WorkflowKind.Sequential,
    Nodes =
    [
        new WorkflowNodeReference { Name = "summarizer", Kind = WorkflowNodeKind.Agent },
        new WorkflowNodeReference { Name = "word-count", Kind = WorkflowNodeKind.Function },
    ],
}
```

`Nodes` and `AgentNames` are mutually exclusive — a definition sets one or the
other. Only `Sequential` supports function nodes: the ready-made builders for
the other four patterns accept only agents.

Each node must take what the node before it passes on. An agent node takes and passes
on a `List<ChatMessage>`, and a run starts by sending the user's message as one, so the
first node must take a `List<ChatMessage>` too. A function's types are the two type
arguments of its registration (`inputType` and `outputType` on
`GET /api/workflows/functions`). A node that takes a wider type, such as
`IEnumerable<ChatMessage>` or `object`, accepts the narrower one; a function that
declares `object` as its output is not checked against the next node. Saving a chain
that breaks this answers `400` and names both nodes and both types: Microsoft Agent
Framework drops a message that no handler takes, without an error, so the chain would
end every run `Completed` with no output. A stored chain that fails this check
fails before its first node runs, with the same message.

The first node must not take `object`. Every start and every resume also sends the first
node Microsoft Agent Framework's turn token, and a node that takes `object` receives it as a
second input: the node would run twice, and a node that writes to an outside system or calls
a paid service would do that work twice. Saving such a chain answers `400`, and a stored one
fails before its first node runs. Declare `List<ChatMessage>` or `IEnumerable<ChatMessage>`
instead. A graph you build in code (`AddWorkflow`) gets the same token on its start
executor; give that executor a `List<ChatMessage>` handler, not an `object` one.

The console builds such a chain too: **Workflows → New workflow**, then *Add an agent*
and *Add a function*, which picks from the functions registered in code. The arrows
reorder the steps and ✕ removes one. The function picker appears only for `Sequential`,
and the pattern stays `Sequential` while the chain holds a function.

A chain of agents only can be stored in either form over HTTP, `agentNames` or `nodes`,
and both keep working. The console writes one form per chain: **`nodes` when the chain
holds at least one function or one agent step [pinned to a version](/concepts/workflows/#pin-an-agent-step-to-a-version),
`agentNames` otherwise.** Removing the last function or pin in the console therefore saves
the chain back as a plain agent list on the built-in sequential pattern, and adding the
first one saves it as a node list. The editor says which form it is about to store. The
difference you can observe is token streaming: an agent step in a node list does not
stream its tokens into the workflow's live event feed (its own run row keeps the full
message history), while the built-in pattern does.

The factory passed to `AddWorkflowFunction` runs once, when the function
registry is built — not once per run. Every workflow compile shares the same
handler closure, so **the handler must be thread-safe**: a captured counter or
non-thread-safe client needs its own guard.

:::note[Code only, same boundary as tools]
A function's body is never written from the UI or the database; only its
*name* crosses that boundary, as `AgentDefinition.ToolNames` does for tools.
`GET /api/workflows/functions` lists what is registered, for a picker.
:::

A function node opens no `runs` row of its own and adds nothing to the token
totals — it made no model call. What it spent that is not tokens, it can report
itself ([below](#report-what-a-node-spent-beyond-tokens)). `ExecutorInvoked` /
`ExecutorCompleted` / `ExecutorFailed` still fire for it as for any node, so
it shows in the run's event stream and live in the graph.

:::caution[The handler must be idempotent]
Resuming from the run's *latest* checkpoint after it already completed does
not call the handler again — there is nothing left to run. Resuming from an
**earlier** checkpoint (the shape a real crash recovery takes) replays the
super-step that follows it, and the handler runs again with the same input. A
handler with a real side effect must tolerate being called more than once.
:::

## Give a function settings

One function often serves several workflows with a different configuration in each: a
voice, a loudness target, a destination folder. Register it with a settings type, and an
operator fills in the values on each workflow's node:

```csharp
tracon.AddWorkflowFunction<List<ChatMessage>, AudioClip, TtsSettings>(
    "tts",
    services =>
    {
        var speech = services.GetRequiredService<ITextToSpeech>();

        return (messages, settings, context, cancellationToken) =>
            speech.SpeakAsync(messages[^1].Text, settings.Voice, settings.LoudnessLufs, cancellationToken);
    },
    options => options.Description = "Text to speech");

public sealed record TtsSettings
{
    public required string Voice { get; init; }

    public double LoudnessLufs { get; init; } = -16;
}
```

```bash
curl -sS -X PUT http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/workflows/narrated \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
       "kind": "Sequential",
       "nodes": [
         { "name": "writer", "kind": "Agent" },
         { "name": "tts", "kind": "Function", "settings": { "voice": "alloy", "loudnessLufs": -14 } }
       ]
     }'
```

In the console the same object goes into the **Settings** field of the function's step,
with the fields the function takes listed under it.

- **The code declares the shape; the operator writes values.** Settings are values, not
  expressions: nothing in them is evaluated, and a run parameter is not substituted into
  them. A function that needs a run's value reads it with `context.GetRunParameters()`.
- **A save checks the settings by reading them into your type.** An unknown field (a
  misspelled name), a missing `required` member, a number written as text, an enum written
  as a number and a `null` where the member does not allow one are all refused with `400`,
  and the message names the node and the member. A node without settings is read as `{}`,
  so a type with a `required` member refuses a node that carries none — you hear about it
  when you save, not in the first run. Names are camelCase and matched without regard to
  case. The function receives exactly the object that was checked.
- **Some settings are refused whatever the type.** Settings on an agent node, settings that
  are not a JSON object, and settings on a function that declares no settings type.
- **A change takes effect on the next run.** The graph is built again for every run, so
  the run in progress keeps the settings it started with. So does a run that waits to be
  resumed: a resume compiles the definition version the run recorded (see
  [Versions, rollback and pinning an agent step](/concepts/workflows/#versions-rollback-and-pinning-an-agent-step)).
  Name the edited version to carry the run over the new settings. The checkpoint stays
  usable: the settings are not part of the node's identity, its name and place in the
  chain are.
- **A settings type that changed since the workflow was saved fails the run by name.**
  The run ends `Failed` before any node runs, and the error names the workflow, the node
  and the member. Save the workflow again with settings that fit. The same happens to a
  function that stopped taking settings while a stored node still carries some.
- **Never put a secret in settings.** They are stored in the workflow definition, appear
  in the audit trail, stay in every [version](/concepts/workflows/#versions-rollback-and-pinning-an-agent-step)
  of its history (a later save does not rewrite them) and are returned to everyone who
  can read the workflow. Make the
  setting the *name* of the configuration key (`"apiKeyConfigurationKey": "Tts:ApiKey"`)
  and read the value from `IConfiguration` inside the factory.
- **A chain uses a function once.** A node's name is its identity in the graph, so the
  same function cannot appear twice in one chain; register it under a second name when it
  should run twice.
- **Wide numbers.** The console reads a JSON number as a double, like any JavaScript
  client, so an integer beyond 9007199254740991 (2^53 − 1) loses its low digits when an
  operator opens the workflow and saves it again. Settings are read strictly, so a string
  cannot fill a numeric member: declare an identifier that wide (a snowflake, a 64-bit
  database key) as a `string`.
- **Size.** One node's settings may be at most `MaxNodeSettingsLength` bytes of JSON
  (16 KiB by default) when a workflow is saved.

`GET /api/workflows/functions` returns each function with `settingsSchema`, the JSON
schema of its settings type, and `null` for a function that takes none. The console lists
the fields from it. It is for display: the check is the read described above, so what the
schema says and what a save accepts cannot drift apart.

## Report what a node spent beyond tokens

A node that speaks, renders or transcribes spends something that is not a token: a
text-to-speech character, a GPU second, a minute of audio. Tracon cannot see that work, so
the node reports it. `ReportUsageAsync` is an extension on the `IWorkflowContext` the
node already receives:

```csharp
tracon.AddWorkflowFunction<List<ChatMessage>, string>(
    "narrate",
    services => async (messages, context, cancellationToken) =>
    {
        var text = messages[^1].Text;

        // ... synthesize the speech with your provider, then report what it billed.
        await context.ReportUsageAsync(new ToolCallUsage
        {
            Unit = ToolUsageUnits.Characters,
            Quantity = text.Length,
            Cost = text.Length * 0.00003m,
            Currency = "USD",
            Provider = "elevenlabs",
            Model = "eleven_multilingual_v2",
        });

        return text;
    });
```

A report is one **item**. The run lists its items, in the order they were reported, at
`GET /api/runs/{runId}/usage` (Reader role, `runs:read` scope); this abridged answer (each item also carries its `id`, `runId` and `createdAt`) is
from a run whose `speak` node reported an estimated, priced item and whose `render` node
reported seconds it has no price for:

```json
[
  {
    "nodeName": "speak",
    "usage": { "unit": "characters", "quantity": 76, "cost": 0.0076, "currency": "USD",
               "isEstimated": true, "provider": "tone", "model": "tone-1" }
  },
  {
    "nodeName": "render",
    "usage": { "unit": "gpu-seconds", "quantity": 1, "cost": null, "currency": null,
               "isEstimated": false, "provider": "local-gpu", "model": null }
  }
]
```

- **Tracon never prices a node's work.** `Cost` is the amount the node computed from its
  provider's rate. `Unit` is free text; `ToolUsageUnits` only names the units Tracon's own
  tools use. `Provider` and `Model` are names for the reader and take no part in a total.
- **The call does not throw.** It returns `false`, logs the cause and lets the node carry
  on when it is called outside a Tracon workflow run, when the item is invalid, and when
  the run already holds 1,000 items, so report once per step and not per chunk. An item is
  invalid when its `Unit` is empty, its quantity or amount is negative, or a value is more
  than its column holds (a unit of 64 characters, a currency of 16, a provider of 100, a
  model of 200, a quantity above 9,999,999,999, an amount above 1,000,000,000). Only a
  `null` argument throws.
- **An item is written the moment it is reported and is not cancelled with the run.** The
  provider billed that work, so a run that is cancelled or fails keeps what its node had
  spent. A node that fails and is [retried](#retry-a-node-on-a-transient-error) keeps the
  items of its failed attempts for the same reason.
- **The item names its node.** A custom `Executor` in a graph built in code is not a
  function node registered with Tracon, so its items carry no node name.
- **Amounts of one currency add up; nothing else does.** The run's **non-token total**
  (`nonTokenCost` on the run, and `treeNonTokenCost` for the run and every run below it)
  adds an item only when the item has a `Cost` and that cost is in `Tracon:Pricing:Currency`;
  an item with no currency label is in it. An item with no amount, or in another currency,
  is listed and counted in `unsummedItemCount`, and is never added or converted. A quantity
  is never added across units, because 76 characters and 1 GPU second make no number. An
  item with no price is *unknown, not free*, so it never counts as zero, and a run that
  reported nothing has `nonTokenCost: null`, not zero. An estimated item adds and marks the
  total `isEstimated`, so a quota ceiling is not passed on a quantity nobody measured.
- **The total stands beside the token cost, not inside it.** A caller that wants "what did
  this run spend" adds the two with `RunSpend.Total`, which leaves the reported amount out
  when the token cost is in another currency.

Where the non-token amount counts:

| Place | What happens |
|---|---|
| The call-tree budget (`AgentGraph.MaxTotalCost`) | An amount that adds is recorded the moment it is reported, so the next model call is refused once the ceiling is passed, and so is the next function node: it does not start (see [below](#a-spent-budget-stops-a-function-node-from-starting)) |
| The tenant's cost quota | Every run of a call tree writes its own entry when it ends, under the root's name: the root (an agent run or a workflow run) and each child run count the token cost plus the reported amount |
| `run.completed` and `run.failed` webhooks | `cost` is the token cost and the reported amount together; `nonTokenCost` is the reported part, so the token part is `cost - nonTokenCost` |

Still token-only: `GET /api/stats`, the dashboard, the `tracon.run.cost` metric, run
comparison and the console's Tools screen. A quota has no limit on a unit such as
characters.

An item reported after the run closed — from a node that outlived its
[timeout](#bound-a-node-with-a-timeout) — stays in the run's detail and does not change the
total, the quota entry or the webhook, because those were already written; a handler that
passes its token on never reaches this case. (A *tool* that outlived its timeout is different:
its amount does reach the quota counter, once.) The items live with their run: erasing a data
subject's runs deletes them too, and they hold no message text, so a data subject export
does not list them. What a *tool* measured stays on `GET /api/runs/{runId}/tools`, and it
joins the same total (see [Tools](/concepts/tools/#report-what-a-tool-spent-beyond-tokens)).

## A spent budget stops a function node from starting

The call-tree budget refuses a function node's **start** once `AgentGraph.MaxTotalCost` or
`AgentGraph.MaxDuration` is spent: the run ends `Failed` with `run_budget_exceeded` and no later
node runs. A node that is already running is never stopped, so the ceiling is not absolute.
`MaxTotalTokens` does not stop a node, and a host that sets neither ceiling sees no change. See
[Function nodes and the budget](/guides/reliability/#function-nodes-and-the-budget).

A node that spends nothing and has to run afterwards, such as a step that stores what the budget
has just paid for, is exempt with `options.StartsWhenBudgetIsSpent = true` in its registration. Its
own spend still counts, and an operator cannot set the exemption in a definition.

A tool call is gated the same way, and `MaxTotalTokens` stops it too: see [a tool call](/guides/reliability/#a-spent-budget-stops-a-tool-call-from-starting).

## Retry a node on a transient error

`AddWorkflowFunction` takes an optional retry policy. For the settings overload it is
`options.RetryPolicy` on the `WorkflowFunctionOptions` callback, and every attempt sees the same
settings:

```csharp
tracon.AddWorkflowFunction<List<ChatMessage>, List<ChatMessage>>(
    "call-shipping-api",
    services => (messages, context, cancellationToken) => CallShippingApiAsync(messages, cancellationToken),
    "Looks up a shipment.",
    retryPolicy: new WorkflowNodeRetryPolicy
    {
        MaxAttempts = 3,
        InitialDelay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1),
        BackoffMultiplier = 2.0,
    });
```

Only a transient failure is retried — a provider error, an open circuit breaker, a
rate limit, or a timeout. Anything else (a bad argument, a permanent downstream
error) is thrown on the first attempt, exactly as without a policy. A failure that
carries a permanent HTTP status — any `4xx` except `408` and `429`, such as a `401`
from `EnsureSuccessStatusCode()` or a `404` from a model provider — is also thrown on
the first attempt: the same request gets the same answer, and a repeated `409` on a
non-idempotent call can repeat its side effect. Tracon reads the status from
`HttpRequestException.StatusCode` or from `HTTP nnn` text in the exception chain,
and a registered `IRunErrorClassifier` cannot make such a failure retry. Neither can
a failure whose stable error type says the next attempt gets the same answer: a
provider the tenant's rules refuse (`tenant_provider_refused`), or a structured
answer cut off at the output limit. The type decides, not the message, which names
the tenant and its providers. A definition that does not compile keeps its retries:
it can fail because a loop criterion or a provider client could not be created for
the moment. The retry loop
runs entirely inside the node's own call: Microsoft Agent Framework invokes the
node once per routed message either way, so retrying costs nothing against
`TraconWorkflowOptions.MaxSuperSteps` — a node that succeeds on its third
attempt still counts as exactly one super-step.

## Bound a node with a timeout

A step that waits on a slow service can hold the whole run. Give the function a
timeout when you register it, with the overload that takes a
`WorkflowFunctionOptions` callback:

```csharp
tracon.AddWorkflowFunction<List<ChatMessage>, List<ChatMessage>>(
    "render-audio",
    services => (messages, context, cancellationToken) => RenderAsync(messages, cancellationToken),
    options =>
    {
        options.Description = "Renders the episode's audio.";
        options.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2);
    });
```

A stored definition can set a node's own `timeout`, which wins over the registered one
for that node; leave it out to use the registration's. `GET /api/workflows/functions`
shows each registered timeout.

```json
{ "name": "render-audio", "kind": "Function", "timeout": "00:05:00" }
```

- When the timeout passes, the token the handler was given is cancelled and the run
  ends `Failed` with the error type `workflow_function_timeout` (class `Timeout`),
  which names the node and the limit. No later node runs. Match the type with
  `TraconWorkflowFunctionTimeoutException.WorkflowFunctionTimeoutErrorType` when you
  read a run's `error`.
- The run stops waiting at the timeout even when the handler ignores its token. Such
  a handler keeps running in the background, its result is discarded, and its late end
  is logged; its side effects still happen. Pass the token on.
- With a retry policy, the timeout applies to each attempt, and a timed-out attempt is
  retried like any transient failure. The longest a node can take is about
  `MaxAttempts × Timeout` plus the delays.
- A caller's cancel or the run's own `RunTimeout` is not a node timeout: the run ends
  `Canceled` with the reason it already had.
- A timeout runs from 1 millisecond to about 49.7 days; a value outside the range is
  refused with `400` on save, or with `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` at registration.
  It is not checked against `RunTimeout`: whichever passes first stops the node.
- `options.MaxConcurrency` limits how many calls of the function run at once in the process;
  [the review-and-revise guide](/guides/review-and-revise-workflow/#limits-that-work-together) says how it
  interacts with retries, the budget and the node's timeout.

An **agent node** of a node list can carry a `timeout` too. It replaces the
installation's `Tracon:AgentGraph:ChildDeadline` for that step, and the hard cutoff for
an agent that ignores its deadline stays 30 seconds after it. A step past it fails the
run with `child_run_timeout`, and the message names the node. A chain with neither a
function step nor a pinned agent step is stored as `agentNames`, which has no node to
carry a timeout, so its steps use the installation's deadline; the console offers the
field only on a chain it saves as a node list.

- [Workflows](/concepts/workflows/) — the five patterns, versions, checkpoints, and asking a human
- [Workflow parameters](/concepts/workflow-parameters/) — run parameters that a function node can read
- [Reliability](/guides/reliability/) — budgets, timeouts, and retries across a call tree

# Workflow parameters

Source: https://tracon.dev/concepts/workflow-parameters/

How do one workflow definition serve many tones, voices or customers without being copied? A workflow declares run
parameters, a run supplies the values, and every step receives the part of them it declared.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: How a run's parameter values reach the steps
    accDescr: The caller supplies values with the run. The workflow's schema checks them before the stream opens. Each agent step is bound with the names its own schema declares, and a function node reads the full set. The run records its final values so a resume or an answer to a waiting request uses them again.
    CALL["Run request<br/>with values"] --> CHECK{"Workflow schema<br/>check"}
    CHECK -->|"invalid"| BAD["400 before the stream"]
    CHECK -->|"valid"| RUN["Run records<br/>the final values"]
    RUN --> AGENT["Agent step:<br/>its own names only"]
    RUN --> FN["Function node:<br/>GetRunParameters()"]
    RUN --> AGAIN["Resume or answer<br/>reads them back"]
```

A stored workflow can declare run parameters, the same `AgentParameter` an agent
declares (name, kind, `Required`, `DefaultValue`, `Description`). The values a run
supplies reach every agent step, so one definition serves many tones, voices or
customers without being copied:

```bash
curl -sS -X PUT http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/workflows/podcast \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
       "kind": "Sequential",
       "agentNames": ["podcast-writer", "podcast-editor"],
       "parameters": [
         { "name": "tone",  "kind": "Text", "required": true },
         { "name": "voice", "kind": "Text", "defaultValue": "alloy" }
       ]
     }'

curl -N -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/workflows/podcast/run \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"message":"Episode 12","parameters":{"tone":"formal","voice":"nova"}}'
```

- **The workflow's schema is the contract.** A missing required value, a name the
  workflow does not declare, or a value over `MaxParameterValueLength` is refused with
  `400` before the stream opens, with the same body an agent run gives
  (`missingParameters`, `unknownParameters`, `tooLongParameters`). The runner checks
  again, so a caller that skips HTTP gets the same refusal.
- **A step receives the values its own schema names.** `podcast-writer` declares only
  `tone`, so it never sees `voice`; `podcast-editor` declares both. A name the step does
  not declare is dropped for that step, and a value the workflow supplies wins over the
  step's own default. The step is bound the way a direct run of that agent would be
  (its instructions, its recording, its tool-approval gate), and its own run row records
  the values it was bound with.
- **Every participant is checked before the first model call.** If an agent in the
  workflow needs a required parameter that has no default and that the workflow does not
  supply, the run ends `Failed` without a single model call, and the error names the
  agent and the parameter. Saving the workflow does not check this, because the agents
  can change after it is saved.
- **A function node reads the values** with `context.GetRunParameters()`, a read-only
  dictionary with the defaults applied:

```csharp
tracon.AddWorkflowFunction<List<ChatMessage>, List<ChatMessage>>(
    "narrate",
    services => (messages, context, cancellationToken) =>
    {
        var voice = context.GetRunParameters().GetValueOrDefault("voice", "plain");
        return ValueTask.FromResult<List<ChatMessage>>([new(ChatRole.User, $"[{voice}] {messages[^1].Text}")]);
    });
```

  Called outside a workflow run it throws `InvalidOperationException` instead of
  returning an empty set, so a forgotten setup is not read as "no values".
- **Resume and respond use the same values.** The run records its final values, and a
  resume from a checkpoint or an answer to a waiting request reads them back and passes
  them on to the run it opens. If the version the run continues with declares parameters
  but the run recorded none, the resume is refused — the agents would otherwise continue
  under their defaults, halfway through the work. That happens when
  `RunRecording:RecordRunInput` is off, so a workflow with parameters that waits for a
  human needs it on. The values are read against the schema of the version the run
  continues with, which by default is the one it recorded (see
  [Versions, rollback and pinning an agent step](/concepts/workflows/#versions-rollback-and-pinning-an-agent-step)).
  When you name a newer version, a name its schema no longer declares is dropped and a
  required name it gained since is refused.
- **A workflow defined in code declares its schema in its registration**
  (`WorkflowRegistrationOptions.Parameters`), checked, queued and recorded like a stored one's.
  Without a schema every value sent is refused.
- **A parameter can choose the version of an agent step built in code**
  (`step.AgentVersionParameter`; see [below](#let-a-run-choose-the-version-of-an-agent-step)).

A workflow row stores no message: the values are the only input it records.

## Let a run choose the version of an agent step

A step of a graph built in code can pin its agent in the graph (`step.AgentVersion = 4`), or read the version
from a run parameter, so one graph serves every version:

```csharp
tracon.AddWorkflow(
    "episode",
    services =>
    {
        var writer = services.GetWorkflowAgentStep("episode", "writer", step => step.AgentVersionParameter = "writerVersion");

        return new WorkflowBuilder(writer).WithOutputFrom(writer).WithName("episode").Build();
    },
    options => options.Parameters = [new AgentParameter { Name = "writerVersion", Kind = AgentParameterKind.Number }]);
```

```bash
curl -N -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/workflows/episode/run \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"message":"Episode 12","parameters":{"writerVersion":"2"}}'
```

- The step reads the value every time it runs. The factory of a graph built in code runs before a run's
  parameters are bound, so it cannot read them; the step does.
- An empty value, or no value, runs the agent's current version. A whole number from 1 runs that version,
  and the step's own run row records it.
- Declare the parameter optional, with no default, when a run may leave it out. A required one is refused
  with `400` at the start of a run that omits it.
- A value that is not a whole number from 1, a parameter name the workflow does not declare, a version the
  agent does not have and an agent defined in code (it keeps no history) fail the step by name before its
  model call. The error for a value that is not a number, and for a name the workflow does not declare,
  names the parameter and never repeats the value; a version the agent does not have is named by its
  number. Earlier steps have already run.
- `AgentVersion` and `AgentVersionParameter` exclude each other: setting both throws when the graph is built.
- A run that continues after a human answer, or a resume, reads the value its first part started with. A
  number keeps that version through the wait, so an edit made while the run waited does not change the
  version its later steps run. An empty value still means the current version, resolved when each step
  runs, so a later step runs an edit made during the wait.
- Whoever may start the run chooses the version, and any stored version of the agent can be chosen. Pass the
  value from your own code, not from an end user's input, unless every version is meant to be reachable.
- A stored workflow has no such setting: a node's `agentVersion` is fixed (see
  [Pin an agent step to a version](/concepts/workflows/#pin-an-agent-step-to-a-version)), and a run chooses the
  version of the whole workflow with `definitionVersion`.

## Read next

- [Workflows](/concepts/workflows/): the patterns, function nodes, versions and recovery these values flow through.
- [A workflow that a person can send back](/guides/review-and-revise-workflow/): parameters on a graph built in code.
