# Workflow requests and time limits

Source: https://tracon.dev/concepts/workflow-requests/

How many people are your workflows waiting on right now, and what happens to a request
nobody answers? This page covers the tenant-wide list of waiting requests and the time
limit a workflow can give them. How a workflow asks, and how an answer resumes it, is in
[Asking a human](/concepts/workflows/#asking-a-human); what an answer leaves behind is in
[Answering a workflow](/concepts/workflow-answers/).

## The list of waiting requests

`GET /api/workflows/requests` lists the human requests that the workflow runs of your
tenant wait on, across every workflow, oldest first. The console shows the same list in
the *Workflow requests* panel of the Approvals screen. Each item is a
[pending request](/http-api/schemas/workflowpendingrequest/) with five more fields. A request
whose `form` is `ToolApproval` is an agent's tool call waiting for a person; the Approvals
screen lists it here with the other requests, and the console answers it on the workflow's
card ([A tool that asks for approval](/concepts/workflow-answers/#a-tool-that-asks-for-approval)):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `workflowName`, `sessionId` | The workflow, and the execution session its runs share |
| `expiresAt` | When the request runs out; `null` when the workflow sets no time limit |
| `answered` | Whether somebody answered the request |
| `lastResponseRunId` | The run that carried out the latest answer; `null` while nobody answered |

| Query | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `state` | `pending` (default): nobody answered. `answered`: answered, but the run still waits. `all`: both |
| `workflowName` | List one workflow |
| `skip`, `take` | A page; `take` is from 1 to 200 and defaults to 50 |

The filter runs before the page, so a page is full unless the list ends. A `state` that is
none of the three is `400`.

**One request is listed once.** An answered run stays `AwaitingInput`, and the run that
continues it publishes the requests that are still open again, with the same request id.
The same request id in the same session is therefore one request, and the item names the
newest run that waits on it: the run to answer. `GET /api/workflows/runs/{runId}/requests`
is unchanged in what it returns — the requests that run published — and carries the same
five fields.

**An answered request stays in the list** until its run is closed, marked `answered`, with
the run that carried the answer out. The default `state=pending` hides it. This is the
same rule that keeps an answered run `AwaitingInput`: a second answer opens a new branch.

The list needs the `Reader` role and read access to runs. A registered
`IRunAuthorizationHandler` that refuses reading runs rejects the whole list with `403`; it
never filters the list, because a filtered page would be shorter than the caller is allowed
to see. A host without the workflow engine answers `501`.

:::note[Runs that started waiting before the list existed are not in it]
The list is built from a row the engine writes when a run starts waiting. A run that
started waiting on an older version has no row: read its requests with
`GET /api/workflows/runs/{runId}/requests` and answer them as before. The row also carries no
copy of the prompt — the list reads it from the run's own event stream, the same text the
run's card shows, with the same content protection.
:::

## Giving a request a time limit

A run that waits for a person keeps its request event, its checkpoints and its input row
for as long as it waits, because answering needs them. An answered run waits too, so these
rows are never deleted. A **request timeout** is how a workflow lets go of them: when the
time passes, the run is closed and retention can delete what it kept.

Set it per workflow:

- `requestTimeout` on `PUT /api/workflows/{name}`, as `d.hh:mm:ss`.
- The *Answer time limit* field in the console's workflow editor, in seconds or `d.hh:mm:ss`.
- For a workflow defined in code, `WorkflowRegistrationOptions.RequestTimeout`:

```csharp
builder.AddWorkflow(
    "publish-approval",
    services => BuildPublishApproval(services),
    options => options.RequestTimeout = TimeSpan.FromDays(7));
```

The value is from one minute to 365 days; a save outside the range is refused with `400`.
Without a value a request waits without limit. The save is a full replace like every other
field, so a client that leaves `requestTimeout` out removes the limit.

The time counts from the moment the run published the request, and it is fixed then. A run
that waits keeps the limit of the version it started with: saving the workflow again
changes it for runs that start afterwards. A continuation that publishes a request again
starts that run's count from its own moment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: The life of a workflow request with a time limit
    accDescr: A run publishes a request and closes as awaiting input with an expiry time. A person answers it, or the time passes. When the time passes the run is closed, failed if a request went unanswered and completed if every request was answered, and retention can then delete what the run kept.
    RUN["run publishes a request"] --> WAIT["run is AwaitingInput<br/>expiresAt is fixed"]
    WAIT -->|"answered"| MARK["request is marked answered<br/>the run still waits"]
    WAIT -->|"time passes"| CLOSE["run is closed"]
    MARK -->|"time passes"| CLOSE
    CLOSE --> FREE["retention can delete the request,<br/>checkpoints and input row"]
```

## When the time passes

A background scan closes the requests whose time has passed, and then the runs that wait on
no other request:

| What the run waited on | The run is closed |
|---|---|
| A request nobody answered | `Failed`, with the error type `WorkflowRequestExpired` (error class `Timeout`) |
| Requests that were all answered | `Completed`, with no error: the answer was given and its work continued on another run |
| Several requests, the last one now due | When the last one passes. A request a slower branch published later keeps the run waiting |

A run that fails this way publishes `run.failed` to the webhooks subscribed to it, with the same
payload any failed workflow run carries, so a pipeline driven by webhooks learns that the review ended
without polling. The event is sent after the run is closed; a publisher that fails is logged and the
close stands. A run closed `Completed` publishes nothing: the answer started a run of its own, which
published its own `run.completed` when it ended.

An answer to a closed run is refused with `400`, as an answer to any run that is not
`AwaitingInput` is, and opens no run. The closed run keeps its usage, cost and event count.
The next retention round deletes its request event, checkpoints and input row by age, like
those of any finished run; the `workflow_requests` retention target deletes the closed rows
of the list after `Tracon:Retention:WorkflowRequests:MaxAgeDays` (30 days by default).

Two settings under `Tracon:Workflows` control the scan:

| Key | Default |
|---|---|
| `RequestExpirationScanInterval` | 1 minute |
| `MaxRequestExpirationsPerScan` | `100` |

A request is closed at most one interval after its time. Only one instance of a cluster
scans at a time. The scan reads an index of the requests that have a limit, so it costs
nothing while no workflow sets one.

:::caution[A request whose row could not be written never expires]
When the row of a request cannot be written, the run still waits and the request can still be
answered from the run, but it is missing from the list and it never expires. That is logged
as a warning.
:::

A scan closes the request first and the run second. If the second write fails, the scan tries
the run again on each scan of the same process. If the process stops between the two writes,
the next instance that takes the scan lease looks for runs that still wait although none of their
requests is open, and closes them the same way.

### An answer that arrives with the time limit

The request and the run are two writes, so an answer can arrive between them.

- An answer **before** the scan closes the request is taken and marks the request answered. At the limit the run closes `Completed`.
- An answer **between** the two writes is taken too, and its work runs: the run still waits, so the check passes. The request is already closed and cannot be marked. The run you answered then closes `Failed` with `WorkflowRequestExpired`, and the run that carried out your answer is not affected.
- An answer **after** the run is closed is refused with `400`, as above. A queued answer (`Prefer: respond-async`) that was accepted before the limit but starts after it fails on its own run for the same reason.

The window is the time between two writes, usually milliseconds.

## Read next

- [Asking a human](/concepts/workflows/#asking-a-human) — how a workflow asks and how an answer resumes it.
- [Answering a workflow](/concepts/workflow-answers/) — the audit entry and the record every answer leaves.
- [Retention defaults](/reference/configuration/#retention-defaults) — what retention keeps for a run that waits, and what it deletes after.

# Workflows

Source: https://tracon.dev/concepts/workflows/

A workflow runs several agents together. Where a callable agent is one agent using
another as a tool, a workflow is an orchestration you define and can watch.

**Tracon does not implement a workflow engine.** A definition compiles onto the
Microsoft Agent Framework's own graph, and `Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows` executes
it. What Tracon adds around that engine is the catalog a definition lives in, the
checkpoint store it resumes from, the quota and cancellation it runs under, and the
`runs` row that records what happened. Five public types are the whole of Tracon's
workflow surface.

Workflows need `Tracon.Workflows`. Without that package registered, definition
management still works and only the execution endpoints answer `501` — the package
stays optional on purpose.

## Five patterns

| Kind | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Sequential` | Agents run in order; each output is the next input |
| `Concurrent` | Agents run at the same time; results are merged |
| `Handoff` | One agent starts and hands off when needed — the **model** decides |
| `GroupChat` | A manager distributes turns among participants |
| `Magentic` | A manager plans, tracks progress, and replans; a manager agent is required |

`MaxIterations` bounds the turn count for `Handoff`, `GroupChat`, and `Magentic` — the
only structural guard against two agents handing off to each other forever. Each
participant call also carries the same two-layer wait limit a callable agent's
sub-call does (see [Agents calling agents](/concepts/agents/#agents-calling-agents)):
a cooperative deadline, then a hard cutoff for a participant that ignores it. The
installation-wide default applies, except to an agent node of a `Sequential` node
list, which can carry its own `timeout` (see
[Bound a node with a timeout](/concepts/workflow-function-nodes/#bound-a-node-with-a-timeout)).

A participant that cannot answer **fails the run**, unlike a callable agent, whose
caller's model reads the refusal and can try another way. No model reads a
workflow step's answer, so the refusal would reach the next node as its input. The
run ends `Failed` and no later node runs: past the wait limit with error type
`child_run_timeout` (class `Timeout`), refused by the call-tree budget with
`run_budget_exceeded` (class `QuotaExceeded`), or with the provider's own error when
the provider never answered. Match the wait-limit type with
`TraconChildRunTimeoutException.ChildRunTimeoutErrorType` when you read a run's `error`.

A tool that asks for approval is not a refusal where the pattern hosts the agent: the
workflow waits for a person ([A tool that asks for approval](#a-tool-that-asks-for-approval)).
It is a refusal for an agent node of a `Sequential` node list, for `GetWorkflowAgentStep` and for
the manager of a `Magentic` workflow. The first two run the agent in a plain function node
that cannot wait, and the manager plans the task rather than being hosted as a participant:
the run ends `Failed` with the message *a workflow step cannot wait for a tool
approval*, and the tool does not run. Give that agent a tool that needs no approval, or an
[approval rule](/concepts/governance/#approvals) for the tool.

```csharp
new WorkflowDefinition
{
    Name = "triage",
    Kind = WorkflowKind.Handoff,
    AgentNames = ["frontline", "billing", "technical"],
}
```

Which fields are required depends on the kind, and the definition is validated when it
is **saved** using the same rules the compiler applies. A shape that could not run is
rejected at write time rather than on the first execution.

## Function nodes

A real pipeline has steps that are not AI calls — a file download, a format
conversion, a database write. `AddWorkflowFunction` registers one by name, and a
`Sequential` definition places it in its `Nodes` list next to catalog agents.
[Workflow function nodes](/concepts/workflow-function-nodes/) covers the
registration, the type rules between nodes, settings, what a node reports beyond
tokens, the budget check, retries, and timeouts.

## Graphs built in code

Workflows can also be built in code with MAF's own builder.

:::caution[The registration key is what routing uses]
When you add a workflow in code, `AddWorkflow("approval-flow", …)` is the key every
URL resolves against. A different name passed to the builder's `WithName(…)` is
cosmetic — and an inconsistency between the two produces a silent `404` or a timeout
rather than an error. Use the same string in both places.
:::

A graph with a way back or a human gate is built in code with `AddWorkflow`. Two helpers give its steps
what a stored chain's steps have: `GetWorkflowFunction` binds a registered function with its time limit,
retry, budget gate and cost line, and `GetWorkflowAgentStep` binds an agent as a plain step that a message
can return to; the step can run a fixed version of its agent or the one a run parameter names (see
[Let a run choose the version of an agent step](/concepts/workflow-parameters/#let-a-run-choose-the-version-of-an-agent-step)).
A registration also takes `RunTimeout` and `Parameters`.
[A workflow that a person can send back](/guides/review-and-revise-workflow/) builds one.

A graph built in code can also raise its own `WorkflowEvent` from an executor
(`context.AddEventAsync`). Tracon has no event type for a type of your own, so it records the
event as a `tracon.workflow.event` event on the workflow run, naming the event's type (and the
executor, when the event derives from `ExecutorEvent`), instead of dropping it. See
[Content and events the run has no type for](/concepts/runs/#content-and-events-the-run-has-no-type-for).

## Parameters

A workflow declares run parameters, the same `AgentParameter` an agent declares. A run supplies the values, each agent
step is bound with the names its own schema declares, and a function node reads them with `context.GetRunParameters()`.
[Workflow parameters](/concepts/workflow-parameters/) has the rules, for a stored workflow and for one defined in code.

## Versions, rollback and pinning an agent step

Every save of a stored workflow appends a version. Nothing rewrites history:

- `GET /api/workflows/{name}/versions` lists full snapshots, newest first. It needs the
  Reader role (the `WorkflowsRead` scope for an API key).
- `GET /api/workflows/{name}/versions/{a}/diff/{b}` returns both snapshots verbatim, as
  `left` and `right`. The client computes the diff.
- `POST /api/workflows/{name}/rollback` with `{"version": 2}` writes the content of
  version 2 as a **new** version. It needs the Admin role (the `WorkflowsAdmin` scope).
  The audit trail records `workflow.rollback`, and a rollback can be rolled back in turn.

A rollback is checked like a save. A version that names a function that is no longer
registered, settings that no longer fit their function, or an agent version that no longer
exists answers `400`; nothing is written and nothing is audited. An unknown version answers
`404`. A workflow defined in code answers `409` to a rollback and `404` ("Workflow has no
version history") to the read calls: its history is your source history.

A version number is never reused. Deleting a workflow keeps its history, and saving the same
name again continues the numbering: after version 3 and a delete, the next save is version
4. The kept versions are not served over HTTP while the workflow is deleted. A workflow
stored before versions were kept starts its history at the version it has today.

### A resume compiles the version the run recorded

The row of a workflow run records the definition version it was compiled from, as
`agentVersion` on `GET /api/runs/{runId}`. It is `null` for a workflow defined in code and
for a row written before versions were kept. A resume and a response are stamped with the
version they ran.

A resume compiles the version the run **recorded**, not the current one. An edit made while
the run waits changes nothing for it: not a setting, a timeout or the parameter schema, and
not a step that was added or removed. A run that recorded no version resumes with the
current definition. A workflow that was deleted is still refused.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Which definition version a resume compiles
    accDescr: A resume or respond request compiles the version named in definitionVersion when the workflow has it, and is refused with 400 when it does not. Without definitionVersion it compiles the version the run recorded, and a run that recorded none uses the current definition.
    REQ["resume or respond"] --> NAMED{"definitionVersion<br/>in the body?"}
    NAMED -->|"yes, the workflow has it"| GIVEN["compile that version"]
    NAMED -->|"yes, it does not"| REFUSE["400 before any stream<br/>opens or job is queued"]
    NAMED -->|"no"| REC{"run recorded<br/>a version?"}
    REC -->|"yes"| RECORDED["compile the recorded version"]
    REC -->|"no"| CURRENT["compile the current definition"]
```

To carry a waiting run over a fix, send the edited version in the optional
`definitionVersion` field of `resume` or `respond`, for example
`{"definitionVersion": 4}`:

- A version the workflow does not have answers `400` ("Definition version not found"),
  and so does a recorded version the workflow no longer has. `0`, a negative number, or a
  version of a workflow defined in code answers `400` ("Definition version invalid"). The
  check runs before a stream opens or a job is queued.
- The checkpoint belongs to the graph that wrote it. A version whose graph differs from it
  — a step added, removed or reordered, another pattern, another stored form — fails the
  run, and the error says the graph's structure differs. A version that differs only in
  settings, timeouts or an agent pin resumes: those are not part of a step's identity.

### Pin an agent step to a version

An agent step in the `nodes` form can run one version of its agent while the agent is
edited. Set `agentVersion` on the node:

```bash
curl -sS -X PUT http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/workflows/narrated \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
       "kind": "Sequential",
       "nodes": [
         { "name": "writer", "kind": "Agent", "agentVersion": 4 },
         { "name": "tts", "kind": "Function" }
       ]
     }'
```

- The step runs version 4's instructions, model and tools, and its own run row records
  version 4. A step with no `agentVersion` runs the agent's current version, resolved each
  time the step runs.
- A save refuses a pin that cannot hold with `400`: a pin on a function node, a number
  below 1, an agent defined in code (it keeps no version history), and a version the stored
  agent does not have. The compile repeats the check, because the agent can be deleted
  after the workflow was saved: the run then fails before its first step.
- A pin is not part of the step's identity. Changing the pin of a step in a node list never
  makes a waiting run's checkpoint unusable.
- A pin reaches the step's agent and the callable agents that version pins. An entry with no
  `version`, and the skills, run their current version.
- Only `Sequential` workflows have `nodes`, so only they can pin. A chain written as
  `agentNames` cannot.

The console lists a workflow's versions, compares two of them and rolls back; its chain
editor pins an agent step (see [the console](/ui/#workflows)). It saves a pinned chain in
the `nodes` form, so pinning the first step of a chain stored as `agentNames` changes the
stored form. A different form is a different graph, and a run that waits keeps resuming
the version it recorded.

## Running one

```bash
curl -N -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/workflows/triage/run \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"message":"My invoice is wrong and the app crashes"}'
```

Events stream over SSE. The first frame reports the run id, and **every agent invoked
inside the workflow opens its own run row** — so the whole thing is readable as a tree
with `GET /api/runs/{runId}/tree`, with each agent's tokens and duration attributed
separately.

The request is checked before the stream opens, so a mistake is a status code, not an
event in a `200` stream. An unknown workflow or run answers `404`, and so does a run of
another tenant. An invalid `sessionId`, a checkpoint the run does not have, a
`definitionVersion` the workflow does not have, and an answer to a run that does not
wait for input answer `400`. None of these opens a run.

The name `functions` is reserved: `GET /api/workflows/functions` lists the function
nodes, so a workflow saved under that name could not be read back. Saving it answers
`400`, and `AddWorkflow` throws.

### Queue a run instead of streaming it

A streamed run belongs to the connection that reads it: if the client stops reading,
the run ends `Canceled`. To run in the background — a render that takes
minutes, a pipeline a deploy must not cut short — send `Prefer: respond-async`:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/workflows/podcast/run \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -H 'Prefer: respond-async' \
     -H 'Idempotency-Key: episode-12' \
     -d '{"message":"Episode 12","sessionId":"episode-12"}'
```

The request passes the same checks a streamed one does — attribution, authorization,
session ownership, quota and parameters — and only then is the run queued. The answer
is `202 Accepted` with a `Location` header and a body that names the run:

```json
{
  "runId": "01a1340e-ad31-75e4-b64b-e3d0a26ab0a1",
  "jobId": "01a1340e-ad31-75e4-b64b-e3d0a26ab0a1",
  "location": "/tracon/api/runs/01a1340e-ad31-75e4-b64b-e3d0a26ab0a1",
  "eventsLocation": "/tracon/api/runs/01a1340e-ad31-75e4-b64b-e3d0a26ab0a1/events"
}
```

The run's row exists at once with the status `Queued`, so `GET /api/runs/{runId}` and
`POST /api/runs/{runId}/cancel` work before a worker picks it up. The job id is the
run id. Read the events from `GET /api/runs/{runId}/events`. A run queued without a
`sessionId` gets one before the `202`, and the row names it.

`resume` and `respond` take the same header. A queued answer is checked before the
`202`: an answer of the wrong shape, a request id that is not pending, a run that
is not waiting, and a `definitionVersion` the workflow does not have are each refused
with `400`, and an unknown run with `404`. A machine
that answers a request when its own work finishes therefore never has a background run
fail on the answer. The queued answer is stored with the job until the job is removed:
do not put a secret in it.

`Idempotency-Key` makes a retried call safe: the same key returns the same `202` and
queues nothing. On these three endpoints the key is accepted only together with
`Prefer: respond-async`. A stream cannot be stored and replayed, so a key on a
streamed call is refused with `400`. A `sessionId` is a correlation, not a
de-duplication: two calls with the same session id and no key are two runs.

Queuing needs a job worker (`Tracon:Scheduling:RunWorker`, on by default), and
`Tracon:AsyncRun:Enabled = false` answers the header with `501`. A queued run is not
something a schedule can start: schedule `tracon.workflow` instead (see
[Background work](/guides/background-work/)).

`GET /api/workflows/{name}/graph` returns the compiled graph. Node ids are identical
to the executor ids in the run events, which is how the console colours nodes live as
the workflow progresses. The response also carries MAF's generated Mermaid text.

A workflow run's `error` follows the [same redaction rule as an agent
run](/concepts/runs/#the-error-message-is-safe-to-display-not-safe-to-debug-from): a
node that throws a `TraconException` keeps its message. Any other exception —
your own node's included — carries only its exception type and a correlation id,
and its message goes to the server log under the same id. Throw a
`TraconException` when a node's message is meant for the person reading the run.

A workflow run ends `Canceled` only when it was cancelled — the
caller's request going away, `POST /api/runs/{id}/cancel`, a worker that stops
gracefully while it runs a queued run, or `Tracon:Workflows:RunTimeout` being
reached. The call-tree budget's
`AgentGraph.MaxDuration` is not one of these: a step it refuses ends the run
`Failed` with `run_budget_exceeded` (see below). A node whose model or tool call
never came back ends the run `Failed` instead, even though .NET surfaces an
`HttpClient` timeout as a `TaskCanceledException`. The same holds for the steps
around the graph: an agent catalog that times out while the workflow resolves, and
a stop at the super-step limit whose cancellation call times out, both end the run
`Failed`. Alert on the two separately: one is a person stopping, the other is an
outage.

`RunTimeout` (10 minutes by default) is **cooperative, and observed between
super-steps**. It cancels the token the run is given and the runner checks it
as each super-step ends. A node without a timeout of its own that ignores its
cancellation token runs to completion, and the run stops at the next boundary;
a node with a timeout stops being waited for at once. To bound one step, give
the node a timeout (see [Bound a node with a timeout](/concepts/workflow-function-nodes/#bound-a-node-with-a-timeout)).
A run stopped this way ends `Canceled` with a `TimeoutException` error that names
`Tracon:Workflows:RunTimeout`.

A definition can set its own `runTimeout`. It may always shorten
`Tracon:Workflows:RunTimeout`; it may be longer only up to
`Tracon:Workflows:MaxRunTimeout`, which is unset by default because a running
workflow holds a slot every tenant shares. A save above the ceiling is refused with
`400`. A run stopped by its definition's value names the definition's `runTimeout`
instead.

The deadline starts when the run starts, so it also counts the time a run waits
for a slot when `MaxConcurrentRuns` workflows are already running. A waiting run
already has its run record and shows `Queued` ([limit it per
tenant](/guides/background-work/#limit-workflow-runs-per-tenant)); a run whose
deadline passes before it gets a slot ends like any other timed-out run.

A workflow stream writes an SSE comment whenever it has sent nothing for
`StreamKeepAliveInterval` (15 seconds by default), so a node that works quietly
for minutes does not look like a dead connection. A closed connection still
cancels the run.

A workflow's root run shares the same call-tree budget every agent run does
(`AgentGraph.MaxTotalTokens`/`MaxTotalCost`/`MaxDuration` — see [Reliable
runs](/guides/reliability/#bound-multi-agent-trees)): every agent node the
workflow invokes spends against the same tree, so a workflow with a long chain
of agent steps is bounded the same way a single agent's own tool loop is. A step
the budget refuses fails the run (see above), and so does a function node it
refuses to start. What a function node
[reported beyond tokens](/concepts/workflow-function-nodes/#report-what-a-node-spent-beyond-tokens) counts against
`MaxTotalCost` too. The budget is [the logical run's](/guides/reliability/#the-ceiling-of-a-workflow-is-the-logical-run): a
run that continues an earlier one starts from what the earlier runs spent. The tenant's cost quota
[stops a node that has not started](/concepts/governance/#a-quota-also-stops-work-that-has-not-started) too.

## Checkpoints

A workflow writes checkpoints as it goes, controlled by
`Tracon:Workflows:EnableCheckpointing` (default `true`).
`GET /api/workflows/runs/{runId}/checkpoints` lists them and
`POST /api/workflows/runs/{runId}/resume` continues from one — omit the id to resume
from the latest.

Resuming opens a **new** run. The original is never rewritten, so the history stays two readable
records, not one edited one. The new run
compiles the definition version the original recorded, unless the request names another
(see [Versions, rollback and pinning an agent step](#versions-rollback-and-pinning-an-agent-step)).

A workflow run whose process stopped is closed as `Failed` by
[run reconciliation](/guides/reliability/#reconcile-runs-left-behind-by-a-crash), like
any other orphaned run. Automatic run continuation does not pick it up or any of its
steps: continuation repeats an agent turn, and a workflow run is
not one. With continuation on, the run's event stream records a
`RunContinuationBlocked` event that names the call to make instead,
`POST /api/workflows/runs/{runId}/resume`. Resuming from the latest checkpoint repeats
the step the stop cut short, so the idempotency rule for function nodes above applies.
A run a job started can be resumed by that job instead, as the next section shows.

### Resume an interrupted run automatically

A run a job started — a queued run, or an item of a `tracon.workflow` batch — has an
owner that outlives the process: the job. With `ResumeInterruptedRuns` on, the job
continues an interrupted run when it is leased again:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddTracon()
    .UsePostgreSql(connectionString)
    .UseWorkflows(options =>
    {
        options.ResumeInterruptedRuns = true;
        options.MaxResumeAttempts = 1;
    });
```

`UsePostgreSql` comes from the `Tracon.PostgreSql` package, which the `Tracon` meta package does not include: `dotnet add package Tracon.PostgreSql --prerelease`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Workflow recovery after a process stops
    accDescr: The job records its run before the run starts. After a crash or a graceful stop the job is leased again, the interrupted run is closed, and a new run continues it from the latest checkpoint in its chain; a finished run is left alone.
    MARK["job records its run id"] --> RUN["run executes<br/>checkpoint after each super-step"]
    RUN --> STOP["process stops<br/>crash, deploy, graceful stop"]
    STOP --> LEASE["lease runs out<br/>a worker leases the job again"]
    LEASE --> CHECK{"last run of the chain"}
    CHECK -->|"Completed or AwaitingInput"| DONE["nothing runs again"]
    CHECK -->|"interrupted, within MaxResumeAttempts"| NEXT["new run from the latest checkpoint<br/>continuedFromRunId names the old one"]
    CHECK -->|"past MaxResumeAttempts<br/>or the job's last attempt"| FAIL["chain closed<br/>item or job fails"]
```

- Before a batch item's run starts, the handler writes the run's id on the item. A
  queued run's id is the job's id from the start.
- When the job is leased again after a crash, a deploy or a graceful stop, the
  handler reads that run. If it is `Completed` or `AwaitingInput`, nothing runs again.
  Otherwise a run left `Running` is closed as `Failed` with the error type
  `interrupted`, and a new run continues it from the latest checkpoint in its chain.
  A continuation that was opened and never started counts as interrupted too.
- A run its job's time limit stopped is not interrupted: it closes `Canceled` with
  the error type `job_max_duration_exceeded` and is never continued, so the limit
  bounds the work, not one attempt of it
  ([Background work](/guides/background-work/#queue-one-workflow-run)).
- The new run's `continuedFromRunId` names the run it continues.
  `GET /api/runs?continuedFromRunId={runId}` walks the chain forward.
- The new run uses the same session, the parameter values the chain recorded, and the
  user and labels of whoever queued the job. It is not counted against the quota or
  asked for authorization again: the job was, when it was queued.
- A continuation from a checkpoint compiles the definition version the run that wrote the
  checkpoint recorded, like any other resume. A save made while the job waits for its
  lease does not change it.
- If no run of the chain wrote a checkpoint — the process stopped before the first
  super-step ended — the run starts again in the same session, or the resume or the
  answer is applied again. A run that starts again compiles the definition version the
  chain's first run recorded, so a save made while the job waited does not change it; a
  workflow defined in code has no versions.
- `MaxResumeAttempts` (default `1`, from `0` to `100`) bounds the continuations of one
  chain. Past it the batch item fails with the chain's last run closed, or the queued
  run's job fails with `tracon.job.workflow-run-not-continued`. With `0`, nothing
  continues, but the interrupted run is still found and closed.
- The worker fails a lease past the job's attempt limit before the handler runs, so
  the job's last attempt never starts a continuation: nothing would close it if it
  were interrupted too. The last attempt closes the chain instead. A queued run's job
  gets `2 + MaxResumeAttempts` attempts: one for the run, one per continuation, and
  the one that closes the chain. A batch job keeps its own attempt limit
  (`Tracon:Scheduling:MaxAttempts`, `3` by default, or the job's `maxAttempts`), so
  give it `2 + MaxResumeAttempts` attempts to get every continuation.

:::caution[The step in progress runs again]
A checkpoint is written as each super-step ends. The steps finished before the stop
are not repeated; the step that was running is. A function step with a side effect
must be idempotent, an agent step repeats its model calls and tool calls, and a
`Loop` agent step repeats every turn it had finished — its turns are not
checkpointed.
:::

The job notices the stop only when its lease runs out (`Tracon:Scheduling:LeaseDuration`,
five minutes by default) and a worker leases it again. A run bound to a connection is
never resumed automatically: its reader is gone. Recovery needs `EnableCheckpointing`
(turning recovery on without it fails at startup) and a SQL provider, so checkpoints
survive the restart. A graceful stop closes the run it stops as `Canceled` and keeps
its checkpoints, even with `KeepCheckpointsAfterCompletion` off: the continuation shares
the session, and the cleanup runs when the continuation finishes. Run reconciliation
still never resumes a workflow run itself: two owners would resume the same run twice.

Checkpoints survive a process restart only with a SQL provider registered
(`UsePostgreSql()`, `UseSqlServer()`, or `UseSqlite()`). The in-memory store keeps at
most 50 checkpoints per session and drops the oldest — enough for local development,
not for a workflow you expect to resume after a restart. They are also a retention
target, so an old run may have none left even on durable storage — except a run
waiting for a human answer, whose checkpoints retention keeps until the run is closed
(see [time limits](/concepts/workflow-requests/#giving-a-request-a-time-limit)).

With `KeepCheckpointsAfterCompletion = false`, a finished run deletes its session's
checkpoints only when no other run of the session still needs them — none is
waiting for an answer and none is running. A run that a stopping worker left to its
job is not finished: with `ResumeInterruptedRuns` on, it keeps its checkpoints for the
continuation. A run that asked a human keeps waiting
even after an answer (a second answer opens a new branch), so a session that
paused for input keeps its checkpoints; retention removes those of its finished
runs.

Attachments that an agent step makes — a generated image, a speech clip — carry
the workflow's session id. That id never gets a session row, so the workflow run
owns the attachments instead: retention keeps them while a run with that session id
waits for input, is still running, or finished after the retention cutoff. After
that they are orphaned, and the `attachments` retention target removes them
together with their stored content.

Turning off `EnableCheckpointing` does not silently disable resumption: a workflow
that stops to wait for a human answer fails outright instead of hanging with no way
to resume.

A checkpoint's state is the Microsoft Agent Framework's own serialized graph;
Tracon does not interpret it and makes no promise that a checkpoint written
by one Microsoft Agent Framework version can be resumed by a different one. See
[Versions and upgrades](/reference/versioning/#persisted-session-and-checkpoint-state)
for the compatibility policy.

`tracon state-check` counts stored checkpoints by the Tracon envelope
generation stamped on them and says which of those the build running the
command understands. That is as far as it can go for a checkpoint: the state
inside has no decoder outside a running workflow, so the command reports a
sampled checkpoint as checked for structure only and never claims to have
resumed it.

## Asking a human

A workflow can stop and wait for input:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Durable workflow input cycle
    accDescr: A workflow request closes the run as awaiting input, writes a checkpoint, then resumes from that checkpoint in a new run after a response.
    RUN["run"] --> ASK["executor raises a request"]
    ASK --> WAIT["run closes as AwaitingInput<br/>a checkpoint is written"]
    WAIT --> LIST["GET .../requests"]
    LIST --> RESP["POST .../respond"]
    RESP --> NEW["a NEW run resumes from the checkpoint<br/>streamed over SSE, or queued with Prefer: respond-async"]
```

A request's prompt and form are read from the run's own event stream — nothing copies
them — and only a run in `AwaitingInput` has any. [Workflow requests and time
limits](/concepts/workflow-requests/) covers the tenant-wide list of them and the time
limit a workflow can give them. The answer is matched to the request that is
re-published with the same id when execution resumes. A very long prompt is cut at
the event payload limit (`RunRecording:MaxPayloadLength`) and marked
`…[truncated]`; the request is still listed and can still be answered.

The answer must fit the request's `form`: `approved` for `Boolean`, `text` for `Text`,
`data` that reads into the port's response type for `Json`, and for `PlanReview`
either an approval or `approved: false` with the revision in `text`, and for `ToolApproval`
`approved`, an optional reason in `text` and an optional `remember`. An answer that
does not fit is refused with `400` before anything runs, and no new run opens. The
detail names the port and the missing or unreadable field. A request recorded by
Tracon 1.0.0-preview.3 or earlier does not carry its response type's assembly: for it,
a `data` value that does not read into the type is still reported on the stream, as a
failed run.

This is the same append-only shape as tool approvals: the waiting run stays as it was,
and the response opens a new one. The new run compiles the definition version the waiting
run recorded, so editing the workflow while a person decides does not change what continues
(see [Versions, rollback and pinning an agent step](#versions-rollback-and-pinning-an-agent-step)).
In the default response mode, a second answer to the same request opens a second new run.

### A tool that asks for approval

Where the pattern hosts the agent, a tool that needs approval stops the workflow instead of
failing it: the request has the form `ToolApproval` and is answered with `approved`, a
reason, and optionally `remember`. [Answering a tool
approval](/concepts/workflow-answers/#a-tool-that-asks-for-approval) has the rules.

The skill tools are tools that ask. A step whose agent names skills stops for an approval at its
first `load_skill` call, unless the agent's definition sets `Skills.DisableReadApproval`.
`run_skill_script` always stops the step. See [Approval of the skill
tools](/concepts/tools/#approval-of-the-skill-tools).

### One answer per request

A workflow can take one answer per request instead (`WorkflowResponseMode.SingleAnswer`):
the same answer given again follows the run the first one started, and a different answer
gets `409 Conflict`. In either mode, every answer that starts a run is written to the audit
trail first and recorded for `GET /api/workflows/runs/{runId}/responses`. [Answering a
workflow](/concepts/workflow-answers/) has the rules, what each answer leaves behind, and
the crash case that needs run reconciliation.

- [A workflow that a person can send back](/guides/review-and-revise-workflow/) — a code graph with a human gate and a bounded revision loop.
- [Runs and recording](/concepts/runs/) — reading the tree
- [Evaluation and experiments](/concepts/evaluation/) — compare agent versions using cases, judges, and experiments.

# Tracon and DevUI

Source: https://tracon.dev/getting-started/devui/

Microsoft Agent Framework already ships a user interface, so the first question about
Tracon is usually why a second one exists. The two answer different questions, and
MAF's own documentation draws the line.

## What DevUI says about itself

[DevUI](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/integrations/by-component/ui/devui/)
introduces itself this way:

> DevUI is a **sample app** to help you visualize and debug your agents and workflows
> during development. It is **not** intended for production use.

Its [security and deployment page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/integrations/by-component/ui/devui/security)
says what to do instead:

> For production deployments, build your own custom interface using the Agent Framework
> SDK with appropriate security measures.

Tracon is one implementation of that production-facing layer, delivered as packages
instead of as an instruction. It is not an official answer to that guidance, and it
does not replace DevUI: DevUI stays the fastest way to look at an agent while you
write it.

## Where the two are documented to differ

Only the rows below are drawn from published documentation. DevUI does not document how
it stores state, so this page makes no claim about that.

| | DevUI | Tracon |
|---|---|---|
| Stated purpose | A sample app for local development | An operational layer for your production host |
| Stated production use | Not intended for it | The reason it exists |
| Network binding | Binds to `127.0.0.1` by default | Loopback by default; remote access is opt-in |
| Authentication | Optional bearer token | Bearer token, scoped API keys, and your own ASP.NET Core authorization policy |

## What the production layer has to carry

These are Tracon's own capabilities, not a judgement about DevUI. They are the work
that the recommendation above leaves to you.

- **Records that outlive the process.** Runs, events, tool calls, timings, and cost,
  written to PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or SQLite in a schema of their own.
- **Definitions you can move backwards.** An agent is data, versioned, with rollback.
- **A tenant boundary.** Optional. When you enable it, a `tenant_id` scopes every query.
- **An audit trail you can check.** `audit_log` is hash-chained, and
  `GET /api/audit/verify` reports whether the chain is intact. The Audit screen runs the same walk with
  its **Verify chain** button.

## What this page does not claim

**DevUI is not deficient.** A sample app that says it is a sample app is doing its job.
The gap it describes is the gap Tracon fills.

**Tracon is not a hosted product either.** It is a package family that runs inside your
own process. You still own authentication, model providers, storage, and outbound
connections.

**Most governance features start switched off.** Tenancy, rate limiting, retention, and
at-rest protection are opt-in. `RequireProductionProfile()` turns each of those, and the
other production decisions, into a decision you make at startup rather than one you
discover later.

## Read next

- [What Tracon is](/getting-started/) — the packages, the four rules, and whether it fits.
- [Capability map](/capabilities/) — every feature with its package, storage need, and limit.
- [Security](/getting-started/security/) — the access layers and the tenant boundary in detail.

# Your first agent

Source: https://tracon.dev/getting-started/first-agent/

Build an ASP.NET Core host, register a model-backed agent, then inspect its run
in the embedded console. MAF executes the agent; Tracon supplies the catalog,
HTTP endpoints, and default-on recording around it.

:::note[Preview release]
This guide uses `1.0.0-preview.6`. Preview packages require explicit selection;
pin the exact version when you need a reproducible build.
:::

## Prerequisites

- The .NET 10 SDK.
- An OpenAI API key and a chat model available to that account. The model request
  is sent to your configured provider and can incur provider charges.

<span id="with-the-template"></span>

## Create the host

Install the published template, then create a project. The template pins every
Tracon package to the same version as the template package. Pass the chat model
your account serves today with `--model`: Tracon ships no model list, so the name
comes from the provider's own documentation. The template writes it to
`appsettings.json`; you do not edit any code.

```bash
dotnet new install Tracon.Templates@1.0.0-preview.6
dotnet new tracon-api -n MyAgents --model gpt-5.4-mini
cd MyAgents
```

Use `--persistence`, `--provider`, and `--ui` to change the generated project.
Run `dotnet new tracon-api -h` to see the available values. The console is
embedded in the host; no separate console server is needed.

Store your provider key in the application's development secrets. The key never
enters the project; `appsettings.json` carries only an empty placeholder. The
project file already carries its secrets ID, so there is no `init` step.

```bash
dotnet user-secrets set "Tracon:Providers:OpenAI:ApiKey" "YOUR_API_KEY"
```

<span id="by-hand"></span>

## Choose the model

The generated `Program.cs` already registers an agent named `support` and one tool,
`get_order_status`, from `Tools/OrderTools.cs`. The agent runs with the model you
passed to `--model`. That name is a setting, not code: it sits in
`appsettings.json` next to the empty key placeholder, and `Program.cs` reads it.

```json
{
  "Tracon": {
    "Providers": {
      "OpenAI": { "ApiKey": "", "DefaultModel": "gpt-5.4-mini" }
    }
  }
}
```

To change the model later, change `DefaultModel` in `appsettings.json`, or
override it with a user secret or an environment variable. Azure OpenAI names a
deployment, so its setting is `DefaultDeployment`.

With an API key set and no model name, the host stops at startup and names
`Tracon:Providers:OpenAI:DefaultModel`, instead of failing on the first model
call. With no key at all, the host still starts, and only a run that calls the
model fails.

The agent definition in `Program.cs` binds that setting to the agent explicitly:

```csharp
tracon.AddAgent(new AgentDefinition
{
    Name = "support",
    DisplayName = "Support Assistant",
    Description = "Answers order and shipping questions.",
    Instructions = "You are a support assistant. Answer briefly and clearly. Always use a tool for order questions.",
    Model = new ModelBinding
    {
        Provider = OpenAIProviderNames.ChatCompletions,
        Model = modelName, // Tracon:Providers:OpenAI:DefaultModel
    },
    ToolNames = ["get_order_status"],
});
```

This first agent uses a chat model only. To let a later agent generate stored image
attachments, add `UseOpenAIImages(...)`, set `Tracon:Images:Enabled`, and choose
an image model explicitly — one the provider serves for image generation, which is
not always the same family as its chat models. An image model is not inferred from
this agent's chat model; see
[image generation providers](/guides/model-providers/#image-generation-providers).

Start the host:

```bash
dotnet run --urls http://localhost:5081
```

The host listens on `http://localhost:5081`. Open
`http://localhost:5081/tracon` for the console. Provider model names are explicit
configuration: Tracon does not ship a built-in model list.

The template source is public at
[github.com/farukatasoy/Tracon](https://github.com/farukatasoy/Tracon/tree/main/src/Tracon.Templates/content/Tracon.Starter).

## Run it

**In the console.** Open `/tracon`, pick **Playground**, choose `support`, and
send a message. The reply streams in; tool calls appear as cards with their arguments
and results.

**Over HTTP.** The same run, as a server-sent event stream:

```bash
curl -N -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/agents/support/run \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"message":"Where is order 4182?"}'
```

**From an OpenAI client.** The compatible endpoint accepts the familiar wire format.
Point the client at Tracon, provide its authentication, and use the agent name as
the `model`:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/v1/responses \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"model":"support","input":"Where is order 4182?"}'
```

Here `model` is the *agent* name. Which model it actually calls is the agent's
business, not the caller's.

## Look at what happened

Run recording is on by default for agents resolved through the catalog. In the
console, open **Runs**: status, duration, token counts, cost when pricing is
configured, and the ordered event stream. Over HTTP it is the same data:

```bash
curl http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/runs
curl http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/runs/{runId}
curl -N http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/runs/{runId}/events
```

No additional recording registration is needed for this catalog-resolved agent. Recording can be disabled. A store
failure is also best-effort: it is logged and the agent still runs, so observability
cannot take down product functionality.

## What you have

An agent defined in code with one tool, a console, and a recorded history — with no
database. With the default `--persistence memory`, every store is in memory, so all of
it ends when the process does.

- [Persistence](/getting-started/persistence/) — retain definitions and run records across restarts.

# What Tracon is

Source: https://tracon.dev/getting-started/

Tracon is a **.NET package family** that adds a **control plane** on Microsoft
Agent Framework (MAF). MAF executes the agent and its model/tool loop. Tracon adds
agent definitions, configurable execution controls, HTTP endpoints, default-on
run recording, and an optional embedded console.

The packages run inside your host process. You choose the model providers,
persistence, identity integration, and operational policies. Recording is
best-effort: a recording-store failure is logged while agent execution continues.

:::note[Preview release]
Packages and templates are published as `1.0.0-preview.6`. The
[first-agent guide](/getting-started/first-agent/) starts with the public template;
pin the exact package version when reproducibility matters.
:::

## What you get

| | |
|---|---|
| **Definitions** | An agent as data: model, prompt, tools, skills, callable agents. Versioned, with rollback |
| **Runs** | Default-on recording — status, timings, tokens, cost, tool calls, traces, and an ordered event stream |
| **HTTP API** | 180 generated operations, plus OpenAI-compatible Responses and Chat Completions surfaces |
| **Console** | 30 screens embedded when you add `Tracon.UI` and call `UseUI()` |
| **Workflows** | Multi-agent execution with checkpoints and human-in-the-loop |
| **Evaluation** | Suites, cases, automatic judges, and A/B experiments between agent versions |
| **Governance** | Roles, scoped API keys, tenancy, approvals, guards, quotas, retention, webhooks, and audit |

See the [complete capability map](/capabilities/) for providers, testing,
RAG, voice, scheduling, external protocols, and production operations.

## What it deliberately is not

**It is not an abstraction over MAF.** `AIAgent`, `AgentSession`, `ChatMessage`, and
`AIFunction` are used directly and appear in the public API as themselves. There is
no parallel type hierarchy to learn and nothing between you and MAF's own extension
points.

**It is not a place to write code.** Tools are defined in your codebase and nowhere
else. An agent can be created and edited from the console, but tool *code* can never
be written through it — see [tools](/concepts/tools/) for the two narrow,
guarded exceptions.

**It is not a hosted service.** Tracon does not provide a managed hosting account.
Your host controls outbound connections: configured model providers, exporters,
webhooks, and integrations can send data outside the process. You can use a cloud
model API or a compatible self-hosted engine such as Ollama or vLLM — see
[picking a model provider](/packages/#picking-a-model-provider).

## Four rules it will not break

These conventions explain the default setup and the extension model.

1. **Explicit infrastructure.** `AddTracon()` supplies in-memory store defaults.
   Configure a model provider or a custom agent source for execution, and choose
   persistence when data must survive a restart.
2. **Tools are code only.** The console selects from registered tools; it never
   defines them.
3. **MAF objects are passed through, not wrapped.**
4. **Replaceable services.** Default registrations of the documented extension
   points use `TryAdd` so a consumer registration can supply the implementation.
   Follow each extension guide for its lifetime and registration contract.
   Interfaces that only Tracon's own packages use are `internal`.

## Is it for you?

It fits when you are building agents in .NET and want the operational layer without
building it: a record of what happened, a console for operators and teams that should
not need to modify application code, and a way to change supported agent
configuration without a deployment.

It does not fit if you want a hosted agent product, or if you are not on .NET. Runtime
packages target `net8.0`, `net9.0`, and `net10.0`, and the testing packages follow the
same matrix, so an app on .NET 8 LTS can be tested on .NET 8. The project template
generates a `net10.0` project pinned to the template package's own Tracon version
(`--TraconVersion x.y.z` overrides it), the `tracon` global tool targets `net10.0`,
and the source generator that ships inside Core targets `netstandard2.0`. The
[compatibility matrix](/reference/compatibility/) carries the per-package detail,
including how long each target framework stays in the matrix.

## Read next

- [Capability map](/capabilities/) — match a system requirement to a feature and its limits.
- [Architecture](/concepts/) — understand MAF and Tracon responsibilities.
- [Your first agent](/getting-started/first-agent/) — build a working host from the published template.

# Persistence

Source: https://tracon.dev/getting-started/persistence/

Without a database every store is in memory and everything ends with the process.
That is deliberate — it makes the first agent work with no infrastructure — but it is
not where you stop.

:::caution[In production, Tracon says so out loud]
Start a host in the `Production` environment while storage is still in memory and
Tracon writes one warning at startup, naming the stores that do not survive a
restart. In-memory storage stays a supported mode — the warning never fails
startup and there is no switch to silence it, because a production installation
losing its runs on the next deployment should not be a quiet fact. The same
judgement is what `GET /api/meta` reports as `storage.persistent`, and what the
console's settings screen shows.
:::

## Pick one

```csharp
builder.AddTracon()
       .UsePostgreSql(connectionString);   // Tracon.PostgreSql
```

The `Tracon` meta package carries no storage engine, so the store you pick is a second
reference: `dotnet add package Tracon.PostgreSql --prerelease`. A host that calls
`UsePostgreSql()` with only `Tracon` referenced does not build (`CS1061`).

| Package | Choose it when |
|---|---|
| `Tracon.PostgreSql` | The default. The only one with vector search for knowledge |
| `Tracon.SqlServer` | You already run SQL Server |
| `Tracon.Sqlite` | One node, or a durable local development setup |

All three implement the same store contracts and pass the same shared contract tests.
Their operational limits differ: only PostgreSQL supports Knowledge, only PostgreSQL
keeps the AOT promise, and SQLite is a single-node choice.

:::caution[The connection string is a secret]
It never belongs in `appsettings.json`. Use `dotnet user-secrets` in development and
the environment or a secret store in production. The same rule runs through the whole
product: a webhook or MCP registration stores the *name* of the configuration key its
secret is read from, never the value.
:::

Binding from configuration is the usual shape:

```csharp
.UsePostgreSql(builder.Configuration.GetSection(TraconPostgreSqlOptions.SectionName))
```

```json title="appsettings.json"
{
  "Tracon": {
    "PostgreSql": {
      "ConnectionString": "",
      "SchemaName": "tracon",
      "AutoApplyMigrations": true,
      "CommandTimeoutSeconds": 30,
      "EnableKnowledge": false,
      "EnableReadViews": false
    }
  }
}
```

## How each provider isolates its tables

| Provider | Namespace | Migration coordination |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | Separate `tracon` schema by default | `pg_advisory_lock`, scoped to the schema |
| SQL Server | Separate `tracon` schema by default; your `dbo` objects stay untouched | `sp_getapplock`, scoped to the schema |
| SQLite | No schema support; `tracon_` table prefix by default | A sidecar file lock next to the database |

Rename `SchemaName` or `TablePrefix` when your conventions require it. A bare SQLite
`Data Source=:memory:` connection is rejected because each opened connection would
see a different database; use a shared in-memory URI for tests.

:::note[Knowledge is opt-in and needs pgvector]
The migration set that creates the `vector` extension and the `document_embeddings`
table only applies when `EnableKnowledge` is `true` — off by default, so a managed
PostgreSQL instance without permission to install extensions works with no
configuration at all. Turn it on only if an agent uses Knowledge:

```csharp
.UsePostgreSql(options =>
{
    options.ConnectionString = connectionString;
    options.EnableKnowledge = true;
})
```

With it off, an agent definition that sets `Memory.EnableVectorSearch` fails
compilation with a clear error instead of a database error at run time. Embedding
`Dimensions` become part of the column type: changing embedding models later needs a
schema migration and a re-embed of existing documents. See
[Knowledge](/guides/knowledge/).
:::

:::note[Read views are opt-in on all three providers]
`EnableReadViews` publishes `runs_v1`, a versioned, read-only SQL view over run
data — off by default, so a deployment that never turns it on never sees the
object. Query it with your own SQL or map it as an EF Core keyless entity. See
[Read contract views](/reference/read-views/).
:::

## Migrations run at startup

The SQL files ship embedded in the assembly and are applied when the application
starts, unless that responsibility is moved to its own deployment step:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Two ways a migration is applied
    accDescr: With AutoApplyMigrations true, the application applies pending migrations itself at startup. With it false, a separate tracon migrate step applies the schema first, and the application only verifies it before starting.
    START["Application starts"] --> CHECK{"AutoApplyMigrations"}
    CHECK -->|"true (default)"| APPLY["Applies pending migrations itself<br/>provider lock serializes concurrent instances"]
    CHECK -->|"false"| SEPARATE["tracon migrate<br/>runs as its own deployment step, no app needed"]
    SEPARATE --> APP2["Application starts, verifies the schema, does not write"]
    APPLY --> READY["Ready"]
    APP2 --> READY
```

Two properties make in-process application safe with several instances starting at
once:

- The runner takes the provider-specific lock shown above, so instances serialize
  instead of racing.
- Each applied file's SHA-256 is recorded. If the content later differs from what was
  applied, startup **fails loudly** rather than running against a schema that is not
  what the code expects.

:::caution[Migrations refuse a non-canonical tenant id]
The tenant identifier is stored in its canonical (lower-case) form — see
[Multi-tenancy](/concepts/governance/#what-a-tenant-identifier-may-be). Before
applying anything, the runner checks every table that carries a `tenant_id` and
**stops, naming the tables**, if any row holds a value that is not canonical.

It does not fold those rows for you. On PostgreSQL and SQLite, which compare
case-sensitively, `Acme` and `acme` may be two real tenants, and merging two
tenants cannot be undone. Decide per table whether the rows belong to one
tenant (lower-case them) or to two (rename one), then start again.
:::

:::caution[A migration can be one-way]
A migration may move data and drop a column in the same file, and Tracon ships no
downgrade. After such a migration an older build of the application cannot read the
table. Back up the database before you upgrade; the release notes name every migration
that drops or rewrites data.
:::

:::danger[Do not edit an applied migration]
The checksum covers the file's whole text, comments included. Editing a file that has
already been applied makes every existing database refuse to start. Add a new
migration instead. If you must take such a change, drop and recreate the schema in
that environment first.
:::

:::caution[A migration can be one-way]
Most migrations only add. Some rewrite or drop a column, and while Tracon is in
preview a release may contain one: the data is carried across by the migration
itself, but there is no downgrade path back to the older schema. Take a backup
before upgrading a database you cannot lose, and roll a version back by restoring
that backup rather than by pointing an older build at the newer schema — the
checksum check will refuse it anyway.

The `run_scores` migration is the current example. It widens the score value from an
integer to a nullable double, adds the score's name and its categorical value, and
rewrites the uniqueness index. Existing rows are carried across: a score written by a
judge keeps that judge's name, every other row is named `overall`. On SQLite the
value column is rebuilt in place, so the table is rewritten — size that step against
your own row count before upgrading a large database.

The `approval_rule_source` migration only adds: a nullable `source_fingerprint`
column on `tool_approval_rules`, which also joins the rule's uniqueness index.
Existing rules keep a `NULL` fingerprint on purpose, so a standing rule for a tool
of an MCP server asks once more after the upgrade
([approval rules](/concepts/governance/)).

The `run_input_parameters` migration only adds: a nullable `parameters` column on
`run_inputs`. Existing rows keep `NULL` on purpose, which means "nothing was
recorded". A replay, a continuation after a crash or an approval resume of such a
run is refused when the agent declares [parameters](/concepts/agents/#parameters),
instead of running on the defaults.

The `job_max_duration` migration only adds: a nullable `max_duration_ms` column on
`jobs`. Existing jobs keep `NULL`, which means "no time limit of its own": the limit
`Scheduling:MaxDurationByHandlerKey` maps the job's handler key to applies, and a key
the map does not list has none ([Background work](/guides/background-work/)).

The `non_token_cost` migration only adds. It creates the `run_non_token_usage` table, whose
rows belong to a run and are deleted with it, and appends four nullable snapshot columns to
`runs` and two (`usage_provider`, `usage_model`) to `tool_invocations`. Existing rows keep
`NULL` on purpose: for a run that closed before the upgrade, `nonTokenCost` is `null`, which
means "nobody reported a number", not zero ([Runs](/concepts/runs/#what-a-run-carries)).

The `workflow_definition_versions` migration only adds: `0059` on PostgreSQL, `0047` on
SQL Server and `0046` on SQLite. It creates the table that keeps every version a stored
workflow has had, and copies each existing workflow's current definition into it as the
first entry of that workflow's history. The versions a workflow had before the upgrade
were never kept, so its history starts at the version it has today. The table has no
foreign key to `workflows`: deleting a workflow keeps its versions, and saving the name
again continues the numbering
([Workflows](/concepts/workflows/#versions-rollback-and-pinning-an-agent-step)).

The `agent_definition_version_counters` migration only adds: `0065` on PostgreSQL, `0053` on
SQL Server and `0052` on SQLite. It creates the table that holds the highest version number
each stored agent has had, and starts the counter of every existing agent at the version it
holds today. An agent that was deleted and created again before the upgrade cannot be
recovered: its earlier numbers were never kept, so its counter starts at the highest number it
holds now. The table has no foreign key to `agent_definitions` and no agent content: deleting
an agent keeps the number, and saving the name again continues the numbering
([Versions](/concepts/agents/#versions)).
:::

Most upgrades are not like that one. The latest `run_scores` migration, which adds
the `evaluator_version` column, is the ordinary shape: a single nullable column
appended to the table, no backfill, and no index change. Existing rows are left
exactly as they are and read back with a null version, so the step costs the same
whether the table holds a thousand rows or a million.

The cache-write migration is of that shape too: `0066` on PostgreSQL, `0054` on SQL Server
and `0053` on SQLite. It appends five nullable columns to `runs`, which hold the
tokens, the charge and the unit prices of prompt-cache writes. Rows written before it read
back with nulls. A database that turned on `EnableReadViews` also gets a second definition
of `runs_v1`: its `total_cost` adds the write charge and the five columns are published
at the end of the view ([Read contract views](/reference/read-views/)).

Set `AutoApplyMigrations = false` when schema changes are their own deployment step.
Tracon then verifies but does not write. The diagnostics endpoint can report
whether the schema is current, but it is deliberately not mapped by default because
it exposes setup details:

```csharp
app.MapTracon("/tracon", options =>
{
    options.EnableDiagnosticsEndpoint = true;
});
```

After that opt-in, `GET /tracon/api/diagnostics` is an Admin surface and still
passes through the configured access layers.

Something still needs to **apply** the schema before the application starts with
`AutoApplyMigrations = false`. The `tracon` CLI does that as its own step,
against the database directly — no running application required:

```bash
tracon migrate --provider postgres --connection "$TRACON_CONNECTION"
```

Running it again applies nothing (`0 applied`) and exits `0`; `tracon migrate
status` lists pending migration names without writing. See the [typed client and
CLI guide](/guides/cli/) for setup and the rest of the commands.

A deployment step that already runs your own code can apply them in process
instead: resolve `IMigrationApplier` and call `ApplyAsync()`. Every SQL provider
registers it, so the same call works whichever provider the application uses.

## Giving your own data source instead of a connection string

Each provider's `Options.DataSource` field accepts a `DbDataSource` you built
yourself instead of `ConnectionString` — most useful when your host already owns
one, for example an EF Core `DbContext` configured with an `NpgsqlDataSource`:

```csharp
.UsePostgreSql(options => options.DataSource = yourDataSource)
```

Tracon never disposes an instance it did not build; ownership stays with
whoever created it. Building two separate data sources from the identical
connection string does **not** share a connection pool — see
[Two data planes, one connection pool or two](/guides/embedding/#two-data-planes-one-connection-pool-or-two)
and, for the full EF Core pattern,
[Two connection planes: EF Core and Tracon](/guides/ef-core/).

## What changes once it is durable

Runs, events, and tool calls survive restarts, so the console shows real history
rather than the current process. Sessions can be read back as chat history rather
than an opaque blob — which is also what makes branching a conversation possible.
Queued runs, schedules, evals, experiments, quotas, and the pending-approval mailbox
all become usable, since they depend on state outliving a request. A resolved
[approval presentation](/concepts/governance/#approvals) is persisted next to the
raw call arguments, so it survives a restart the same way the arguments do.

It is also what makes recovering from a crash possible at all: a run's recorded
tool calls are what an [automatically continued run](/guides/reliability/#continue-an-interrupted-run-automatically)
replays instead of repeating, and orphan reconciliation itself only has a stale
`Running` row (or a `Queued` one that was waiting for a workflow slot) to find because
that row, and every tool call it already made, outlived the process that opened it.

Session and workflow checkpoint rows carry a version stamp of their own, separate
from the schema migrations above: Tracon's envelope around the row, and the
Microsoft Agent Framework version that wrote the opaque state inside it. See
[Versions and upgrades](/reference/versioning/#persisted-session-and-checkpoint-state)
for what that stamp promises and what happens when an old row can no longer be read.

Durable state is also state an upgrade has to keep being able to read, and the
stamp is what makes that answerable ahead of time rather than in production:

```bash
tracon state-check --provider postgres --connection "$TRACON_CONNECTION"
```

Run with the **new** version of the tool, it counts your stored rows by stamp,
says which of them the new build understands, and decodes a sample of each. It
writes nothing, so it is safe against the live database. See [the supported
upgrade window](/reference/versioning/#the-supported-upgrade-window).

An agent definition keeps its content in one JSON column. A field that a new version adds
to the definition, such as the list of agent extensions, needs no migration: a row that
was written before the field existed reads the field as empty, and it keeps running as it did.
A row without `skills` reads back with the approval on for all three skill tools.
A row that holds the callable agents as a list of names (`callableAgentNames`) reads back as
entries with no version, and takes the new shape the next time it is saved.

## Keeping it from growing forever

A recorded run is data, and recorded runs accumulate. Retention policies set an age
or row limit per target — run events, tool calls, traces, jobs, webhook deliveries,
eval results, checkpoints, and more.

Database policies take precedence. When no database policy exists and
`Tracon:Retention:Enabled` is true, configuration falls back to built-in target
defaults, such as 30 days for run events and 14 days for spans. With retention
disabled, nothing is deleted. An `archive: true` policy also deletes nothing when no
`IArchiveSink` is registered; data loss is the failure mode the worker avoids. With a
sink, each batch deletes only the rows the sink received — see
[Retention](/concepts/governance/#retention).

Cleanup runs through the job queue. Preview a policy before you execute it:

```bash
curl 'http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/retention/preview'
curl -X POST 'http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/retention/run'
```

## Durability also enables governance

A durable `audit_log` can be **verified**: `GET /api/audit/verify` walks a
hash chain and reports whether any entry was altered or deleted after it was
written. Set a chain key and the hash is an HMAC that only your host can produce
([Sign the audit chain with a key](/guides/audit-chain-key/)). And because sessions, runs, conversations, and workflow checkpoints are real
rows now, a data subject's content can be found and erased by identity, not just aged
out — see [Data subject rights](/concepts/governance/#data-subject-rights).

Both endpoints accept an optional `tenantId` filter; leaving it out never means
"every tenant" — it resolves to the caller's own ambient tenant. A custom
`IAuditLog` implementation must apply this same fallback (see
[Write your own store](/guides/write-your-own-store/)).

Durable rows are also what
[content protection](/getting-started/security/#at-rest-content-protection) encrypts.

A durable `sessions` row is also what
[session ownership](/concepts/sessions/#session-ownership) writes its owner into.
The column is added by a migration, is nullable, and stays NULL until you turn
ownership on — so enabling persistence costs nothing here, and enabling ownership
later is a configuration change rather than a data change. The listing filter is a
`WHERE` clause on that column, applied before paging, which is precisely what an
in-memory setup cannot offer.

## Read next

- [Securing the endpoints](/getting-started/security/) — required reading
before this leaves your machine.
- [Write your own store](/guides/write-your-own-store/) — implement `IRunStore`
  (or another store interface) against a persistence engine none of the three
  built-in providers cover.
