# Securing the endpoints

Source: https://tracon.dev/getting-started/security/

Configure who can reach Tracon, what they can do, and which tenant they can access.
Protected endpoints restrict non-loopback callers by default. This restriction does
not replace host authorization or correct proxy configuration; the metadata endpoint
is an explicit exception.

## The layers

Four independent layers, applied in this order. Use as many as you need.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    accTitle: HTTP authorization layers
    accDescr: A request passes authentication, role policy, optional API-key scope, and optional tenant isolation before an endpoint runs.
    REQ["Incoming request"] --> META{"path = /api/meta ?"}
    META -->|yes| OK["Endpoint runs"]
    META -->|no| POL{"Authorization policy set?"}
    POL -->|"set, fails"| F403["403 Forbidden"]
    POL -->|"unset or passes"| LB{"Remote access off<br/>and caller not loopback?"}
    LB -->|yes| F403b["403 Forbidden"]
    LB -->|no| HDR{"Authorization header present?"}
    HDR -->|no| TOKU{"AuthToken configured?"}
    TOKU -->|yes| F401["401 Unauthorized"]
    TOKU -->|no| ANON{"No policy, and the caller is remote<br/>or a web page of another site?"}
    ANON -->|"remote"| F401
    ANON -->|"foreign Host or Origin"| F403d["403 Forbidden"]
    ANON -->|no| OK
    HDR -->|yes| TOK{"Matches the static token?"}
    TOK -->|yes| OK
    TOK -->|no| KEY{"Valid API key?"}
    KEY -->|no| F401
    KEY -->|yes| SC{"Endpoint needs a scope<br/>the key lacks?"}
    SC -->|yes| F403c["403 Forbidden"]
    SC -->|no| OK
```

### 1. The loopback restriction

On protected routes, non-loopback requests receive `403` by default. A request that a
reverse proxy forwarded counts as remote too: if it still carries `X-Forwarded-For`,
`Forwarded`, or `X-Real-IP`, nothing consumed the header, so the connection address is
the proxy's and not the caller's. Review the host and proxy boundary before allowing
remote access:

```csharp
app.MapTracon("/tracon", options => options.AllowRemoteAccess = true);
```

:::danger
Never turn this on without a token, an API key, or a policy behind it. With remote
access on and no authentication method configured, Tracon refuses an anonymous remote
request with `401`; an API key still works. Anonymous access stays a same-machine
convenience.
:::

With no token and no policy, an anonymous caller counts as the local operator only
when it is not a web page of another site. The request's `Host` must be a loopback
name (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`), and an `Origin` header, when
present, must name one too. Otherwise the request receives `403`: another name that
resolves to this machine (DNS rebinding) or a page on another site is how a browser
takes over a local service. A request with a token or a key is not judged by its host
or origin.

### 2. A bearer token

A single shared token, compared in constant time:

```csharp
options.AuthToken = builder.Configuration["Tracon:AuthToken"];
```

Good enough for one operator or a private network. It cannot be revoked
individually, carries no identity, and gives everyone the same rights.

### 3. API keys

Issued from `/api/api-keys`, stored hashed, scoped per capability, revocable, and
optionally expiring. Each key belongs to a tenant.

Scopes **narrow** a role, they never widen it: what a caller may do is the
intersection of its role and its key's scopes. Scope values use the closed JSON enum;
for example, a key with only `RunsWrite` cannot
administer agents no matter what role the caller has.

The [compatibility reference](/reference/compatibility/#api-key-scopes)
lists all 17 values and the capability each one grants.

A key also proves which tenant is calling — which is why it outranks any claim or
header for tenant resolution. A secret is proof; a header is a claim.

### 4. An authorization policy

The production path. Hand Tracon a policy name and it runs inside your own
authentication pipeline:

```csharp
options.RequireAuthorization("TraconAdmin");
```

## Roles

Three policy names — `Reader`, `Operator`, `Admin` — that you bind to your own claims:

| Role | Can |
|---|---|
| Reader | Read agents, runs, sessions, traces, statistics |
| Operator | Reader, plus start runs, decide approvals, delete sessions |
| Admin | Everything: write definitions, add MCP servers, manage tenants and approval rules, read the audit trail |

Tracon stores no users and no roles. If a policy is not registered in your
application, that endpoint group simply falls back to the layers above — so upgrading
never breaks a working deployment. Turn on `RequireRolePolicies` and a missing policy
becomes a **startup** error instead of a silent gap. If your
`IAuthorizationPolicyProvider` throws while `MapTracon` resolves a role name, that
role is treated as not registered and a `Warning` is logged in the
`Tracon.RolePolicies` category; with `RequireRolePolicies` on, the startup error
carries the provider's exception as its inner exception.

### Acting on another tenant

A few endpoints take the tenant from the request instead of the caller: another
tenant's provider bindings, egress policy and tool policy (`/api/tenants/{tenantId}/providers`,
`/api/tenants/{tenantId}/egress`, `/api/tenants/{tenantId}/tools`) and the tenant records (`/api/tenants`). The
caller's own tenant needs only the role and scope the endpoint names. Another tenant
needs platform authority, and each identity proves it differently:

| Caller | Platform authority |
|---|---|
| API key | The key also carries the `PlatformAdmin` scope |
| Static `AuthToken` | Always — it identifies the installation, not a tenant |
| Claims principal, multi-tenancy on | The `TraconPolicies.PlatformAdmin` policy (`Tracon.PlatformAdmin`) passes |
| Anonymous, same machine | Always — the zero-configuration local operator |

Unlike the three role policies, a missing `Tracon.PlatformAdmin` registration
**denies**: a claims-authenticated Admin of one tenant does not reach another tenant's
secrets by default. With multi-tenancy off, a claim resolves no tenant, so a
single-tenant installation needs no new policy.

:::caution[Reverse proxies change the network boundary]
The loopback rule sees the connection presented to ASP.NET Core. A proxy on the same
machine connects over loopback or a Unix socket, so Tracon also treats a request that
still carries `X-Forwarded-For`, `Forwarded`, or `X-Real-IP` as remote. Configure the
`ForwardedHeaders` middleware with your trusted proxies, so it consumes the header and
the client address becomes the connection address, and HTTPS at the proxy. In
production, require role policies even when the proxy already authenticates users.
:::

## Two deliberate exemptions

**`/api/meta`** answers without authentication. The console has to learn which
authentication method to present before it can ask for anything. It returns no
sensitive data.

**The console shell** — its HTML, JavaScript, and CSS — is exempt from the bearer
layer only. A browser cannot attach an `Authorization` header to a `<script src>`
request, so a locked shell would mean the user could never reach the screen that asks
for the token. The shell carries no data. The loopback restriction and the
authorization policy still apply to it, and every data endpoint behind it is fully
protected.

The real-time voice WebSocket is not an exemption: a browser cannot set a header on a
handshake either, so the token travels in the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` subprotocol and
is verified in constant time. A query string was rejected — it would be written to
server and proxy logs. A WebSocket is not bound by CORS, so an anonymous socket is held
to the same host and origin rule as an anonymous request.

## Outbound requests are guarded too

Tracon reaches the network from three places, and each one accepts an address that
ultimately came from a user. That makes all three an SSRF risk — cloud metadata
endpoints (`169.254.169.254`) included, which often hand out unauthenticated temporary
credentials.

| Surface | Address comes from |
|---|---|
| Webhook delivery | A subscription's `url` |
| MCP server connections | A server definition's `endpoint` |
| Model provider calls | A tenant's provider binding `endpoint` (BYOK) |

One guard covers all three. Private network targets are refused by default:

```json
{
  "Tracon": {
    "Egress": {
      "AllowPrivateNetworkTargets": false
    }
  }
}
```

Refused ranges include `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, `169.254/16`, loopback,
CGNAT, and the IPv6 equivalents. An IPv6 address that *embeds* an IPv4 address is
reduced to that IPv4 address first and judged by the same rules, so
`::ffff:169.254.169.254`, `::169.254.169.254`, `64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe` (NAT64) and
`2002:a9fe:a9fe::` (6to4) are all refused as well.

Turn the setting on if your MCP servers really do run inside the private network. The
rejection message names the setting, so an operator who hits it knows what to change.

The check lives inside the socket connect callback, so the address that is validated
is the address the socket connects to. Validating a URL and then calling it would
leave a time-of-check/time-of-use gap: `HttpClient` would resolve the name a second
time, and an attacker can change the answer between the two lookups (DNS rebinding).
Because the guard runs per connection, a name that passed when it was saved is checked
again every time it is used.

Webhook delivery keeps two extra rules of its own: only `https` is accepted (unless
`AllowInsecureHttp` is on, which permits loopback only), and redirects are not
followed — a redirect is an escape route into a private network.

### Configuration keys are fenced too

A stored record never holds a secret value; it holds the **name** of the configuration
key the value is read from. That alone is not enough, so each name must sit under an
allowed prefix. Without it, a record could name `ConnectionStrings:Default` as its
"API key" and Tracon would send that value to a remote server.

| Record | Field | Default prefix |
|---|---|---|
| Inbound trigger | `signingSecretConfigurationName` | `Tracon:TriggerSecrets:` |
| Tenant provider binding | `apiKeyConfigurationName` | `Tracon:ProviderKeys:` |
| MCP server | `headerConfigurationKeys`, `oauthClientSecretConfigurationKey` | `Tracon:McpSecrets:` |
| Webhook subscription | `headerConfigurationKeys`, `secretConfigurationKey` | `Tracon:WebhookSecrets:` |

The prefix is one per installation, so a name must also sit inside its record's
tenant. A tenant names keys under `{prefix}{tenant}:` — for tenant `acme`,
`Tracon:McpSecrets:acme:GithubToken`. A flat name directly under the prefix, such as
`Tracon:McpSecrets:GithubToken`, belongs to the default tenant, so a single-tenant
installation keeps its names unchanged. Without the tenant segment, one tenant could
name another tenant's key and point the record at an address it controls. The segment
matches the tenant id without regard to case, like configuration keys themselves.

Each prefix is configurable through the matching options section, and both rules are
enforced twice: where the record is saved, and again where the value is resolved — so
a record written before a rule existed cannot quietly read outside it.

### Credential headers are declared by key name

An MCP server or a webhook receiver often wants a credential in a header other than
`Authorization` — `X-Api-Key`, `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key`, `Cookie`. Declare it in
`headerConfigurationKeys`, a map from the header name to the configuration key its
value is read from:

```json
{
  "endpoint": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
  "headerConfigurationKeys": { "X-Api-Key": "Tracon:McpSecrets:acme:SearchKey" }
}
```

Every name in the map goes through the same prefix and tenant rules as the fields
above, on save and again on every connection or delivery. A webhook delivery whose
subscription names a key outside its tenant is dropped, and an MCP server in that
state does not connect. A response returns the map as stored: it holds names, not
values.

The extra plain `headers` of an MCP server or a webhook subscription are the one
free-text exception: they are stored in plain text and sent as given. A save rejects a
plain header whose name looks like a credential — `Authorization`, any name containing
`api-key`, `token`, `password` or `secret`, `Cookie`, or any name ending in `-key` —
with `400`, and the response names `headerConfigurationKeys` as the place for it. A
header name may appear only once across both maps, compared without regard to case.

The name rule is a heuristic. It also catches `X-Idempotency-Key`, which is harmless:
move the value into configuration. It misses names such as `X-Auth`, `X-Signature` or
`X-Session-Id`, so a credential under such a name would still be stored in plain text.
That is why no response returns a stored plain header value — every read and save
response carries the header names with the value `***`, and the audit trail records
the names only. A save that sends `***` back as a value is rejected with `400`: a
client that reads, edits and saves a record must send the real value of every header
again.

A save that leaves `headers` or `headerConfigurationKeys` out, or sends `null`, keeps
the stored map; `{}` removes it. The admin forms send neither map, so saving a server
or subscription from the UI keeps its headers. The side effect: changing only the
address in the form keeps the headers, so the stored plain values and the credential
values resolved from configuration go to the **new** address. The server logs a
warning with the header names when that happens. Change the maps in the same save, or
clear them with `{}`, when an address moves to a party that should not receive them.

## What is stored in the clear

By default, Tracon does **not** encrypt content at rest. Your database holds
these in plain form unless you turn on [content protection](#at-rest-content-protection)
below, so plan for that before storing regulated data:

| Column | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `sessions.state` | Microsoft Agent Framework's serialized session state |
| `workflow_checkpoints.state` | A workflow run's serialized checkpoint, which carries its messages |
| `conversation_items.item` | One stored chat message |
| `run_inputs.messages` | The prompt a run was started with |
| `run_inputs.parameters` | The parameter values a run was started with |
| `run_events.text`, `run_events.payload` | Streamed output and event detail |
| `tool_invocations.arguments`, `.result` | What a tool was called with, and what it returned |
| `attachments.content`, `agent_files.content` | Uploaded bytes and agent file contents |
| `responses.payload` | Reserved for provider responses; no store writes to this table today |

Secrets are the exception and are handled separately: a credential value is never
written to the database. Only the **name** of the configuration key is stored, and the
value is resolved at call time from your configuration. API keys are stored as a
SHA-256 hash, never as a recoverable value.

Two columns hold operator text that can still carry a credential: the plain `headers`
of `mcp_servers` and `webhook_subscriptions`. A save rejects credential-looking names
there, but a credential under a name the rule misses (`X-Auth`, `X-Signature`) is
stored in plain text. Declare such a header in `headerConfigurationKeys` instead. Rows
written before that rule existed keep working; each connection or delivery logs a
warning that names the header, never its value.

## At-rest content protection

`AddContentProtection(...)` encrypts the twelve columns above with AES-256-GCM before
they reach the database, and decrypts them transparently on read — the rest of
Tracon, and your own code, never sees ciphertext. It is off by default (no
surprises); turning it on is a deliberate, explicit call.

```csharp
builder.AddTracon()
       .AddContentProtection(options =>
       {
           options.ActiveKeyId = "2026-08";
           options.Keys["2026-08"] = "ContentProtectionKeys:2026-08";
       })
       .UsePostgreSql(connectionString);
```

`UsePostgreSql` comes from the `Tracon.PostgreSql` package, which the `Tracon` meta package does not include: `dotnet add package Tracon.PostgreSql --prerelease`.

`Keys` never holds a key's raw material — it maps a key id to the **name** of
another configuration key, the same indirection Tracon uses for provider
credentials. The raw 32-byte, base64-encoded key lives only in `dotnet user-secrets`
or an environment variable:

```
dotnet user-secrets set "ContentProtectionKeys:2026-08" "<32-byte base64 key>"
```

Three limits are worth knowing before you rely on this:

- **It protects data at rest, not a running process.** A process holding the key
  still sees plaintext once a value is read back — this closes a stolen backup, a
  discarded disk, or a misconfigured table permission, not a compromised
  application server. What leaves the process is plaintext too: a data subject
  export, and the rows a retention policy hands to your `IArchiveSink`. Encrypt the
  archive in the sink if it must stay encrypted at rest. The same holds for
  [conversation memory](/guides/context-and-memory/#remember-a-user-across-sessions):
  it stores the text of what a user and the agent said in your own vector store, in
  plain text, whatever protects the session tables. Protect that store yourself.
- **A protected column cannot be searched or filtered on the server.** Agent file
  search still returns correct results, but the server-side prefilter is skipped
  and every candidate file is decrypted and matched on the client instead.
- **Only new writes are protected.** Turning protection on does not retroactively
  encrypt existing rows, and turning it off does not decrypt them — each row stays
  readable either way, because Tracon decides whether a value is encrypted by
  looking at the value itself, never at configuration. Key rotation is lazy for the
  same reason: an old key id stays configured for as long as any row still carries
  it, and losing that key makes those rows unrecoverable.

Protect what this does not cover at the layer below: full-disk or tablespace
encryption, a managed database with encryption at rest, and retention policies that
delete what you no longer need.

## The boundaries Tracon enforces

The layers above are what you configure. This table is the other question — which
boundaries exist at all, what each one refuses, and where the detail lives. A security
report is assessed against this list; see the [security
policy](/reference/security-policy/) for what is in and out of scope.

| Boundary | What it refuses | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint access | An unauthenticated or unauthorized caller | [The layers](#the-layers) |
| Tenant isolation | Reading or writing another tenant's rows | [Multi-tenancy](/concepts/governance/#multi-tenancy) |
| Session ownership | Continuing a conversation the caller does not own | [Session ownership](/concepts/governance/#below-the-tenant-session-ownership) |
| Tool authorization | A tool call the caller is not entitled to make, or a tool the tenant's tool policy does not name | [Tool authorization](/concepts/governance/#tool-authorization), [Per-tenant tool policy](/concepts/tools/#per-tenant-tool-policy) |
| Tool approval | An unapproved tool call, until a human decides | [Approvals](/concepts/governance/#approvals) |
| Tool definition | A tool written from the console — tools exist only in code | [Tools](/concepts/tools/) |
| Script execution gates | A skill script starting without a grant or with an interpreter off the allowlist, or a stored or code-defined one starting after its content changed since the grant | [Skill scripts](/concepts/tools/#skill-scripts--the-strict-exception) |
| Outbound egress | A request to a private network target or a disallowed host | [Outbound requests](#outbound-requests-are-guarded-too) |
| Tenant provider policy | A tenant's data reaching a model, speech, live voice, image or embedding provider its egress policy does not name, or a call billed to the shared key while the tenant has its own | [Per-tenant provider credentials and egress](/concepts/governance/#per-tenant-provider-credentials-and-egress) |
| Content guards | Input or output a configured guard rejects | [Content guards](/concepts/governance/#content-guards) |
| Secret handling | A secret value reaching storage, a log, or a response | [What is stored in the clear](#what-is-stored-in-the-clear) |
| At-rest protection | Readable content in a database you do not fully trust | [At-rest content protection](#at-rest-content-protection) |
| Audit trail | Eight operations proceeding without their record | [What is guaranteed to be written](/concepts/governance/#what-is-guaranteed-to-be-written) |
| Quotas and rate limits | Spend and request volume above the configured ceiling | [Quotas and rate limits](/concepts/governance/#quotas-and-rate-limits) |
| Production profile | A host starting with a security decision never made | [Requiring a production decision](/concepts/governance/#requiring-a-production-decision) |

Individual .NET types restate the boundary they sit on in their own API reference
page, so the constraint is visible at the point of use as well as here.

This table says what each boundary refuses. For who it refuses — the attacker
profiles behind "unauthenticated", "another tenant", "a malicious MCP server" — and
which combinations are accepted risk rather than a covered boundary, see the [threat
model](/reference/threat-model/).

## A short checklist

- [ ] `AllowRemoteAccess` is on only together with a token, a key, or a policy
- [ ] A multi-tenant installation registers `Tracon.PlatformAdmin` for its operators, and each tenant's secrets sit under `{prefix}{tenant}:`
- [ ] Secrets are in user-secrets, the environment, or a secret store — never a file
- [ ] Roles are bound to your claims, and `RequireRolePolicies` is on
- [ ] Quotas are set, so one caller cannot spend the whole model budget
- [ ] Retention policies exist for run events and traces
- [ ] Encryption at rest is provided by the database or the disk, `AddContentProtection(...)`, or both
- [ ] Skill script execution is left off unless you have read what it does; when it is on,
      scripts run in a container under an unprivileged user, or in your own
      [script executor](/guides/write-your-own-script-executor/) bound with
      `RequireCustomBinding<ISkillScriptExecutor>()`
- [ ] `Tracon:Egress:AllowPrivateNetworkTargets` is on only if your MCP servers or
      provider endpoints really are on the internal network
- [ ] `IToolAuthorizationHandler` is implemented for any tool that should not be callable
      by every caller — see [Tools: authorization and timeout](/concepts/tools/#authorization-validation-and-timeout) —
      or, in a multi-tenant host, `Tracon:Tools:RequireTenantPolicy` is on and each tenant has a
      [tool policy](/concepts/tools/#per-tenant-tool-policy)
- [ ] `RequireProductionProfile()` is called, so the production decisions (tenant
      separation, role policies, tool authorization, tenant egress and the rest) cannot be
      skipped in silence — see
      [Make a production decision required](/guides/embedding/#make-a-production-decision-required)

- [Security policy](/reference/security-policy/) — reporting a vulnerability, and scope
- [Governance](/concepts/governance/) — audit trail, quotas, tenancy
- [Architecture](/concepts/) — how the pieces fit

# Adding a tool

Source: https://tracon.dev/getting-started/tools/

An agent without tools can only talk. A tool is a method in your codebase that the
model may call.

## Register one

Mark the method and let the source generator find it:

```csharp title="Tools/OrderTools.cs"
using Tracon;

internal class OrderTools
{
    /// <summary>Returns the shipping status of an order.</summary>
    /// <param name="orderId">The order number.</param>
    [TraconTool("get_order_status", "Returns the shipping status of an order.")]
    public static string GetOrderStatus(string orderId)
        => $"Order {orderId} has shipped. Estimated delivery: 2 days.";
}
```

```csharp title="Program.cs"
builder.AddTracon()
       .AddGeneratedTools();
```

`AddGeneratedTools()` is filled in at compile time — no reflection, no trimming or
AOT warning. A method without the attribute is not a tool, so adding a helper to the
class does not quietly expose it to a model.

Then name it on the agent:

```csharp
tracon.AddAgent(new AgentDefinition
{
    Name = "support",
    // …
    ToolNames = ["get_order_status"],
});
```

An unknown tool name fails **definition compilation**, not C# compilation. A database
definition is rejected when you validate or save it. A code definition is compiled
when the catalog first resolves it and does not resolve until the registration is
fixed. In either case, the model never receives a tool name Tracon cannot bind.

### The other two ways

```csharp
.AddTool(GetOrderStatus)      // from a delegate — uses reflection
.AddToolsFrom<OrderTools>()   // scans a type — uses reflection
```

Both work and both carry `[RequiresUnreferencedCode]` and `[RequiresDynamicCode]`.
The warning is handed to you rather than suppressed. Use `AddGeneratedTools()` unless
your tools live in an assembly you do not compile.

### Tools in a class library

`AddGeneratedTools()` is generated into every assembly that has a tool, and it is
`internal`: it registers that assembly's tools only. A library hands its tools to a
host through its own extension, which calls the generated one from inside:

```csharp title="ContosoToolsExtensions.cs (in the library)"
public static class ContosoToolsExtensions
{
    public static ITraconBuilder AddContosoTools(this ITraconBuilder builder)
        => builder.AddGeneratedTools();
}
```

The host calls `AddContosoTools()` next to its own `AddGeneratedTools()`. Nothing is
scanned at run time, so the trimming and AOT guarantee holds across the two
assemblies.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: Each assembly registers its own generated tools
    accDescr: The host's AddGeneratedTools registers the host's tools. The host also calls the library's public AddContosoTools, which calls the library's own internal AddGeneratedTools from inside the library.
    HOST["Host Program.cs"] -->|"AddGeneratedTools()"| HT["Host tools<br/>internal, generated in the host"]
    HOST -->|"AddContosoTools()"| LIB["Library extension<br/>public, written by the library"]
    LIB -->|"AddGeneratedTools()"| LT["Library tools<br/>internal, generated in the library"]
```

## The rule that trips people up

:::danger[A tool sees an empty service provider]
`AddTool(delegate)` and `AddToolsFrom<T>()` build the tool with
`AIFunctionFactory.Create`, which binds an `IServiceProvider` parameter from
`AIFunctionArguments.Services`. MAF always supplies that as an **empty** provider.
Resolving a dependency inside a tool body fails — and it fails at run time, in a model
call, not at startup.

Take dependencies at **registration**:

```csharp
// Wrong — services is empty when the model calls this
public static string GetOrderStatus(string orderId, IServiceProvider services)
    => services.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>().Find(orderId).Status;

tracon.AddTool(GetOrderStatus);

// Right — the dependency is captured when the tool is registered.
// The factory runs once, on the final service provider, when Tracon builds its
// tool registry at start. Register before builder.Build(): the service collection
// is read-only after it, and a registration added then throws.
tracon.AddTool(provider =>
{
    var repository = provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>();

    return AIFunctionFactory.Create(
        (string orderId) => repository.Find(orderId).Status,
        "get_order_status",
        "Returns the shipping status of an order.");
});
```

`[TraconTool]` catches the same mistake earlier: the source generator does not
support an `IServiceProvider` parameter, so the method fails to compile instead of
failing on the first call.

The same problem reaches instance methods picked up by `AddToolsFrom<T>()` — the
instance has to come from somewhere, and MAF cannot supply it. Tracon rejects an
instance method there too, but at scan time, when `AddToolsFrom<T>()` runs at startup,
not on the first call.
:::

Taking a dependency at registration only works for a **singleton**. When the
dependency has to be fresh per call — a repository, a `DbContext` — use
`AddScopedTool` instead of `AddTool`:

```csharp
tracon.AddScopedTool(AIFunctionFactory.Create(
    (string orderId, AIFunctionArguments arguments) =>
        arguments.Services!.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>().Find(orderId).Status,
    "get_order_status",
    "Returns the shipping status of an order."));
```

`AddScopedTool` opens a real dependency-injection scope for every call and exposes
it through `AIFunctionArguments.Services` — the empty-provider trap above does not
apply to a tool registered this way. See
[Write your own tool](/guides/write-your-own-tool/#scoped-dependencies) for the
full mechanism.

## Tools that need a human

Some tools should not run unattended:

```csharp
[TraconTool("issue_refund", "Refunds an order.", RequiresApproval = true)]
public static string IssueRefund(string orderId) => /* … */;

// or, for a tool registered from a delegate:
tracon.AddTool(IssueRefund, configure: options => options.RequiresApproval = true);
```

For the full singleton, scoped-dependency, timeout, and output contract, see
[Write your own tool](/guides/write-your-own-tool/).

The tool is wrapped in the registry — the single place where "an agent may only point
at a registered tool" is enforced, so there is no code path that skips the wrapper.
When the model calls it, the run pauses and an approval request appears in the
console. What happens next depends on how the run was started: a streaming run
carries the approval in its next turn, while a queued run stops at
`AwaitingApproval` and waits in the approval mailbox.

Standing decisions are possible too — an approval rule pre-approves a tool, or one
exact set of arguments, so it stops asking. Those rules are visible and revocable
under **Governance**.

## Try it

```bash
curl -N -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/api/agents/support/run \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"message":"Where is order 4182?"}'
```

The stream carries `ToolInvoking` and `ToolInvoked` events around the model's reply,
and each call is written to the run with its arguments, its result, its duration, and
its error if it had one.

- [Persistence](/getting-started/persistence/) — keep the history
- [Tools, skills, and MCP](/concepts/tools/) — the whole picture, including
  the two exceptions to "code only"

# AG-UI front ends

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/ag-ui/

How does a front end built on the [AG-UI protocol](https://docs.ag-ui.com) — CopilotKit, or your own
React code on `@ag-ui/client` — run a Tracon agent? Through one extra endpoint,
`POST /tracon/agui/{agentName}`. The request is a Tracon run: it is recorded, the tenant is resolved,
roles are enforced, the quota is counted and the cost is written. Session ownership applies when
[`Tracon:SessionOwnership`](/concepts/sessions/#session-ownership) is on; it is off by default, and until then a thread
is whatever the front end chooses and any operator of the tenant can continue it. Only the dialect on the wire is AG-UI.

## Map the endpoint

AG-UI lives in its own package, so an application whose front end does not speak it never carries the
AG-UI SDK.

```bash
dotnet add package Tracon.AGUI --prerelease
```

```csharp
builder.AddTracon()
       .UseOpenAI(apiKey)
       .AddClientTool(
           "read_shopping_cart",
           "Reads the items in the customer's shopping cart in the browser.",
           JsonSerializer.Deserialize<JsonElement>("""{"type":"object","properties":{}}"""))
       .AddAgent(new AgentDefinition
       {
           Name = "support",
           Instructions = "You are a support assistant.",
           Model = new ModelBinding { Provider = "openai", Model = "gpt-5.4-mini" },
           ToolNames = ["read_shopping_cart"],
       });

app.MapTracon();
app.MapTraconAGUI();
```

`MapTraconAGUI` must come after `MapTracon`. It inherits the same access protection from there: loopback
by default, the bearer token, your authorization policy, the `Operator` role and the `runs:write` API key
scope. The path is `/tracon/agui` unless you pass another prefix.

The body is an AG-UI `RunAgentInput` and the answer is `text/event-stream`, one `data:` frame per event:

```bash
curl -N -X POST http://localhost:5081/tracon/agui/support \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"threadId":"t1","runId":"r1","messages":[{"id":"m1","role":"user","content":"hello"}],
       "tools":[{"name":"read_shopping_cart","description":"Reads the cart in the browser.","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{}}}],
       "context":[]}'
```

The agent carries a client-side tool, so the request declares it; an empty `tools` list would be refused (see
[Front-end tools](#front-end-tools)).

## Connect a front end

CopilotKit's runtime reaches a remote AG-UI agent through `HttpAgent` from `@ag-ui/client`. Point it at
the Tracon endpoint and pass the credential as a header:

```ts
import { HttpAgent } from "@ag-ui/client";
import { CopilotRuntime } from "@copilotkit/runtime/v2";

const runtime = new CopilotRuntime({
  agents: {
    support: new HttpAgent({
      url: "https://your-host/tracon/agui/support",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.TRACON_API_KEY}` },
    }),
  },
});
```

When the browser itself calls the endpoint, add its origin to `AllowedOrigins`: the AG-UI path gets the
same [CORS answer](/guides/client-side-tools/#cors) as the rest of Tracon, and nothing wider.

## How a request is read

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: How an AG-UI request becomes a Tracon run
    accDescr: The front end sends a RunAgentInput. Tracon reads only the new messages, checks the declared tools against the client-side tools in code, answers pending approvals and requests, runs the agent through the same gates as the management API, and streams AG-UI events back.
    FE["Front end<br/>RunAgentInput"] --> MAP["Read the request<br/>new messages · tools · resume"]
    MAP --> GATES["Same gates as<br/>POST /api/agents/{name}/run"]
    GATES --> RUN["Tracon run<br/>recorded · priced"]
    RUN --> EV["AG-UI events<br/>text · tool calls · interrupts"]
    EV --> FE
```

| AG-UI field | What Tracon does |
|---|---|
| `threadId` | It is the session. At most 200 characters; a thread belongs to the tenant that opened it, and with session ownership on also to the user |
| `messages` | The server keeps the conversation. Only the messages after the **last assistant message** are new input: the user's text, and the results of the client-side tool calls that message made. Earlier messages are already in the session and are not added again. System and developer messages are not read — the instructions are the agent's |
| `tools` | Must name every client-side tool the agent carries. The schema is always the one in code |
| `resume` | Answers a tool approval or a request for user input |
| `context` | Becomes run documents, kept apart from the instructions |
| `state`, `forwardedProps` | Not used |

Text is the only input kind read: image, audio, video and document parts of a message are ignored.

## Front-end tools

A tool that runs in the browser is a [client-side tool](/guides/client-side-tools/): its declaration lives
in code, the server never runs it, and the result comes back with the next request. In AG-UI terms the model's
call arrives as `TOOL_CALL_START`, `TOOL_CALL_ARGS` and `TOOL_CALL_END`, the run finishes, the front end runs
the tool, and the next request carries the result as a `tool` message with the same `toolCallId`.

An AG-UI front end declares its tools on every request. Tracon treats that as information, not as
instruction:

- A tool the request declares and the agent carries as a client-side tool is run by the front end. The model
  sees the **code's** schema, never the request's.
- A client-side tool the agent carries and the request does not declare is refused with `400`, and the
  response names it. The model would call a tool nobody can run.
- A tool the request declares and the agent does not carry is **ignored**. The model never sees it, and the
  run records its name under the `tracon.agui.tools.ignored` event.

A front end cannot add a tool or change a schema through this endpoint. Tools are defined only in code.

## Approvals and requests for input

A tool that [waits for approval](/concepts/governance/), and an MCP server that [asks the user for
input](/concepts/tools/#a-server-asks-the-user-for-input), end the run with an **interrupt** in
`RUN_FINISHED`. The run stays open on the Tracon side (`AwaitingApproval` or `AwaitingInput`).

```json
{
  "type": "RUN_FINISHED",
  "threadId": "t1",
  "runId": "r1",
  "outcome": {
    "type": "interrupt",
    "interrupts": [{
      "id": "ficc_call_YhKBs3eWkkfjxpTyfphRGAnV",
      "reason": "tool_call",
      "message": "Cancel order ORD-1001 for Priya Shah.",
      "toolCallId": "call_YhKBs3eWkkfjxpTyfphRGAnV",
      "responseSchema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "approved": { "type": "boolean" },
          "reason": { "type": "string" },
          "remember": { "type": "boolean" },
          "rememberArgumentsOnly": { "type": "boolean" }
        },
        "required": ["approved"]
      },
      "metadata": { "toolName": "cancel_order", "entityType": "order", "entityId": "ORD-1001", "entityName": "Order ORD-1001" }
    }]
  }
}
```

The `message` and `metadata` come from the tool's approval presenter when one is registered. The answer is the `resume`
of the next request, on the same thread. For an approval, `remember: true` saves
the decision as a standing rule, exactly as it does on the management API; without `rememberArgumentsOnly`
the rule covers every call of the tool:

```json
{
  "threadId": "t1",
  "runId": "r2",
  "messages": [],
  "resume": [{ "interruptId": "ficc_call_YhKBs3eWkkfjxpTyfphRGAnV", "status": "resolved", "payload": { "approved": true } }]
}
```

- A `cancelled` status is a refusal for an approval, and a cancellation for a request for input. It is never
  an approval.
- For a request for input (`reason: input_required`) the interrupt carries the server's own field schema, and
  the `payload` is an object of those fields. A value that does not fit is refused with `400` before anything
  runs again.
- An interrupt id that is not pending in the thread — unknown, already answered, or another tenant's — is a `400`.
- The decision is written to the audit trail before it is applied, with `"surface": "ag-ui"`. A decision that
  cannot be recorded is not applied.

## What comes back

The first event after `RUN_STARTED` is a `CUSTOM` event named `tracon.run`. Its value carries the Tracon run
id, which is how a front end finds the run in the console and in `GET /api/runs/{id}`.

A failure after the stream began is a `RUN_ERROR` event: its `code` is the exception type and its message
says what failed. The provider's address and the exception text never reach the front end; the server log
holds them under a correlation reference, which an exception Tracon does not recognize also puts at the end
of the message as `(ref: …)`.

A front end that closes the connection mid-run stops the run, and the run is recorded as `Canceled`.

## Limits

- One thread, one run at a time. Two overlapping runs of the same thread behave as on the management API: the
  second to save loses, and its stream ends with `RUN_ERROR`.
- No `Idempotency-Key` and no `Prefer: respond-async`: an AG-UI run is always live.
- No run parameters and no culture: an agent with a required [parameter](/concepts/agents/#parameters) cannot be started
  from AG-UI, and instructions resolve in the agent's default culture.
- Attachments are not read; only the text of a message is.
- The package is not Native AOT compatible.

## Read next

- [Client-side tools and the embeddable widget](/guides/client-side-tools/) — how the front-end tool mechanic works without AG-UI.
- [Governance](/concepts/governance/) — what an approval is and where its rules and audit trail live.
- [Security](/getting-started/security/) — the access layers `MapTraconAGUI` inherits.

# Use any Microsoft Agent Framework feature

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/any-maf-feature/

Does Tracon block a Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) feature that it does not model?
No. Every MAF feature runs under Tracon when your code builds the agent. The real
question is what the agent loses on the way. This page puts the ways in order, lightest
first, and says what each one keeps and loses.

Every code block on this page comes from `samples/Tracon.Samples.MafFeatures`. That
sample builds against the packed packages. Its test project checks eight claims: the
decorator sees the tool calls of every door, the custom source uses the tenant's own
key and records cost, a factory agent that declares its model does the same, the egress
policy reaches the custom source and the factory agent that declares its model, it does
not reach a factory agent that declares none, that agent uses the setup key and records no
cost, and Tracon says so once, an agent extension adds a context provider to an agent
defined as data without losing the tenant's key or cost, and a chat client ring that an
extension adds sees every model call of that agent.

## The coverage ladder

Four levels say how far a feature reaches into Tracon:

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Unavailable | You cannot use the feature, or using it turns off the run record or the tenant boundary. |
| Runs | You use the feature from code. The run of the agent is recorded. Some Tracon rings can be lost. |
| Recorded | The events, usage, and cost of the feature enter the run record and the span. The tenant boundary applies. |
| Managed | You turn the feature on with data: a definition, the HTTP API, or the console. Tracon validates it, versions it, and puts it under roles and the audit trail. |

The rule is: code defines, data selects. Anything that executes is registered in
code — a tool, a context provider, middleware. A definition picks it by name. A feature
that you wire in from code reaches **Runs** at once. It does not reach **Managed** by
itself.

## Pick the lightest door

Start at the top of the diagram and stop at the first door that fits.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Which door reaches a framework feature
    accDescr: A decision tree. A workflow graph goes to a code workflow. A Microsoft.Extensions.AI type that Tracon reads from the container is registered in the container. Agent middleware, tool middleware, or a message context provider goes in an agent decorator. A framework option, a full context provider, or a chat client ring on an agent that a definition describes goes in an agent extension. Anything else needs an agent that code builds. An agent that does not live in your code, such as one from a repository or another runtime, comes from a custom agent source. An agent in your code that calls a model through Tracon is a factory agent that declares its model, and it keeps the tenant key, the egress policy, and cost. An agent in your code that does not call a model through Tracon is a factory agent that declares none.
    START["A framework feature you want to use"] --> GRAPH{"Is it a workflow graph?"}
    GRAPH -->|yes| WF["Code workflow<br/>AddWorkflow"]
    GRAPH -->|no| DI{"Does Tracon read the type<br/>from the container?"}
    DI -->|yes| REG["Register it<br/>in the container"]
    DI -->|no| MW{"Is it agent middleware, tool middleware,<br/>or a message context provider?"}
    MW -->|yes| DEC["Agent decorator"]
    MW -->|no| OPT{"Is it a framework option, a full context provider,<br/>or a chat client ring, on an agent that a definition describes?"}
    OPT -->|yes| EXT["Agent extension"]
    OPT -->|no| LIVE{"Does the agent live<br/>in your code?"}
    LIVE -->|no| SRC["Custom agent source"]
    LIVE -->|yes| MODEL{"Does it call a model<br/>through Tracon?"}
    MODEL -->|yes| FACM["Factory agent<br/>that declares its model"]
    MODEL -->|no| FAC["Factory agent<br/>that declares none"]
```

| Door | Use it when | What you keep | What you lose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Container registration | Tracon reads the type from the container | Everything | Nothing |
| Agent decorator | The feature is agent middleware, tool middleware, or a message context provider | Everything: the model rings, the tenant key, the egress policy, cost | A full context provider |
| Agent extension | The feature is a framework option, a full context provider, or a chat client ring, and a definition describes the agent | Everything a decorator keeps, plus the definition: console editing, versions, validation | The options the definition owns are protected. A tool that your provider adds skips the tool chain |
| Factory agent that declares its model | Code builds the agent and it calls a model through Tracon | The run record, the model rings, the tenant key, the egress policy, cost, the wrapped tools | Console editing, the request fields on the binding (set them in the factory), and the features the compiler wires |
| Factory agent that declares none | Code builds the agent and it does not call a model through Tracon, such as a wrapper of another runtime | The run record and the wrapped tools; the model rings if you build the client from the registry | The tenant key, the egress policy, cost |
| Custom agent source | The agents live outside your code: a repository, or another runtime | The same as a factory agent that declares its model | Console editing and the features the compiler wires |
| Code workflow | The feature is a graph | The graph, in full | Events that Tracon does not map |

## Register it in the container

Some Microsoft.Extensions.AI types need no agent at all. You register the type, and
Tracon uses it where it needs one. An `IEmbeddingGenerator` serves knowledge search, an
`ITextToSpeechClient` or `ISpeechToTextClient` serves voice, and an `IEvaluator` serves
evaluation. Register the type with the extension of its own package, then bind it as the
page of the feature says. Each page also says what the feature records:

- [Knowledge and RAG](/guides/knowledge/) — the embedding generator
- [Voice and live conversation](/guides/voice/) — speech clients
- [Evaluation and experiments](/concepts/evaluation/) — evaluators

## Wrap the agent with a decorator

An `IAgentDecorator` wraps every agent that the catalog resolves. A decorator can add
MAF middleware with `AIAgentBuilder`. It can add run middleware, function-invocation
middleware that sees each tool call, or a `MessageAIContextProvider`. The decorator
wraps the agent that the catalog already built, so the agent keeps every Tracon ring.

```csharp
public sealed class ToolCallLogDecorator(ToolCallLog log) : IAgentDecorator
{
    public int Order => 100;

    public AIAgent Decorate(AIAgent agent, AgentDescriptor descriptor)
        => agent.AsBuilder()
            .Use(async (innerAgent, context, next, cancellationToken) =>
            {
                log.Record(descriptor.Name, context.Function.Name);
                return await next(context, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);
            })
            .Build();
}
```

Give the decorator an `Order` above `0`. Run recording sits at `0` and hands the agents
inside it a plain `AgentRunOptions`. MAF function middleware accepts that type. A
decorator outside run recording receives Tracon's own run options, and the middleware
rejects them.

The decorator sees every agent. To act on one agent only, check `descriptor.Name`. The
sample tests run this decorator against four agents: one defined as data, two from
factories, and one from a custom source. It sees the tool call of all four.

A decorator cannot add a full context provider, one that adds tools or instructions.
`UseAIContextProviders` takes only message providers. For a full provider on an agent that
a definition describes, use an agent extension. For an agent that code builds, use one of
the doors after it.

The sample registers the decorator together with the log it writes to:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ToolCallLog>();

return builder.AddAgentDecorator<ToolCallLogDecorator>();
```

See [Write your own agent decorator](/guides/write-your-own-agent-decorator/) for the
full contract.

## Add an option, a provider, or a ring with an agent extension

An agent extension is code that you register once and a definition selects by name. It
reaches the options that Tracon builds the agent from, so it can set a framework option or
add a full `AIContextProvider`. It can also put a chat client ring into the model pipeline
of the agent. The agent still goes through the definition compiler. It keeps the model
rings, the tenant's own key, the egress policy, and cost, and the console can still edit and
version it.

The sample adds a provider that puts a policy notice into the instructions of every model
call:

```csharp
return builder.AddAgentExtension(
    ExtensionName,
    context =>
    {
        // Add after the providers Tracon built; the compiler refuses a change to them.
        var options = context.ChatAgentOptions!;
        options.AIContextProviders = [.. options.AIContextProviders ?? [], new PolicyNoticeProvider()];
    },
    description: "Adds the refund policy to the instructions of every model call.");
```

```csharp
private sealed class PolicyNoticeProvider : AIContextProvider
{
    protected override ValueTask<AIContext> ProvideAIContextAsync(InvokingContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
        => new(new AIContext { Instructions = Notice });
}
```

The sample puts the name in the definition of the agent. A stored definition does the same
with `extensionNames`, and the console offers the registered names in the agent editor:

```csharp
ExtensionNames = [PolicyNoticeExtensionRegistration.ExtensionName],
```

### Add a chat client ring

`context.UseChatClient` puts a `Microsoft.Extensions.AI` chat client into one of two fixed
places in the model pipeline that Tracon builds. A client that the framework documents as
one that must see every model call belongs here: a check on each call, a log of each call,
or a reducer of the request. The sample logs every model call:

```csharp
return builder.AddAgentExtension(
    ExtensionName,
    context =>
    {
        var log = context.Services.GetRequiredService<ModelCallLog>();
        var agent = context.Definition.Name;

        context.UseChatClient(ChatClientSlot.ModelCall, inner => new ModelCallLogChatClient(inner, log, agent));
    },
    description: "Logs the role of the last message of every model call.");
```

The ring derives from `DelegatingChatClient`. The sample's ring records the role of the last
message and passes the call on:

```csharp
public override Task<ChatResponse> GetResponseAsync(
    IEnumerable<ChatMessage> messages,
    ChatOptions? options = null,
    CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
{
    var request = messages as IReadOnlyList<ChatMessage> ?? [.. messages];
    Record(request);

    return base.GetResponseAsync(request, options, cancellationToken);
}
```

The sample test runs an agent that calls a tool. The ring sees two calls: the question, and
the call that takes the tool result to the model.

The two slots, from the outside of the pipeline in:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    accTitle: Where a chat client ring sits
    accDescr: The model pipeline of a compiled agent from the outside in. Error normalization, finish-reason detection, the fallback chain, the circuit breaker, and attachment resolution are outermost. The Turn slot is next, above the tool-call loop. The ModelCall slot is right below the loop. The run budget, the response cache, hosted tool usage, the chat span, the content guard, and the concurrency limit are below it, and the provider's raw client is innermost.
    N["Error normalization · finish reason"] --> FB["Fallback chain · circuit breaker"]
    FB --> A["Attachment resolution"]
    A --> T[["Turn slot"]]
    T --> L["Tool-call loop"]
    L --> M[["ModelCall slot"]]
    M --> B["Run budget · response cache · hosted tool usage"]
    B --> O["chat span"]
    O --> G["Content guard · concurrency limit"]
    G --> R["Provider client"]
```

| Slot | What the ring sees | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `ChatClientSlot.ModelCall` | Every model call of a turn, including the call that takes a tool result to the model | A check or a log of each call, a change to each request |
| `ChatClientSlot.Turn` | One call for each agent turn. The tool-call loop runs inside it | A reducer of the conversation, a log of each turn |

What follows from the order:

- **The content guard inspects the messages that the ring sends.** A user, assistant, or
  tool message that the ring adds reaches the guard before the model. The guard does not
  inspect a system message or the instructions in `ChatOptions`, on any agent. Do not let a
  ring put text that it did not write there, for example a retrieved document. The ring also
  receives the answer after the guard has checked it.
- **The budget counts the calls that the ring sends.** A ring that answers by itself and
  does not call the client below it spends nothing and leaves no `chat` span.
- **The response cache keys on the request after the ring.** Two requests that the ring
  makes the same share one cache entry.
- **The fallback chain gets the same ring.** When a fallback model answers in place of the
  agent's model, the ring factory builds a ring for that model's pipeline too.
- **A provider failure passes up through the ring.** The circuit breaker counts it, the
  fallback chain moves on, and normalization masks it as before. An exception that the ring
  throws by itself is your code's: it is not counted and not masked, the same as an exception
  from a wrapper that `context.Use` adds.
- **The compaction summarizer and the judge of a loop criterion get no ring.** They serve
  their own call, not the agent's turn.

The ring factory runs each time the pipeline is built: when the agent is compiled, and when
a fallback model is first used. Keep it cheap and keep state that belongs to one run out of
it. With several rings in one slot, the first one added is the innermost. Derive the ring
from `DelegatingChatClient`. A `Turn` ring that hides the tool-call loop from `GetService`
fails the compilation, because the framework would add a second loop above it. A host that
replaces `IModelProviderRegistry` with its own cannot place a ring: an agent that selects a
ring extension fails to compile on that host, with an error that names the extension.

What to know about this door:

- **`Configure` runs when the agent is compiled, not on every run.** The compiled agent is
  cached for each tenant, agent name, and definition, so the runs that follow share it. Two
  runs that start before the cache holds the agent can each compile it. A run with parameter
  values, and an agent of a tenant that holds its own provider key, is not cached and runs
  the extension each time.
- **The extension gets one options object.** `ChatAgentOptions` is set for a chat agent and
  `HarnessAgentOptions` for a harness agent. `context.Use` adds a wrapper around the
  compiled agent, inside Tracon's own wrappers and decorators. `context.UseChatClient` adds
  a ring to the model pipeline of both kinds of agent.
- **Some options are protected.** A definition or a tenant and security decision owns the
  tool chain, the tool approval settings, the instructions and sampling settings (including the seed,
  top-k, stop sequences, penalties, tool mode, and `AllowMultipleToolCalls`), the chat
  history provider, file access, the working-directory skill scan, file memory, web search,
  compaction, the loop, and the sub-agent tree. Some other options are protected because
  they change a protected setting indirectly. `UseProvidedChatClientAsIs` removes the
  framework's default chat client stack, and with it the approval binding and the per-call
  history writer. `AllowConcurrentInvocation` turns on concurrent tool calls in the tool loop
  that Tracon builds. For concurrent tool calls, set `ToolLoop.AllowConcurrentToolCalls` in the model
  binding of the definition. `ChatOptions.RawRepresentationFactory` replaces the model,
  sampling, and provider settings of the definition on the wire. Two options are protected
  because they do not work under Tracon. `EnableMessageInjection` and
  `RequirePerServiceCallChatHistoryPersistence` act on each model call only when they are under
  the tool loop. Tracon's tool loop is inside the model client, so these layers are above it. An
  injected message does not reach the running turn, and the history is written once per turn.
  A layer of this kind belongs in the `ModelCall` slot of a chat client ring.
  An extension that changes a protected option fails the compilation with
  an error that names the extension and the option. Tracon does not undo the change. The
  provider list is append-only. The other options are yours, for example
  `ThrowOnChatHistoryProviderConflict`. The check covers the options object. It does not look inside a
  provider or a wrapper that the extension adds, so a provider you add can still read files
  or load skills by itself. Register only extension code that you trust, as you do for a tool.
- **A provider can add tools, and Tracon does not run them through the tool chain.**
  Authorization, approval, and the timeout apply to the tools that the tool registry gives
  an agent. A tool that your own provider adds skips them. The run record still shows the
  call.
- **A replay that plays tools back does not run the extension**, for the same reason.
- **Model options for one run follow the same rule.** Code can run a catalog agent with
  `ChatClientAgentRunOptions`. The run may add instructions and tool declarations, and it may
  turn parallel tool calls off (`AllowMultipleToolCalls = false`), which a handoff step does. A
  model id, a sampling setting, a tool mode, a response format, a chat client factory, or a tool
  that runs throws `ArgumentException` before the run starts. No HTTP endpoint takes model options for one run. To change a run, change the
  definition, run an experiment, or declare a parameter.

## Build the agent in a factory

`AddAgent(name, model, factory)` takes the model the agent calls and a factory that returns
any MAF `AIAgent`. Tracon builds the chat client for that model, with the tenant's own
provider key and the tenant's egress policy, and hands it to the factory as
`context.ChatClient`. Tracon records the run and applies its decorators. The agent skips
the definition compiler, so the factory has to ask for each other piece it wants to keep:

```csharp
return builder.AddAgent(
    AgentName,
    model,
    context =>
    {
        // The registry returns the wrapped tool: authorization, validation,
        // timeout, truncation, and approval stay on.
        if (!context.Services.GetRequiredService<IToolRegistry>().TryGet(SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName, out var searchOrders))
        {
            throw new InvalidOperationException($"The tool '{SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName}' is not registered.");
        }

        // The client carries the model rings (run budget, circuit breaker, fallback,
        // response cache, content guards, the 'chat' span), the tenant's key, and the
        // egress policy. Build the agent around it and nothing else.
        return context.ChatClient.AsAIAgent(new ChatClientAgentOptions
        {
            Name = context.AgentName,
            ChatOptions = new ChatOptions
            {
                Instructions = "Answer questions about orders. Look orders up with the search tool.",
                Tools = [searchOrders],
            },

            // Tracon's history store, so the console and /v1/conversations show the
            // turns. With SQL storage, leaving this out leaves both of them empty.
            ChatHistoryProvider = context.Services.GetService<ChatHistoryProvider>(),

            // Any framework provider or option is now yours.
            AIContextProviders = [new TodoProvider(new TodoProviderOptions())],
        });
    },
    description: "A factory agent that declares its model and answers questions about orders.");
```

What a factory agent that declares its model keeps, and how:

| Piece | Kept? | How |
|---|---|---|
| Run row, events, tool-call record, usage, cancellation, webhooks, error class, input record, replay | Yes | Automatic. Run recording wraps every agent. |
| `invoke_agent` span and saved approval rules | Yes | Automatic. |
| Sessions, `/v1/*`, A2A and MCP publication, being called as a sub-agent | Yes | Automatic. |
| The model rings | Yes | Build the agent around `context.ChatClient`. |
| The tenant's own provider key and the egress policy | Yes | The client in `context.ChatClient` is built for the tenant of the run. |
| Cost, model breakdown, cost quota, and `POST /api/agents/{name}/estimate` | Yes | The declared model is the model of the agent in the catalog. |
| The tool chain: authorization, validation, timeout, truncation, approval flag | Yes | Take the tool from `IToolRegistry.TryGet`. |
| History in the console and in `GET /v1/conversations/{id}/items` | Yes | Pass the `ChatHistoryProvider` from the container. |
| The request fields: temperature, maximum output tokens, response format and the rest | **No** | The factory builds its own `ChatOptions`. A binding that sets one is refused when you register, with the field named. Set it in the factory. |

Four facts about this door:

- **The history provider matters on SQL storage.** With the in-memory store, the turn
  shows in the console and in `/v1/conversations/{id}/items` whether or not the agent
  uses the provider from the container. With a SQL store, both stay empty unless the
  agent uses it. The sample passes it.
- **The factory runs on every resolve, and Tracon keeps nothing.** The client holds the
  key of one tenant. Do not keep the agent, or the client, in a field or a cache that
  outlives the call: another tenant would use the first tenant's key. Keep the factory
  cheap, and keep state out of it. A factory that awaits takes
  `Func<AgentFactoryContext, CancellationToken, ValueTask<AIAgent>>` and gets the token of the
  resolve.
- **The factory builds the agent. It does not call the model.** The detail view of the agent
  (`GET /api/agents/{name}`) calls the factory to read the instructions, and builds the
  client without the tenant's key.
- **Tracon warns when the agent does not use the client it was given.** If the agent's chat
  client is not `context.ChatClient`, because it comes from another registry call or from
  outside the registry, Tracon writes one warning for that agent name the first time the
  catalog resolves it. The run would be priced at a model that did not answer. An agent that
  exposes no chat client gets no warning.

### Declare no model

`AddAgent(name, factory)` declares no model. Use it for an agent that does not call a model
through Tracon, such as a wrapper of another runtime. The sample keeps one for the
comparison:

```csharp
return builder.AddAgent(
    AgentName,
    services =>
    {
        // This synchronous call applies no tenant key and no egress policy.
        var chatClient = services.GetRequiredService<IModelProviderRegistry>().CreateChatClient(model);

        // ...the same tool and agent options...
    },
    description: "A factory agent that declares no model.");
```

Tracon does not know which model this agent calls. The client the factory builds from the
registry has the model rings, but it uses the key set up at start and skips the tenant's egress
policy. The run record has no model and no cost, and a cost quota does not stop the agent.
Tracon writes one warning for the agent name when it sees an agent of this kind call a model
through the registry, and one when the chat client does not come from the registry at all.
Both warnings name `AddAgent(name, model, factory)` as the way out.

## Build the agent in a custom source

Write a custom source when the agents do not live in your code: they come from a
repository, a database of your own, or another runtime. An agent that code builds needs no
source, because `AddAgent(name, model, factory)` gives the factory the same client. An
`IAgentSource` builds its agents on demand. Its `ResolveAsync` is asynchronous, so it can call
`CreateChatClientAsync`, which applies the tenant's own provider key and egress policy.
Its `ListAsync` returns a descriptor that names the model, and run recording prices the
run from that model. The sample describes its agent like this:

```csharp
// The model named here is what run recording prices. Leave it out and the
// run is recorded with no model and no cost.
private AgentDescriptor Descriptor => new()
{
    Name = AgentName,
    Description = "A custom-source agent that answers questions about invoices.",
    Origin = AgentDefinitionOrigin.Custom,
    SourceName = SourceName,
    Model = model,
    ToolNames = [SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName],
};
```

`ResolveAsync` then builds the agent:

```csharp
// The asynchronous call applies the tenant's own provider key and the tenant's
// egress policy, on top of the model rings.
var chatClient = await models.CreateChatClientAsync(model, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false);

if (!tools.TryGet(SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName, out var searchOrders))
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException($"The tool '{SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName}' is not registered.");
}

return chatClient.AsAIAgent(new ChatClientAgentOptions
{
    Name = AgentName,
    ChatOptions = new ChatOptions
    {
        Instructions = "Answer questions about invoices. Look orders up with the search tool.",
        Tools = [searchOrders],
    },
    ChatHistoryProvider = history,
});
```

The sample tests run this agent for a tenant that has its own key. The chat client is
built with that key, and the run record carries the model and a cost. The same tests run
the factory agent that declares its model for the same tenant, with the same result, and
the factory agent that declares none: its client is built with the setup key, and its run
record has no model and no cost. They also set an egress policy that forbids the provider.
The custom source and the factory agent that declares its model are refused. The factory
agent that declares none still runs.

A custom source does not run the definition compiler. It owns the whole shape of the
agent. Do not cache an agent whose client carries a tenant's own key across tenants.
[Write your own agent source](/guides/write-your-own-agent-source/) explains the
lifecycle, the priority, and the contract tests.

## Build the workflow in code

`AddWorkflow(name, factory)` runs a MAF `WorkflowBuilder` graph. Every builder feature
runs, and Tracon records a root run. Tracon maps the started, output, error, warning,
super-step, executor, request, and agent-response-update events into the run record. It
records every other event — the plan and ledger events of a Magentic workflow, or an event
class that you define — as a `tracon.workflow.event` with its type name and its data as
text ([Runs and recording](/concepts/runs/)). Such an event has no card of its own in the
console.

If you write executors with MAF source-generated handlers (`[MessageHandler]`), add the
`Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows.Generators` analyzer package to your own project.
Tracon does not reference it for you.

See [Workflows](/concepts/workflows/) for the registration key, the helpers that give a
code graph the time limit, retry, and budget of a stored one, and the full recording
model.

## Ready-made pieces from the framework

Some framework packages ship a finished piece instead of a hook. Three of them were tried
under Tracon on 2026-10-21 with Microsoft Agent Framework 1.25. The shell tool and the
remote agent ran against a real host; Purview was read from its package, because it needs a
Microsoft 365 tenant.

- **A shell tool in a container** (`Microsoft.Agents.AI.Tools.Shell`, preview).
  `DockerShellExecutor.AsAIFunction()` returns an ordinary tool. Register it with `AddTool`
  and name it in the definition: authorization, approval, the timeout, and the audit trail
  apply. Use `ShellMode.Stateless`, so every call runs in a new container and no tenant or
  conversation sees another's files. The persistent mode keeps one shell for one
  conversation, and a registered tool serves every run, so do not register a persistent
  executor. The executor starts the `docker` command line on the Tracon host, and access
  to a Docker socket is root access on that machine: point it at an engine that runs
  nothing else. The executor asks for approval by default, and Tracon reports that tool as
  one that needs approval. Do not use `LocalShellExecutor` on a shared host: it runs the
  command on the host itself.
- **A remote agent** (`Microsoft.Agents.AI.A2A`, preview). `A2AClient.AsAIAgent()` returns
  an agent that sends each turn to another A2A server. Register it with
  `AddAgent(name, factory)`. The run is recorded at the agent level, and the session keeps
  the remote `contextId`, so the next turn on the same Tracon session continues the remote
  conversation. The remote server runs its own model and tools: the record has no model,
  usage, or cost, and the remote run is not a child of the run that called it. The HTTP
  client that you give the agent does not go through Tracon's egress policy.
- **Microsoft Purview** (`Microsoft.Agents.AI.Purview`, release candidate).
  `PurviewExtensions.PurviewAgentMiddleware(...)` returns agent middleware: apply it with
  an agent extension or a decorator. Build it once at startup, because each call builds its
  own cache, background queue, and HTTP client. Purview checks the input and the final
  answer of a run. When it blocks, it returns its message as an ordinary answer, so the run
  closes `Completed`, not as blocked content. Its check of every model call is a chat client
  and needs a seat below the tool loop: the `ModelCall` slot of a chat client ring. That form
  was not tried under Tracon. Its calls to Microsoft Graph do not go through Tracon's egress
  policy.

## What you cannot win back today

These losses have no door that removes them:

- **A protected option on an agent defined as data.** An agent extension can set any
  framework option that the definition and the tenant do not own. The tool chain, the chat
  history provider, the approval settings, the file access and skill-scan options, and the model
  settings stay with Tracon as options. A feature that needs one of them needs an agent that your code builds. That agent is code, so the
  console cannot edit it.
- **The tool chain for a tool that your own provider adds.** An extension's provider can
  add a tool, and that tool skips authorization, approval, and the timeout. Register the
  tool in the tool registry instead, and name it in the definition.
- **Tracon's managed skills, compaction, MCP resources, and loop recording on a
  code-built agent.** The definition compiler wires skills with their script gates,
  context compaction with its record, MCP tools and resources, loop recording, and the
  budget of the agent tree. It does this only when it compiles a definition. A factory
  agent or a custom-source agent gets none of them from Tracon.
- **A file store that is scoped to the tenant and the agent.** The agent file store in
  the container is not built for a provider of your own. The in-memory default has no
  tenant prefix and no agent prefix: every tenant and agent of the process shares it. The
  SQL stores scope every call to the tenant and to the agent of the current run, so a
  provider of your own shares the space of that agent's file memory, and it fails outside
  a run. Do not give the in-memory store to an agent that serves more than one tenant.
  For files that belong to one conversation, use the
  [session workspace](/guides/context-and-memory/#give-an-agent-files-in-each-session)
  instead: it is scoped to the tenant, the agent and the session, its file tools run through
  the tool chain, and its files go with the session.
- **Everything a definition gives.** A code-built agent cannot take parameterized,
  per-culture, or shared instructions. It has no versions, experiments, rollback, or
  validation when you save, and you cannot edit it in the console.
- **The response format of a factory agent.** `ResponseFormat` is a request field, so a
  factory agent cannot declare it, and the validator that checks a structured response runs
  for agents defined as data. Set the format in the factory's `ChatOptions` and validate the
  answer in your own code.

## Checklist

Answer these five questions before you write a factory agent:

1. Can a decorator or an agent extension do the job? If the feature is middleware, a
   message provider, a framework option, a full context provider, or a chat client ring, one
   of them can, and you keep every ring.
2. Does the agent call a model through Tracon? If yes, declare the model with
   `AddAgent(name, model, factory)`, so you keep the tenant's own key, the egress policy,
   and cost. If the agents live outside your code, use a custom agent source.
3. Does the factory build the agent around `context.ChatClient`? If not, the model rings,
   the key, and the egress policy are off, and Tracon logs a warning.
4. Does the agent take its tools from `IToolRegistry` and its history from the
   container? If not, tool policy is off, and the console may show an empty history.
5. Can the agent live as code? Without console editing, versions, and rollback, and
   without Tracon's skills, compaction, and MCP resources, is it still the agent you
   want?

# Sign the audit chain with a key

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/audit-chain-key/

The audit trail is a per-tenant hash chain: each entry carries a hash of its own content and
of the entry before it, and `GET /api/audit/verify` walks it (see [Tamper
detection](/concepts/governance/#tamper-detection) for the four answers it gives). Without a key
that hash is a plain SHA-256 of a public form, so anyone who can write to the audit table can change
an entry, recompute every hash after it and still get `Valid`. With a chain key the hash is an
HMAC-SHA256 under a value only your host holds, and each entry names the key's **id**, never its value.
The console's Audit screen runs the same walk with its **Verify chain** button.

## Turn the key on

The key value lives in configuration and nowhere else; the entry stores only the key's id.

```json
{
  "Tracon": {
    "Audit": { "ChainKeyId": "2026-10" },
    "AuditChainKeys": { "2026-10": "<base64, at least 32 bytes>" }
  }
}
```

```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
dotnet user-secrets set 'Tracon:AuditChainKeys:2026-10' '<the value>'
```

- A key decodes to at least 32 bytes. An id is 1 to 64 characters of lowercase letters, digits,
  `.`, `_` and `-`; lowercase only, because configuration keys ignore case and the id is stored as
  written.
- The host reads every key at start and refuses to start when one is missing a value, is not
  base64, is too short or has an id outside the pattern. The message names the configuration key and
  never carries a value. A change needs a restart.
- The value is never written to the database, a log, the diagnostics report or a response.
- Every replica carries the same set of keys. During a rollout two replicas may sign with different
  ids; both ids must be in both replicas' configuration.
- Entries written before the key was set keep their plain SHA-256 and are checked with it. They are
  not re-signed, because re-signing would rewrite history. The walk counts them in `unkeyedEntries`.
  After the first signed entry, an unsigned entry is a downgrade and the walk reports `Broken`.

## Turn the key on across replicas

Upgrade every replica to this release **first**, with no key. Then give every replica the same `ChainKeyId` and the
same values and restart them together. A replica that writes without the key after another has written a signed entry
for the same tenant leaves an unsigned entry behind a signed one: the walk reads that as a downgrade and reports
`Broken` from that entry on, for good, because the entry cannot be re-signed without rewriting history. Two things
produce it: a replica that has not restarted yet, and a replica still on an older release. Tracon's own tests pin
this (`AuditLogContract.Two_writers_with_a_mixed_key_configuration_leave_the_chain_broken_at_the_unsigned_entry_for_good`).

## Rotate the key

Add a new key under a new id, set `ChainKeyId` to it and restart. Keep the old
value in configuration: the entries it signed are checked with it for as long as they exist. Remove it
and those entries report `UnknownKey`. The same answer appears when a row's `key_id` was changed by hand to an id
no one holds, and the walk cannot tell the two apart: it is never `Valid`, so compare the id the row names with the
history of your keys.

## Turn the key off

Remove `ChainKeyId` and restart. Audit entries are still written (an audit trail
must not lose a record), unsigned; the host logs one warning per tenant, and the walk reports `Broken`
from the first unsigned entry on.

## Ask for it in production

`RequireProductionProfile()` asks about the key as `UnkeyedAuditChain`. It is not asked while the audit
log is Tracon's in-memory one, because that chain lives in the process and goes with it; a database
audit log, or one you registered, is asked. See [Make a production decision
required](/guides/embedding/#make-a-production-decision-required).

## What the key protects against, and what it does not

The key protects against an actor who can **write to the audit table but cannot read this host's
configuration**: a database administrator, a restored backup, another application's connection. They
can no longer change an entry and recompute the hashes after it, because a valid hash needs the key.

It does not protect against an actor who can read the configuration **and** write the table: they hold
the key. It does not anchor the chain outside the database, so an attacker who rewrites every entry from
the first signed one onward without a key leaves a chain the walk calls `Valid`; the signal is
`unkeyedEntries` equal to `entriesChecked`, which a host that has been signed from its first entry never
shows. `?after=` and `?before=` walk a range and cannot see a signed entry before it: the whole-history walk
is the one to trust. Without a key the chain still catches a change made without recomputing it (a manual
edit, a partial restore, a bug in another writer) and nothing more: anyone who can write the table can
recompute every hash, and the walk reports `Valid`.

- [Governance](/concepts/governance/#tamper-detection) — the four answers of `GET /api/audit/verify` and what each means
