# Embedding into a host application

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/embedding/

`AddTracon()` plus `MapTracon()` is a complete, working setup on its own;
[Your first agent](/getting-started/first-agent/) starts from it. Embedding Tracon into an application that already has its own tenants,
users, permissions, event bus, or object storage is a different job: it means
replacing built-in defaults with bindings into systems you already run. There are
seven embedding points. The six below are wired the same way, are all optional, and
can be added one at a time; the seventh, `IToolApprovalPresenter`, is covered with
[Approvals](/concepts/governance/#approvals).

## The six points

| Contract | What you give it | Built-in default when unbound |
|---|---|---|
| `ITenantContext`, `ITenantStore` | The current tenant, resolved from your own identity layer | A single fixed tenant |
| `IRunAttributionContext` | The current user and job labels a run belongs to | `UserId` and `Labels` are always `null` |
| `IToolAuthorizationHandler` | A decision for every tool call that runs through the tool chain ([which tools](#which-tools-reach-the-tool-authorization-handler)): allowed or denied | Every call is allowed |
| `IRunAuthorizationHandler` | A decision for every run start, every access to a run's resources, and every session access: allowed or denied | Every run starts, every run is readable, and every session is reachable |
| `IRunEventSink` | A bridge that receives every run event as it is written | No bridge; events reach only `IRunStore` |
| `IAttachmentStorage` | A place to write attachment bytes outside the database | Content is stored as `bytea` in the database |

Each interface is registered with `TryAdd`, so a registration made **before**
`AddTracon()` wins over the built-in default. A registration made after it is
where module order starts to matter: a `TryAdd` registration is dropped, because
Tracon's default already holds the slot, while a plain `Add` still wins the
resolve and leaves Tracon's unused registration behind it. Register first and
neither case can bite you. `GET /api/diagnostics` (once you turn it on) reports which
of the six are still built-in and which your application replaced — see
[Extension points](#extension-points-in-diagnostics) below; to turn a missed binding
into a failed startup instead of a report nobody reads, see
[Make a binding required](#make-a-binding-required).

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddSingleton<ITenantContext, YourTenantContext>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ITenantStore, YourTenantStore>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IRunAttributionContext, YourRunAttributionContext>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IToolAuthorizationHandler, YourToolAuthorizationHandler>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IRunAuthorizationHandler, YourRunAuthorizationHandler>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IRunEventSink, YourRunEventSink>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IAttachmentStorage, YourAttachmentStorage>();

var tracon = builder.AddTracon()
    .UseOpenAI(builder.Configuration.GetSection(OpenAIProviderOptions.SectionName))
    .UsePostgreSql(builder.Configuration.GetSection(TraconPostgreSqlOptions.SectionName));
```

`UsePostgreSql` comes from the `Tracon.PostgreSql` package, which the `Tracon` meta package does not include: `dotnet add package Tracon.PostgreSql --prerelease`.

The order above — bindings first, `AddTracon()` second — is the only order that
works. `AddTracon()` calls `TryAdd*` for all six; called first, it claims every
slot and your registrations that follow do nothing.

### 1 — Tenant resolution

```csharp
public sealed class YourTenantContext(IYourIdentityService identity) : ITenantContext
{
    public string TenantId => identity.CurrentTenantId;
}
```

`YourTenantContext` replaces the built-in resolver entirely — the claim/header
resolution chain [Governance](/concepts/governance/#multi-tenancy) describes only
applies when you leave the default in place and turn it on with `UseTenancy()`.
Bind your own `ITenantContext` instead when the tenant already lives in a service,
a claim shape, or a header your identity layer owns. Bind `ITenantStore` alongside
it only if you also want Tracon's tenant admin endpoints
(`/api/tenants`) to read and write your own tenant records instead of its
in-memory default.

For work that runs outside an HTTP request — a queued job, a scheduled task — no
`HttpContext` exists for `ITenantContext` to read. Open an ambient scope for the
duration of that work instead. It composes with
[`AmbientRunAttributionScope`](/concepts/runs/#who-ran-it-and-for-what) — a
background job binds both together, since neither has a request to read from:

```csharp
using (AmbientTenantScope.Begin(job.TenantId))
using (AmbientRunAttributionScope.Begin(job.RequestedByUserId, labels: null))
{
    await agent.RunAsync(job.Message);
}
```

**Open the scope inside the method that starts the run**, in that method's own
body — not in a helper it calls — and reopen it before every `MoveNextAsync` on a
streaming path. `AmbientTenantScope` is an `AsyncLocal<T>`; a value set upstream of
an `await` boundary does not flow back down through one opened later. A dropped
scope reads as "empty tenant", not as an exception, so it fails silently.

### 2 — Run attribution

Attributes a run to a user and, optionally, job labels — see
[Runs: who ran it and for what](/concepts/runs/#who-ran-it-and-for-what) for the
full contract, including why the value is never read from the run request body.

### 3 — Tool authorization

Decides whether a caller may invoke a specific tool at all, separately from
approval — see [Tools](/concepts/tools/#authorization-validation-and-timeout) for the binding
pattern and how authorization and approval order relative to each other. If your
widget renders its own approval card instead of the built-in console's, register
[`IToolApprovalPresenter`](/concepts/governance/#approvals) too — it turns a raw
`{ "orderId": "ORD-1001" }` into a name your widget can show directly, and it reaches
your widget the same way the built-in one reads it: an `approvals` frame on the
streaming run endpoint, keyed by the pending request's `requestId`. A widget that shows
the streamed reply of an agent with a [loop](/concepts/agents/#run-until-the-work-is-done)
needs one more frame: `loop.iteration-completed` marks where an iteration ends, because
nothing in the `update` frames does. The [embeddable chat widget](/ui/#embeddable-chat-widget)
does not stream (it sends `Idempotency-Key`), so it gets the final iteration only.

#### Which tools reach the tool authorization handler

The handler is asked for every tool call that runs through Tracon's tool chain:

- tools you register in code (`AddTool`, `AddToolsFrom`, `AddScopedTool`) and the built-in tools
  `speak`, `transcribe` and `generate_image`;
- the tools of the MCP servers of the tenant;
- the `file_access_*` tools of a [session workspace](/guides/context-and-memory/#give-an-agent-files-in-each-session),
  with the effect `Read`, `Write` or `Destructive`;
- `search_knowledge`, the search tool of a [knowledge base](/guides/knowledge/), and
  `search_conversation_memory`, the on-demand search of
  [conversation memory](/guides/context-and-memory/#remember-a-user-across-sessions), both with the effect `External`:
  the text of the query leaves the process for the embedding provider and the vector store.

It is not asked for a tool that Tracon does not run or does not own: a hosted tool (it runs at the model provider), an
agent called as a tool, the skill tools, the file memory, todo and harness tools, and the tools a provider
that an agent extension adds brings with it. The two search tools are not in the tool registry, so `GET /api/tools` does
not list them: write their names in your policy as fixed text.

The same list is what a tenant's [tool policy](/concepts/tools/#per-tenant-tool-policy) covers: the policy is
checked first, and a call it refuses is not shown to your handler.

### 4 — Run event bridge

Bridges every run event to your own queue or bus, in addition to the run store —
see [Runs: observing events beyond the store](/concepts/runs/#observing-events-beyond-the-store)
and [Troubleshooting a slow sink](/guides/observability/#troubleshooting) for the
full contract.

**The one rule that matters most:** `OnEventAsync` must queue the event and
return. Tracon awaits it directly on the run's own hot path, before the
response keeps streaming to its caller — a sink that does its own network I/O
inline ties the model's response speed to that network call's latency.

Tracon holds **no queue of its own** in front of your sink, so the buffer is
yours to own: write to a bounded channel and return. Size that channel to drop
the event and log it when it is full rather than block, so a slow consumer of
yours never slows the run down to match its queue depth.

### 5 — Attachment storage

```csharp
public sealed class YourAttachmentStorage(IYourBlobClient blobs) : IAttachmentStorage
{
    public async ValueTask<Uri> WriteAsync(
        string tenantId, Guid id, Stream content, string mediaType, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
        => await blobs.PutAsync($"{tenantId}/{id}", content, mediaType, cancellationToken);

    public ValueTask<Stream?> ReadAsync(Uri uri, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
        => blobs.OpenReadAsync(uri, cancellationToken);

    public ValueTask DeleteAsync(Uri uri, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
        => blobs.DeleteAsync(uri, cancellationToken);
}
```

`IAttachmentStore` keeps the metadata row either way; `IAttachmentStorage` only
decides where the bytes live. Tracon takes no dependency on any cloud SDK —
you write this class against whichever client your object store already uses.

### 6 — Run and session authorization

Tracon draws ownership at the **tenant** level by default; without this
binding, every caller with the `Operator` role in a tenant can start a run as,
read, cancel, score, and delete every other user's runs, attachments,
approvals, and sessions in the same tenant.

:::note[Sessions have a built-in answer too]
Turning on [session ownership](/concepts/sessions/#session-ownership) makes
Tracon record which user opened a session and narrow the session list to
that user, with no handler at all. It covers **sessions only**; runs,
attachments, approvals, and scores still need the handler below. The two
compose — with ownership on, a handler no longer has to reject a whole session
listing just to keep users apart.
:::

#### Ownership and attribution are not the same promise

Both read the user from `IRunAttributionContext`, and it is worth being exact
about how differently they treat a failure there:

| | Attribution | Session ownership |
|---|---|---|
| What the value does | Names the user on a cost report | Decides who may reach a session |
| If your implementation throws | The run continues; the column stays `NULL` | The session is not opened: `403` |
| If it returns an over-long value | Dropped whole; the run continues | Treated as no identity: `403` |
| When it is read | Every run | Only when a session is **opened** |

Same service, two contract strengths. The rule "observability never breaks
functionality" holds for attribution and deliberately does **not** hold once a
deployment has asked for that value to be an authorization input. If you bind
`IRunAttributionContext` and later turn ownership on, re-read your
implementation with that in mind: a path that used to degrade quietly now
refuses.

`AuthorizeRunAsync` answers two different questions, told apart by
`request.Access`. `RunAccess.Start` asks whether a run may **begin**;
every other value asks whether an existing run's **resource** may be reached,
and carries `request.RunId` so you can look that run up in your own records:

| `RunAccess` | What the caller is asking to do |
|---|---|
| `Start` | Start a run — including a replay, which carries the source run's `RunId` |
| `Read` | Read the run: summary, tree, event stream, recorded input, span tree, tool calls, scores |
| `Cancel` | Request cancellation of the run |
| `Feedback` | Write or delete a score for the run |
| `Attachment` | Upload, download, list, or delete an attachment |
| `Approval` | List, read, or decide an approval request |

```csharp
public sealed class YourRunAuthorizationHandler(IYourOwnershipService ownership) : IRunAuthorizationHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<RunAuthorizationResult> AuthorizeRunAsync(
        RunAuthorizationRequest request, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    {
        // Starting a run: there is no run yet, so the question is about the agent.
        if (request.Access == RunAccess.Start && request.RunId is null)
        {
            return await ownership.CanStartAsync(request.TenantId, request.UserId, request.AgentName!, cancellationToken)
                ? RunAuthorizationResult.Allow()
                : RunAuthorizationResult.Deny("This user cannot run this agent.");
        }

        // Everything else is about an existing run. RunId is null only for a
        // list, and for an attachment uploaded before any run existed.
        if (request.RunId is not { } runId)
        {
            return RunAuthorizationResult.Allow();
        }

        return await ownership.OwnsRunAsync(request.TenantId, request.UserId, runId, cancellationToken)
            ? RunAuthorizationResult.Allow()
            : RunAuthorizationResult.Deny("This run belongs to a different user.");
    }

    public async ValueTask<RunAuthorizationResult> AuthorizeSessionAsync(
        SessionAuthorizationRequest request, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    {
        // request.SessionId is null only for SessionAccess.List, which has no
        // single session identity to check ownership of.
        if (request.Access == SessionAccess.List)
        {
            return RunAuthorizationResult.Allow();
        }

        return await ownership.OwnsAsync(request.TenantId, request.UserId, request.SessionId!, cancellationToken)
            ? RunAuthorizationResult.Allow()
            : RunAuthorizationResult.Deny("This session belongs to a different user.");
    }
}
```

Both methods are called explicitly at every endpoint concerned — there is no
single filter they all share, because these endpoints have no route shape in
common, so each one calls this binding in its own body:

- **Six run-starting endpoints:** the agent run endpoint, the workflow run
  endpoint, the inbound trigger accept endpoint, the OpenAI-compatible
  `/v1/responses` and `/v1/chat/completions` endpoints, and `POST
  /api/runs/{id}/replay`. The check runs **before** the quota check, so a
  denied call never consumes the tenant's quota.
- **Every run resource:** the run summary, its tree, its event stream, its
  recorded input, its span tree, its tool calls, its scores, its
  cancellation, its attachments, and its approval requests.
- **Every session access:** list, read, delete, branch, and opening a
  real-time voice conversation (`SessionAccess.Voice`) — including the
  OpenAI-compatible routes that reach the same sessions under another name,
  `GET`/`DELETE /v1/conversations/{id}` and `GET /v1/conversations/{id}/items`.
  `POST /v1/conversations` is not among them: it reserves an identifier and
  writes nothing, so there is no session yet to authorize.

**How a denial answers depends on what was asked for.** A denied single
resource — a run, a session, an attachment, an approval request — returns
`404`, with a body **identical** to the one that resource gets when it
genuinely does not exist. A `403` there would confirm the resource exists to
a caller who should not even know it, and wording that differed between
"denied" and "missing" would leak the same thing through a side channel. A
denied **list** returns `403` instead: a list is an operation, not a single
resource, so there is no existence to leak, and the response is never
silently filtered — filtering there would break the `skip`/`take` paging
contract. A denied **run start** and a denied **attachment upload** also
return `403`: neither addresses an existing resource. A denied voice
handshake is refused before the socket upgrades, with the same `404` an
unreachable session already gives.

A voice session that does not exist yet is **not** an error: the first turn
opens it, and the handler is still asked, so you decide for yourself whether
a caller may open a conversation under that id.

If this handler throws, the call is denied (fail-closed); a gate that fails
open on an exception is not a gate. When it denies a single resource, the
`Reason` you supply is deliberately **not** returned — the response has to
stay identical to a missing resource's.

A throw is a failed check, not a decision, and Tracon reports it that way:

- It writes one `Error` log line in the `Tracon.RunAuthorization` category.
  The line names your handler type, the access kind and the tenant, agent, run
  and session ids, and carries the exception. The exception text never goes
  into the HTTP response.
- A `403` (a run start, a list, a replay, a workflow resume or respond) says
  *The run authorization check failed. Retry the request.* instead of claiming
  that your handler denied the call. A `404` does not change: it stays
  identical to a missing resource's.
- An `OperationCanceledException` that the request itself did not cause (for
  example, an `HttpClient` timeout inside your handler) is a failure like any
  other and is denied. Only the caller's own cancellation travels on.

If your `IRunAttributionContext` throws while a request is authorized, the
caller is treated as having no identity, and one `Error` line per request is
written in the same category.

## Reading identity inside a tool body

A tool cannot reach `AgentSession`, so it cannot read `ITenantContext` or
`IRunAttributionContext` through the normal request pipeline. It reads the same
values from `TraconRunContext.Current` instead — a static, `AsyncLocal`-backed
snapshot the run pipeline populates before every tool call:

```csharp
[TraconTool("current_account", "Returns the tenant, run, session, and caller identity of the current run.")]
public static string CurrentAccount()
{
    var scope = TraconRunContext.Current;

    return scope is null
        ? "no run in progress"
        : $"tenant={scope.TenantId} run={scope.RunId} session={scope.SessionId} user={scope.UserId}";
}
```

This is the only place a tool can read the run's identity — there is no parameter
Tracon injects for it. `scope.UserId` is the same value `IRunAttributionContext`
resolved for the run record, not a new concept — just a second place to read it
from. `AgentRunScope` also carries `RootRunId` (the top of an
agent-calls-agent tree) and `Budget` (the shared token/depth/count ceiling for that
tree).

## Two data planes, one connection pool or two

Your application's own schema and Tracon's tables can live in the same
PostgreSQL database. Tracon writes only inside its own schema (`SchemaName`,
default `tracon`; see
[Choose a migration strategy](/guides/production/#choose-a-migration-strategy)) and
never reads or writes yours.

**Giving both sides the same connection string does not share a pool.** Npgsql
pools a `NpgsqlDataSource` **instance**, not a connection string — two separate
`NpgsqlDataSource` objects built from an identical string open two separate
pools (measured: with 5 concurrent commands held open on each of two data
sources built from the same string, the server showed 10 simultaneous
backends, not 5). If your application uses Entity Framework Core (or any other
Npgsql consumer) and you want Tracon sharing its actual pool, build **one**
`NpgsqlDataSource` and give the same instance to both sides:

```csharp
var dataSource = new NpgsqlDataSourceBuilder(connectionString).Build();
builder.Services.AddDbContext<YourDbContext>(o => o.UseNpgsql(dataSource));
builder.AddTracon()
       .UsePostgreSql(o => o.DataSource = dataSource);
```

See [Two connection planes: EF Core and Tracon](/guides/ef-core/) for the
full pattern, including startup/shutdown ownership. Without a shared
`DataSource`, pointing `Tracon:PostgreSql:ConnectionString` at the same
string your application uses is still fine — the two sides simply keep
independent pools against the same database, exactly as if they pointed at two
different databases.

Give Tracon a **separate** connection string (or data source) — same
server, different database, or a fully different server — when you want its
connection ceiling, credentials, or failure blast radius kept independent of
your application's own database traffic. Nothing in Tracon requires this;
it is purely an operational choice, and it can be changed later since only the
connection string moves.

`AutoApplyMigrations` (default `true`) applies to Tracon's own schema only. In
an embedded setup where your application already owns a controlled migration step
for its own schema, set it to `false` and call `ApplyAsync()` on the registered
`IMigrationApplier` from that same step — Tracon's schema then
migrates alongside yours instead of at every instance's startup. See
[Choose a migration strategy](/guides/production/#choose-a-migration-strategy) for
the fleet-deployment version of this same setting.

## Make a binding required

Reporting a missed binding is not the same as refusing to run without it. An
application that means to enforce its own rule can declare the binding required, and
the host then does not start while Tracon's built-in default is what resolves:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IRunAuthorizationHandler, YourRunAuthorizationHandler>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IToolAuthorizationHandler, YourToolAuthorizationHandler>();

builder.AddTracon()
    .RequireCustomBinding<IRunAuthorizationHandler>()
    .RequireCustomBinding<IToolAuthorizationHandler>();
```

The check runs while the host starts, and the message names the contract, the type
that resolved instead, and how to fix it:

```text
IRunAuthorizationHandler was declared as a required custom binding, but Tracon's
built-in default AllowAllRunAuthorizationHandler is what resolved. Register your own
IRunAuthorizationHandler on IServiceCollection BEFORE the AddTracon() call.
```

Four properties are worth knowing before you rely on it:

- **It is off by default.** An application that never calls `RequireCustomBinding`
  behaves exactly as it did before, and the call resolves nothing extra at startup.
- **It is not an HTTP concern.** The check runs at host start, so an embedded host
  that never calls `MapTracon()` gets the same guarantee.
- **`IRunEventSink` and `IAttachmentStorage` are judged by absence.** Tracon
  registers nothing for those two, so "still on the default" means no registration at
  all rather than a particular type.
- **It is a composition gate, not a security proof.** It tells you your
  implementation is the one bound. It cannot tell you that your implementation
  decides correctly — that is what your own tests are for.

Any type that is not one of the seven contracts also stops the host, with a message
listing the seven that are accepted.

## Make a production decision required

`RequireCustomBinding<T>()` covers the bindings. Its sibling covers the settings:
`AddTracon()` also brings every security-sensitive switch up permissive, so a
deployment can reach production having never separated tenants, never decided who
owns a session and never registered a content guard — in silence.

```csharp
builder.AddTracon()
    .RequireProductionProfile(profile => profile
        .Accept(TraconProductionRisk.SingleTenant));
```

These decisions are asked about, and each is either answered by turning the feature on
or accepted by name. This table is the one list; other pages point here rather than
repeat it:

| Risk | What the permissive default means | Answer it with |
|---|---|---|
| `SingleTenant` | Every call resolves to the same default tenant | Bind your own `ITenantContext`, or `UseTenancy(options => options.Enabled = true)` |
| `UnownedSessions` | No session records the user it belongs to | `Tracon:SessionOwnership:Enabled` |
| `UnencryptedContentAtRest` | Prompts, responses and tool arguments are stored as clear text | `AddContentProtection(...)` |
| `UninspectedContent` | No prompt or response is inspected | `AddPatternContentGuard(...)` or `AddContentGuard<TGuard>()` |
| `UnlimitedRequestRate` | One caller can take the whole model budget | `Tracon:RateLimit:Enabled` |
| `UnboundedRetention` | Nothing is ever deleted | `Tracon:Retention:Enabled`, or a policy per target |
| `UnregisteredRolePolicies` | At least one of the `Tracon.Reader`, `Tracon.Operator` and `Tracon.Admin` policies is not registered, so the endpoints it guards get no role check | Define the three policies in `AddAuthorization(...)` with `TraconPolicies.Reader`, `Operator` and `Admin`, and set `TraconEndpointOptions.RequireRolePolicies` so a missing one stops `MapTracon` too |
| `UncheckedToolCalls` | The built-in tool authorization handler allows every call for every caller | Register your own `IToolAuthorizationHandler`, or set `Tracon:Tools:RequireTenantPolicy` to `true` and save a [tool policy](/concepts/tools/#per-tenant-tool-policy) for each tenant, the default tenant included |
| `UnrestrictedTenantEgress` | A tenant with no egress policy may call every provider | `Tracon:TenantProviders:RequireEgressPolicy`, then save a policy for each tenant |
| `UnverifiedTenantHeader` | The tenant is read from a request header and no claim takes precedence, so a client names the tenant it acts as | Set `ClaimType` in `UseTenancy(...)`, or leave `AllowHeaderResolution` off |
| `UnlimitedTenantWorkflows` | One tenant can take every workflow slot | `Tracon:Workflows:MaxConcurrentRunsPerTenant`. Any value the options validator accepts answers the decision; a value equal to `MaxConcurrentRuns` still lets one tenant take every slot, so size it |
| `UnkeyedAuditChain` | The audit trail's hash chain has no key, so anyone who can write to the audit table can change an entry and recompute every hash after it | Put a key under `Tracon:AuditChainKeys:<id>` and set `Tracon:Audit:ChainKeyId` to `<id>`; see [Sign the audit chain with a key](/guides/audit-chain-key/) |

Some rows are not asked in every composition:

- `UnrestrictedTenantEgress`, `UnverifiedTenantHeader` and `UnlimitedTenantWorkflows`
  are about one tenant reaching what another should not. They are reported as not
  applicable and never stop a host that does not separate tenants (the built-in
  single-tenant context, or `UseTenancy(options => options.Enabled = false)`). This is
  also why `SingleTenant` and these three are never open together: a host is one or the
  other.
- `UnverifiedTenantHeader` and `UnlimitedTenantWorkflows` exist only when
  `UseTenancy(...)` or `UseWorkflows(...)` is in the chain. `UnlimitedTenantWorkflows`
  is also not asked while `Tracon:Workflows:Enabled` is `false`.
- `UnkeyedAuditChain` is not asked while the audit log is Tracon's in-memory one: that chain lives in the process
  and goes with it, so no one writes to a table behind the host's back. A database audit log, or one you
  registered, is asked.
- `UnregisteredRolePolicies` is known only once `MapTracon` has run, so it is asked of a
  host that mapped the endpoints before it started. A host with no HTTP surface is not
  asked it.

The startup failure names every open decision at once — the setting, what it is
today, and how to answer it — so one restart clears all of them rather than one per
round:

```text
RequireProductionProfile() was called, and 2 production decisions are still on the
permissive default, so the host does not start.

  SingleTenant
    Setting: ITenantContext
    Today:   resolves to Tracon's built-in SingleTenantContext, so every call runs as the default tenant
    Fix:     register your own ITenantContext before the AddTracon() call, or on an ASP.NET Core host call UseTenancy(options => options.Enabled = true)
```

Five properties are worth knowing before you rely on it:

- **It changes no setting.** It sets no value, chooses no policy and turns nothing
  on. The only thing it does is turn a skipped decision into a startup failure.
- **It is off by default.** An application that never calls it behaves exactly as it
  did before, and the call resolves nothing extra at startup.
- **Accepting is per item.** There is no way to accept them all at once, so each
  accepted risk is one reviewable line — and every accepted risk is written to the
  log at information level, by name, each time the host starts.
- **The set of decisions is a versioned contract.** A later release that adds one
  stops a host that calls this method until the new decision is answered or
  accepted. See
  [Compatibility](/reference/compatibility/#the-production-profile-is-a-versioned-contract).
- **It is a composition gate, not a security proof.** It reports that a feature is
  switched on. It cannot tell you the policy behind it is right.

The tenant decision is answered by which `ITenantContext` is bound, so an embedded
host that resolves its tenant from a message header answers it the same way an HTTP
host does. `UseTenancy(options => options.Enabled = false)` is the one case where
that is not enough, and the HTTP package adds its own check for it: two checks can
carry the same risk, and the stricter answer wins. The same seam is open to you —
register your own `IProductionProfileCheck` to add a decision of your own, or to
narrow one of Tracon's.

## Extension points in diagnostics

`GET /api/diagnostics` (off by default; turn it on with
`TraconEndpointOptions.EnableDiagnosticsEndpoint`) reports an `extensionPoints`
array: one entry per contract above, naming the bound implementation's type and
whether it is still Tracon's built-in default.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Binding and verification order
    accDescr: Register the six implementations, then call AddTracon so TryAdd claims whatever is still unbound, then read the diagnostics endpoint to confirm each binding actually took.
    A["Register ITenantContext, IRunAttributionContext,<br/>IToolAuthorizationHandler, IRunAuthorizationHandler,<br/>IRunEventSink, IAttachmentStorage"] --> B["AddTracon call<br/>TryAdd claims any still-open slot"]
    B --> C["GET /api/diagnostics<br/>reads extensionPoints"]
    C --> D{"isBuiltInDefault?"}
    D -->|false| E["binding is active"]
    D -->|true| F["registered too late, or against<br/>the wrong interface"]
```

```json
{
  "extensionPoints": [
    { "contract": "ITenantContext", "implementation": "YourTenantContext", "isBuiltInDefault": false },
    { "contract": "IRunAttributionContext", "implementation": "DefaultRunAttributionContext", "isBuiltInDefault": true }
  ]
}
```

A fresh installation shows all seven (the six above, plus `IToolApprovalPresenter` —
see [Approvals](/concepts/governance/#approvals)) as built-in. Read this endpoint right after
adding a binding to confirm it actually took — `isBuiltInDefault: true` on a
contract you meant to replace means the registration ran too late, or against the
wrong interface.

## Verification checklist

- [ ] Every binding you need is registered **before** `AddTracon()`
- [ ] Bindings your deployment must not run without are declared with `RequireCustomBinding<T>()`
- [ ] Production decisions your deployment must not skip are declared with `RequireProductionProfile()`
- [ ] `GET /api/diagnostics` shows `isBuiltInDefault: false` for each contract you bound
- [ ] A background job opens `AmbientTenantScope.Begin(tenantId)` in the method that starts the run, and the scope covers every `await` on that path
- [ ] `IRunEventSink.OnEventAsync` never performs blocking I/O inline — it queues and returns
- [ ] `Tracon:PostgreSql:SchemaName` (or the equivalent SQL Server/SQLite setting) does not collide with a schema your own application already owns
- [ ] `AutoApplyMigrations` matches your deployment's migration strategy, not just the default

## Read next

- [Runs](/concepts/runs/) — attribution and the event sink in full
- [Governance](/concepts/governance/) — the built-in tenant resolution chain `ITenantContext` replaces
- [Production](/guides/production/) — migration strategy and process topology

# Connect and expose agents

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/external-agents/

Tracon supports three different external-agent directions. Keep them separate:

| Direction | Purpose | Registration | HTTP surface |
|---|---|---|---|
| MCP client | Bring remote tools, prompts, and resources into Tracon | `UseMcp()` | Managed through `/api/mcp-servers/*` |
| MCP server | Publish a Tracon agent as an MCP tool | `UseMcpServer()` | `/tracon/mcp` by default |
| A2A server | Publish an agent through the agent-to-agent protocol | `UseA2A()` | `/tracon/a2a/{agent}` by default |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: The three external-agent directions
    accDescr: As an MCP client Tracon calls remote servers to gain tools. As an MCP server and as an A2A server Tracon is called by outside callers, and each of those directions has its own allowlist, budget, and credential requirement.
    subgraph Inbound["Who can call your agents"]
        MCPC["MCP caller"] --> MCPS["UseMcpServer<br/>allowlist · run budget · ExternalInvoke key"]
        A2AC["A2A caller"] --> A2AS["UseA2A<br/>one agent card per exposed agent"]
    end
    MCPS --> AGENT["Your agent"]
    A2AS --> AGENT
    AGENT --> CLIENT["UseMcp<br/>discovery, refreshed on an interval"]
    CLIENT --> REMOTE["Remote MCP server<br/>tools · prompts · resources"]
```

The first direction expands what your agents can call. The other two expand who can
call your agents. They have different trust boundaries and must be enabled separately.

## Consume a remote MCP server

Add the non-AOT `Tracon.Mcp` package and register discovery:

```csharp
var tracon = builder.AddTracon()
    .UseOpenAI(builder.Configuration.GetSection(OpenAIProviderOptions.SectionName))
    .UsePostgreSql(connectionString)
    .UseMcp(options =>
    {
        options.RefreshInterval = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5);
        options.ConnectionTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
        options.MaxToolsPerServer = 100;
    });
```

`UsePostgreSql` comes from the `Tracon.PostgreSql` package, which the `Tracon` meta package does not include: `dotnet add package Tracon.PostgreSql --prerelease`.

Create server records through the console or management API. Only the configuration
key name is persisted; the credential value stays in your secret provider:

```json
{
  "endpoint": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
  "headerConfigurationKeys": {
    "Authorization": "Tracon:McpSecrets:ExampleToken",
    "X-Api-Key": "Tracon:McpSecrets:ExampleKey"
  }
}
```

```bash
dotnet user-secrets set "Tracon:McpSecrets:ExampleToken" "Bearer ..."
dotnet user-secrets set "Tracon:McpSecrets:ExampleKey" "..."
```

Each key name sits under `Tracon:McpSecrets:`, and a tenant other than the default one
uses `Tracon:McpSecrets:<tenant>:`. A credential in plain `headers` is refused with
`400` — see [credential headers](/getting-started/security/#credential-headers-are-declared-by-key-name).
The value is read on every connection, but a changed value does not reconnect by
itself: call the refresh endpoint below after rotating it.

Discovery is asynchronous and does not block startup. Refresh immediately after a
configuration change with `POST {prefix}/api/mcp-servers/refresh`. A server that
cannot be reached produces a warning; other servers continue. If the server was
listed before and its definition is unchanged, its last tool list is kept for
`StaleToolRetention` (15 minutes) after that listing, so one network blip does not
stop the agents that use it. After that the tools drop out, and an agent that names
one is refused until the server lists them again. A server that is edited, deleted
or disabled drops its tools at once.

An agent compiled against a tool also follows what the server says about it: when
a refresh lists a changed description or input schema, the next run compiles again
and the model sees the new definition.

### The MCP client security boundary

- Only HTTP and HTTPS transports are accepted. Tracon does not start MCP `stdio`
  processes on the host.
- Discovered tool names are `{server}_{tool}`. A code-defined tool with the same name
  wins, so a remote server cannot replace it.
- New MCP tools require approval by default.
- Discovery is tenant-scoped and limited to 100 tools per server by default.
- OAuth tokens live in memory. Plan for reauthorization after a process restart.

An agent can also receive static MCP resources at run start through
`AgentDefinition.McpResourceUris`. Each entry is `{server}:{uri}`. The limits are
64 KB per resource and 256 KB total. `UseMcp()` is required. This field is currently
code/HTTP-only; the console editor does not preserve it.

## Publish agents as MCP tools

Choose the allowlist before the application is built, then map the management API
before the MCP endpoint:

```csharp
var tracon = builder.AddTracon()
    .UseOpenAI(builder.Configuration.GetSection(OpenAIProviderOptions.SectionName))
    .UsePostgreSql(connectionString)
    .UseMcpServer(options =>
    {
        options.ExposedAgents.Add("support");
        options.ToolNamePrefix = "acme";
        options.Budget = new AgentRunBudget
        {
            MaxDepth = 1,
            MaxTotalRuns = 4,
            MaxTotalTokens = 40_000,
        };
    });

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapTracon("/tracon", options =>
{
    options.AllowRemoteAccess = true;
    options.RequireRolePolicies = true;
});
app.MapTraconMcpServer();
```

No agent is exposed by default. `ExposeAllAgents` exists, but an allowlist is safer
for a catalog that operators can edit. Each MCP call creates a fresh run budget; the
default maximum depth is one, so an external caller cannot open an unbounded agent
tree.

The endpoint inherits the loopback, bearer, and authorization settings from
`MapTracon`. Remote exposure also requires at least one active, unexpired API key
with the exact `ExternalInvoke` scope. A static bearer token alone is rejected at
startup. Create the key before enabling remote access.

An exposed agent cannot contain an approval-required tool. A tool needs approval when its
registration sets `RequiresApproval`, or when the function is already wrapped in
`ApprovalRequiredAIFunction` — the default of Microsoft Agent Framework's
`DockerShellExecutor.AsAIFunction()`. The application waits
until the catalog is queryable, checks the selected agents, and prevents MCP requests
from running if an approval boundary would be crossed. An external protocol caller
cannot act as the missing human. A tool that gains approval after the agent was exposed
is refused at the call, and the run closes `Failed` with the error type
`approval_unanswerable`: nobody can ever answer it, so it does not wait.

The skill tools follow the same rule. They are not in the tool registry: Microsoft Agent
Framework adds them when it builds the agent, and it makes all three ask for approval. An
exposed agent that names skills must set `Skills.DisableReadApproval` on its definition
(see [Approval of the skill tools](/concepts/tools/#approval-of-the-skill-tools)). Without it,
the host refuses to open the agent and the message names the agent and the setting. With it,
`load_skill` and `read_skill_resource` run. `run_skill_script` keeps its approval, so the check does
not count it; a model that calls it ends the run with `approval_unanswerable`, unless a standing
approval rule covers the tool.

The file tools of a [session workspace](/guides/context-and-memory/#give-an-agent-files-in-each-session)
are not in the registry either. The tools that change a file always ask for approval, so an exposed
agent may have a workspace only if it is read-only and asks for no approval to read:
`Workspace.ReadOnly` and `Workspace.DisableReadApproval` together. Any other workspace on an
exposed agent stops the host from opening it, and the message names the agent and the settings.

The check reads the catalog once, when the host starts, with no request in scope. An agent that you
save through the API after that is not checked, and neither is an agent that a callable agent
reaches. The run-time refusal is the boundary for those agents.

### Long-running calls as MCP tasks

By default, a `tools/call` for a published agent holds the connection open until the
agent finishes. A client that speaks the `2026-07-28` revision gets the response
headers together with the result, not before it, so a proxy that times out while it
waits for the first byte cuts a long call. Set `EnableTasks` to serve long-running calls
as MCP tasks instead: a task-aware client gets an immediate task id back, closes the connection, and polls
`tasks/get` for the result — useful when an agent's response can take longer than a
client is willing to keep a connection open.

```csharp
.UseMcpServer(options =>
{
    options.ExposedAgents.Add("support");
    options.EnableTasks = true;
    options.TaskTimeToLive = TimeSpan.FromHours(2);
    options.TaskPollInterval = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5);
});
```

`EnableTasks` is `false` by default: a client that never asks for the tasks
capability keeps getting today's immediate response either way. The task id is the
same id the run itself uses, so a task also shows up as an ordinary run in the
management API and cost reports. An agent that ends up needing approval never
surfaces as a task waiting on input — it is reported as a completed task carrying
the same rejection message the synchronous path returns, for the same reason an
approval-required tool cannot be exposed in the first place: an external protocol
caller cannot act as the missing human.

## Publish agents through A2A

A2A exposes a distinct identity and agent card for each selected agent:

```csharp
var tracon = builder.AddTracon()
    .UseOpenAI(builder.Configuration.GetSection(OpenAIProviderOptions.SectionName))
    .UsePostgreSql(connectionString)
    .UseA2A(options =>
    {
        options.ExposedAgents.Add("support");
        options.Budget = new AgentRunBudget
        {
            MaxDepth = 1,
            MaxTotalTokens = 40_000,
        };
    });

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapTracon("/tracon", options =>
{
    options.AllowRemoteAccess = true;
    options.RequireRolePolicies = true;
});
app.MapTraconA2A();
```

The invocation URL is `/tracon/a2a/support`; its card is under
`/tracon/a2a/support/.well-known/agent-card.json`.

A2A names are frozen during service registration because the underlying hosting API
registers one server per name. The agent implementation is still resolved from the
catalog on every call, so updating a database definition changes later behavior, but
adding a new name requires an application restart and registration change. There is
no expose-all switch.

Tracon declares streaming, push notifications, and background A2A runs as
unsupported. The same `ExternalInvoke`, approval, tenant, and budget boundaries as
the MCP server apply.

### A2A conversations

A message that carries a `contextId` continues a conversation. Tracon stores the
session of each conversation, so the agent sees the earlier turns of the same
`contextId`. A message without a `contextId` is a single turn: the response carries
a new `contextId` that the caller can send next.

A conversation belongs to the caller. Tracon stores it under the tenant, the agent,
the caller, and the `contextId`. A `contextId` is a handle, not a credential: a
caller that sends the `contextId` of another caller starts a new conversation and
cannot read or extend the first one.

| The request carries | The caller is |
|---|---|
| A signed-in user | That user. The user is read the way the audit trail reads its actor, so `Tracon:Audit:ActorClaimType` applies |
| An API key | That key |
| The static `AuthToken` | The installation |
| Nothing (loopback, no token) | The local operator. All such requests share one conversation space |

A signed-in user whose identity cannot be read is refused. Tracon does not move that
user into the local operator's space.

Keep these effects in mind:

- **Cost.** Each turn sends the whole history to the model, so the tokens per message
  grow with the conversation. Send a new `contextId` to start over.
- **Storage.** Every message Tracon answers leaves a session, also a message with no
  `contextId`: Tracon makes one up and the reply carries it. Session retention is off by
  default because a session is user data. Set a maximum age for the `sessions` target to
  bound the table; see [Retention defaults](/reference/configuration/#retention-defaults).
- **Parallel messages.** Two messages on one `contextId` at the same time cannot both
  be stored. One succeeds. The other fails and the caller receives a JSON-RPC
  internal error (`-32603`). Send the messages one after the other.
- **Refusals.** A refusal reaches the caller as the same opaque `-32603` error. The
  cause is in the server log at `Error` level.
- **Session ownership.** When session ownership is on and
  `RequireAuthenticatedOwner` is `true`, a message whose identity Tracon cannot
  attribute is refused **before** the model is called, and so is a message that resumes
  a conversation another user owns. This matters when one API key speaks for several
  users: the key is one caller, the owner is the end user. Bind `IRunAttributionContext`
  to the identity pipeline, or an A2A caller cannot open a conversation.
- **A turn that needs an approval.** If a tool that needs approval reaches an exposed
  agent after startup, the turn ends with the same error and stays in the conversation;
  the call is recorded as declined, and the next message goes through.
- **The console.** A conversation is a session. The Sessions page lists it under the
  exposed agent, with an identity that starts with `a2a:`.

To store conversations somewhere else, register an `AgentSessionStore` keyed by the
agent name, or without a key; Tracon uses yours. To name the caller differently,
register an `AgentIsolationKeyProvider`. Both types come from Microsoft Agent
Framework and are marked experimental there. A store of your own receives the caller
as the `isolation` partition of the key and must keep the callers apart.

Both surfaces are configured in code, never from the console:
`TraconMcpServerOptions` for the MCP server and `TraconA2AOptions` for A2A.
They do not carry the same settings.

`ExposeAllAgents` and `ToolNamePrefix` are **MCP-server settings only**:
`ExposeAllAgents` opts out of naming published agents one by one, and
`ToolNamePrefix` keeps the published tool names from colliding with another
server's. A2A has neither — its names are fixed at registration, which is why
there is no expose-all switch for it.

`Budget`, which bounds what an external caller may spend, is on both.

## Production checklist

- [ ] Expose only names whose input contract is safe for another system.
- [ ] Expect token use to grow with each turn of a `contextId`; decide how a caller starts a new conversation.
- [ ] Create a tenant-bound `ExternalInvoke` key and test revocation and expiry.
- [ ] Keep approval-required and high-impact tools out of exposed definitions.
- [ ] Set `Skills.DisableReadApproval` on every exposed agent that names skills, and keep script
      skills off exposed agents.
- [ ] Give an exposed agent no session workspace, or a read-only one with `Workspace.DisableReadApproval`.
- [ ] Set token, depth, and child-run budgets for externally initiated work.
- [ ] Terminate HTTPS at a trusted proxy and preserve the request path.
- [ ] Alert on external run error rate, token use, latency, and rejected credentials.
- [ ] Test catalog availability when migrations are applied outside the process.

MCP server and A2A routes are protocol surfaces, not management endpoints. They do
not appear in the generated OpenAPI operation count. Their runs still use the normal
recording, tenancy, trace, cost, quota, and audit infrastructure.

- [Tools, skills, and MCP](/concepts/tools/) — the other direction: consuming an MCP server rather than publishing one
- [Securing the endpoints](/getting-started/security/) — bind exposed agents to authentication, tenant scopes, and execution limits
- [Compatibility matrices](/reference/compatibility/) — which protocol revisions and transports are supported

# Move an agent from AddAIAgent to Tracon

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/from-maf-hosting/

You built an agent with `AddAIAgent` from Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) hosting. What
is the Tracon call for it? This page maps each hosting call to the Tracon call that does the
same work, and says what you keep and gain on the way. Read it with the code of the
`samples/Tracon.Samples.MafFeatures` sample open: its tests run the agent mappings against the
packed packages. The tool block comes from `samples/Tracon.Samples.CustomTool`.

Tracon does not read `AddAIAgent` registrations. An agent you registered with `AddAIAgent`
is not in the Tracon catalog until you register it again with a Tracon call. The table is
the list of calls to change.

## Pick the Tracon call

Start from how your MAF agent gets its model, and follow the arrow to the Tracon call.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    accTitle: From a hosting call to the Tracon call
    accDescr: A decision tree. An AddAIAgent call with instructions only becomes an agent definition with a model binding. An AddAIAgent call with a factory that calls a model becomes AddAgent with a declared model, and Tracon gives the factory the chat client. A factory for an agent that calls no model through Tracon becomes AddAgent with no model. WithAITool becomes AddTool, and a tool that takes a dependency uses the factory form of AddTool.
    START["An AddAIAgent call"] --> FORM{"What does it take?"}
    FORM -->|"instructions"| DEF["AddAgent(new AgentDefinition)<br/>with a Model binding"]
    FORM -->|"a factory"| CALL{"Does the agent call a model<br/>through Tracon?"}
    CALL -->|yes| DECL["AddAgent(name, model, factory)<br/>Tracon builds the chat client"]
    CALL -->|no| PLAIN["AddAgent(name, factory)<br/>no model declared"]
    TOOL["A WithAITool call"] --> DEP{"Does the tool take<br/>a dependency?"}
    DEP -->|no| ADD["AddTool(tool)"]
    DEP -->|yes| ADDF["AddTool(provider => tool)"]
```

## The mapping

| MAF hosting call | Tracon call | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| `AddAIAgent(name, instructions)` | `AddAgent(new AgentDefinition { … })` | The agent is data. Tracon compiles it and gives it versions, validation, and console editing. |
| `AddAIAgent(name, instructions, chatClient)` | `AddAgent(new AgentDefinition { … })` with a `Model` binding | The chat client becomes a model binding that names a provider and a model. See [the model client](#the-model-client). |
| `AddAIAgent(name, (sp, key) => agent)` | `AddAgent(name, model, context => agent)` | The factory is yours. Tracon builds the chat client and hands it over as `context.ChatClient`. |
| `AddAIAgent(name, (sp, key) => agent)`, an agent that calls no model through Tracon | `AddAgent(name, sp => agent)` | The agent declares no model. Tracon records the run and nothing more. |
| `WithAITool(tool)`, `WithAITools(…)` | `AddTool(tool)`, and the agent lists the tool name in `ToolNames` | The tool is registered once, with its policy, and every agent finds it by name. |
| `WithAITool(sp => tool)` | `AddTool(sp => tool)` | The factory runs once, at start. |
| `WithSessionStore(…)`, `WithInMemorySessionStore()` | Nothing to write | Tracon keeps the session. Pick a store with `UsePostgreSql` (package `Tracon.PostgreSql`), `UseSqlServer` (`Tracon.SqlServer`), or `UseSqlite` (`Tracon.Sqlite`). |
| `AddWorkflow(name, (sp, key) => workflow)` | `AddWorkflow(name, factory)` from `Tracon.Workflows` | See [Workflows](/concepts/workflows/). |

## An agent with instructions only

`AddAIAgent(name, instructions)` becomes a definition. The definition names the model, so
Tracon can build the chat client, price the run, and apply the tenant's own provider key:

```csharp
builder.AddTracon()
       .AddAgent(new AgentDefinition
       {
           Name = "support-agent",
           Instructions = "Answer questions about orders. Look orders up with the search tool.",
           Model = model,
           ToolNames = [SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName],
       });
```

## An agent that your code builds

`AddAIAgent(name, (sp, key) => agent)` gives you the whole agent. In Tracon you keep that, and
you declare the model the agent calls. Tracon then builds the chat client for the model, with
the tenant's own provider key and the tenant's egress policy, and the factory builds the agent
around it:

```csharp
return builder.AddAgent(
    AgentName,
    model,
    context =>
    {
        // The registry returns the wrapped tool: authorization, validation,
        // timeout, truncation, and approval stay on.
        if (!context.Services.GetRequiredService<IToolRegistry>().TryGet(SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName, out var searchOrders))
        {
            throw new InvalidOperationException($"The tool '{SearchOrdersToolRegistration.ToolName}' is not registered.");
        }

        // The client carries the model rings (run budget, circuit breaker, fallback,
        // response cache, content guards, the 'chat' span), the tenant's key, and the
        // egress policy. Build the agent around it and nothing else.
        return context.ChatClient.AsAIAgent(new ChatClientAgentOptions
        {
            Name = context.AgentName,
            ChatOptions = new ChatOptions
            {
                Instructions = "Answer questions about orders. Look orders up with the search tool.",
                Tools = [searchOrders],
            },

            // Tracon's history store, so the console and /v1/conversations show the
            // turns. With SQL storage, leaving this out leaves both of them empty.
            ChatHistoryProvider = context.Services.GetService<ChatHistoryProvider>(),

            // Any framework provider or option is now yours.
            AIContextProviders = [new TodoProvider(new TodoProviderOptions())],
        });
    },
    description: "A factory agent that declares its model and answers questions about orders.");
```

Three differences from the hosting factory:

- **You do not use the key.** The hosting factory receives a service key that selects a
  chat client in the container. Tracon does not read the container for the chat client. The
  model you declare selects a provider, and the provider holds the credential.
- **A request field is refused.** The factory builds its own `ChatOptions`, so a binding that
  sets `Temperature`, `MaxOutputTokens`, `ResponseFormat`, or any other request field fails
  when you register, and the message names the field. Set the field in the factory.
- **Tracon keeps nothing between calls.** The factory runs on every resolve, and the client
  holds the key of one tenant. Do not keep the agent, or the client, in a static field or a
  cache.

## The model client

A hosting agent takes its chat client from the container, selected by a key. That client is
a `Microsoft.Extensions.AI` `IChatClient` that you registered yourself. In Tracon the
equivalent is a model provider: `UseOpenAI`, one of the other provider packages, or
`AddModelProvider` for your own. The provider builds the client from a model binding, which
is a provider name and a model name. The tenant's key and the egress policy apply to that
path, and a client you register in the container does not use it.

## A tool that takes a dependency

`WithAITool(sp => tool)` and `AddTool(sp => tool)` are the same idea. The factory gets the host's
service provider when Tracon builds its tool registry at start, and the tool keeps what the factory
resolved. A tool does not get the container at call time, in MAF or in Tracon.

```csharp
return builder.AddTool(
    static provider => provider.GetRequiredService<OrderFulfillmentTool>().CreateFunction(),
    static options =>
    {
        options.RequiresApproval = true;
        options.Effect = ToolEffect.External;
        options.RequiredPermission = "orders.submit";
        options.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
        options.SafeToRepeat = true;
        options.MaxOutputBytes = 768;
    });
```

Do not ask the factory for `IToolRegistry`. The registry is built from the result of the
factory, and Tracon stops the host with an error that says so. For a dependency that must be
new on every call, use `AddScopedTool`.

## What you gain

The agent you move keeps its code. It gains the parts that hosting does not have:

- a run record for every run, with events, usage, and cost;
- the tenant's own provider key, the egress policy, and the cost quota;
- the tool chain: authorization, approval, timeout, and output limits;
- the catalog, the console, and the HTTP API.

## Read next

- [Use any Microsoft Agent Framework feature](/guides/any-maf-feature/) — the full list of doors, and what each one keeps
- [Agents and definitions](/concepts/agents/) — how the catalog gets its agents
- [Write your own tool](/guides/write-your-own-tool/) — approval, permission, and timeout for a tool

# Gemini speech and two-voice dialogue

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/gemini-speech/

How do you speak with a Gemini text-to-speech model, and voice a two-host dialogue with it? You register the model
with `UseGoogleSpeech`, and a caller names the provider `gemini`. This page covers the provider. The speech
layer it plugs into, the tenant's checks and the dialogue contract are in [Voice and live
conversation](/guides/voice/).

`UseGoogleSpeech` registers a Gemini text-to-speech model as a named provider. It shares the
client of `UseGoogle`, so call that first. The same provider speaks one voice and voices a
dialogue of two.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: How a Gemini speech call reaches the model
    accDescr: A caller names the provider gemini. The resolver applies the tenant's egress policy to the name google and chooses the setup key or the tenant's own key. The synthesizer sends one voice, or a dialogue of two voices in the speaker format the model takes, and returns a WAV file or raw 16-bit PCM.
    CALL["Caller<br/>provider: gemini"] --> RES["Resolver<br/>egress policy on google<br/>setup key or tenant key"]
    RES --> SYN["UseGoogleSpeech<br/>synthesizer"]
    SYN --> ONE["One voice"]
    SYN --> TWO["Dialogue of two voices<br/>PartMetadata or TextLabels"]
    ONE --> GEM["Gemini text-to-speech model"]
    TWO --> GEM
    GEM --> OUT["WAV file or<br/>raw 16-bit PCM"]
```

## Register it

```csharp
builder.AddTracon()
    .UseGoogle(builder.Configuration.GetSection(GoogleProviderOptions.SectionName))
    .UseGoogleSpeech(options =>
    {
        options.Model = "gemini-3.8-flash-tts";
        options.Voices.Add(new VoiceDescriptor { VoiceId = "Kore", Name = "Kore" });
        options.Voices.Add(new VoiceDescriptor { VoiceId = "Puck", Name = "Puck" });
    });
```

```http
POST /tracon/api/voice/speak
{ "text": "Your order is on its way.", "provider": "gemini", "voiceId": "Kore" }
```

## Voice a dialogue

The same provider voices a dialogue. Take the capability from the resolver, as [the voice
guide](/guides/voice/#voice-a-dialogue-with-several-speakers) describes:

```csharp
var dialogue = await speech.GetDialogueSynthesizerAsync("gemini", cancellationToken);
var result = await dialogue.SynthesizeDialogueAsync(
    new SpeechDialogueRequest
    {
        Turns =
        [
            new SpeechDialogueTurn { Text = "Welcome back.", VoiceId = "Kore" },
            new SpeechDialogueTurn { Text = "Glad to be here.", VoiceId = "Puck" },
        ],
    },
    cancellationToken);
```

A synthesizer of your own refuses the same requests, in the same words, with
`DialogueCapabilities.Check(request, ProviderName)`.

`result.Audio` is one WAV file. `GET /api/voice/providers` shows `dialogue` for `gemini` as
`maxVoices: 2` and `supportsSegmentTimestamps: false`.

## Options

`Model` is the only required option of `GoogleSpeechOptions`: Tracon carries no Gemini model or voice list. The provider
name is `google`, the name the chat provider uses, so one egress rule covers chat, images, and speech.
A prebuilt voice name such as `Kore` is the `voiceId`.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Model` | none | The text-to-speech model. A request can name another model. |
| `Name` | `gemini` | The registration name. |
| `DialogueSpeakerMode` | `PartMetadata` | How a dialogue names its speakers. See the rule below. |
| `MaxCharactersPerRequest` | `5000` | The limit `speak` enforces. Tracon's own guard: Gemini bounds a request by tokens. |
| `MaxDialogueCharactersPerRequest` | `2000` | The most characters one dialogue request carries. |
| `Voices` | empty | The voices `GET /api/voice/voices` lists. |
| `UseAsDefault` | `false` | Also register the synthesizer as the unnamed default, with `TryAdd`. Call `UseGoogleSpeech` before `UseVoice` for it to take effect. The `speak` tool then sends `Tracon:Voice:OutputFormat`, which defaults to `mp3_44100_128` and which Gemini cannot produce: set it to `wav`. Keep Gemini a named provider for the live conversation socket, which streams the raw PCM the shipped panel cannot play. |

## Rules that follow from the Gemini service

- **The speaker format follows the model generation.** The `gemini-3.8` models want the speaker
  on each text part and refuse a label in the text; `gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts` and
  `gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview` want a label in the text (`Speaker1: …`) and refuse the part
  metadata. Set `DialogueSpeakerMode` to `PartMetadata` or `TextLabels` to match the model. The wrong
  one answers `400`, and the error names the other mode. With `TextLabels`, a turn that has a line
  starting with a speaker label would change the voice, so Tracon refuses that turn before the call
  and does not rewrite it.
- **A dialogue takes exactly two voices.** One voice or three is refused before the call. Voice
  a single-voice text with `SynthesizeAsync`.
- **Timing is refused.** `IncludeTimestamps` fails on a speech and on a dialogue: Gemini reports no
  timing, so a dialogue result has no `Segments`.
- **The audio container follows the model.** The `gemini-3.8` models answer a WAV file with a `C2PA`
  provenance chunk after the samples; the older models answer raw 16-bit PCM. `OutputFormat` takes
  `wav` (the default) or `pcm`, and another format is refused. A `wav` result is the model's own
  file, or the samples in a new header. A `pcm` result is the samples alone, at the sample rate the
  answer states (24 kHz so far).
- **Streaming yields raw PCM** and never a WAV header, because a header carries the length of the
  audio. A `wav` request on a stream is refused. Whether the model streams in many parts depends on
  the model: `gemini-3.8-flash-tts` sends the first part after about a second, and
  `gemini-2.5-flash-preview-tts` sends the whole audio as one part.
- **A tenant with its own Google key is served with that key,** on the same client its chat
  requests use. A binding with an endpoint override is refused: the synthesizer calls the address
  it was built with.
- **Billing is an estimate.** Gemini bills speech by tokens and the answer carries no character
  count, so Tracon records the length of the text and marks it as estimated. A character price under
  `Tracon:Pricing:Voice:google:{model}` gives the cost; the price reader comes with `UseVoice()`.
- **Provider settings are refused.** Gemini speech reads no `google.*` setting.
- **A failure is a `502`** that carries the HTTP status and Google's status name
  (`HTTP 400 (INVALID_ARGUMENT)`), never the service's text.
- **The sample application** registers this provider when `Tracon:Providers:Google:ApiKey` is set.

## When a Gemini dialogue fails

The run's error names the cause. `takes exactly 2 voices` means the dialogue used one voice. `starts with
a speaker label` means a turn of a `TextLabels` dialogue would change the voice; rephrase the line. An
`HTTP 400` whose message names `DialogueSpeakerMode` means the model wants the other speaker format.
`GET /api/voice/providers` shows `dialogue: null` for a provider that cannot voice a dialogue at all.

- [Model providers](/guides/model-providers/) - `UseGoogle`, the client this provider shares
- [Packages](/packages/) - when to add `Tracon.Google`

# Hosted tools - web search, code interpreter, file search

Source: https://tracon.dev/guides/hosted-tools/

How does an agent use a tool that the model provider runs, not your code? You register the tool in code
with `AddHostedTool`, the agent definition selects it by name, and Tracon records and prices each call.

## What a hosted tool is

A function tool is code in your process. A hosted tool runs on the provider's side, inside the model
call. The provider decides when to run it. The response carries the call and its outcome.

| | Function tool | Hosted tool |
|---|---|---|
| Who runs it | Your process | The model provider |
| Registered with | `AddTool` and the other `Add*Tool` calls | `AddHostedTool` |
| Selected with | `ToolNames` | `ToolNames`, the same list |
| Approval, permission, timeout | Yes | No. Tracon has nothing to put in front of it |
| Billed | By your own cost | By the provider, per call |
| Where its calls are recorded | Tool events | Tool events, under the registered name |

Three kinds exist: `WebSearch`, `CodeInterpreter` and `FileSearch`. Image generation and hosted MCP
servers are not kinds. For images, see [Multimodal input and output](/guides/multimodal/).

## Register a hosted tool

```csharp
builder.AddTracon()
    .AddHostedTool("web_search", HostedToolKind.WebSearch, _ => new HostedWebSearchTool(),
        description: "Searches the web.")
    .AddHostedTool("docs_search", HostedToolKind.FileSearch,
        context => new HostedFileSearchTool
        {
            Inputs = [new HostedVectorStoreContent(Docs.VectorStoreFor(context.TenantId))],
        },
        description: "Searches the product documentation.");
```

The tool is code, like every tool. Registration is the only way to add one. The console and the HTTP API
can select a registered tool and cannot create one.

The factory has to follow these rules:

- **Return the type that matches the kind.** `HostedWebSearchTool` for `WebSearch`, `HostedCodeInterpreterTool`
  for `CodeInterpreter`, `HostedFileSearchTool` for `FileSearch`. Another type stops the compilation.
- **Return a new instance on every call.** Tracon remembers the name a tool was built under. An instance that
  another hosted tool returned too stops the compilation.
- **Keep it cheap.** The factory runs on every run of an agent that selects the tool. Tracon compares what it builds
  with the cached compiled agent and compiles again only when they differ. Do not call the network.
- **Read tenant values from `context`.** `context.TenantId` names the tenant. The identifier of a tenant's
  own vector store belongs here. An identifier is not a secret. Never put a credential in a hosted tool.

A tenant that replaces its vector store reaches the next run. Tracon compares what the factory builds, not only
the definition, before it reuses a compiled agent. It compares text, numbers, booleans, enums, lists and dictionaries of
those, the identifiers of vector stores and files, and the bytes of a code interpreter input. A tool that holds anything
else, such as a provider SDK object in `AdditionalProperties`, cannot be compared: the agent is compiled again for every
run, and the response cache never serves an answer for it.

A name is unique among all tools. A hosted tool and a function tool with one name stop the host at start.

## Select it in a definition

```json
{
  "name": "research",
  "instructions": "Answer from the web. Cite what you found.",
  "toolNames": ["web_search", "lookup_order"],
  "model": { "provider": "openai-responses", "model": "gpt-5.4-mini" }
}
```

An agent that does not list the name is not offered the tool. An agent selects at most one hosted tool of each
kind: the provider's response names the kind and not your tool, so two tools of one kind could not be told apart
in the run record.

`GET /api/tools` lists hosted tools with a `hostedKind` and no argument schema. The console shows a badge. Listing
runs no factory.

## Which provider runs which kind

The provider's API surface decides. The table is what the shipped adapters send, checked against the request body
each adapter writes (2026-10-20).

| Kind | `openai` (Chat Completions) | `openai-responses` | `anthropic` | `google` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `WebSearch` | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `CodeInterpreter` | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `FileSearch` | No | Yes | No | No |

`azure-openai` uses the Chat Completions surface and runs none. On Chat Completions the adapter drops a code
interpreter and a file search without an error, and the model answers as if it had none. For that reason an
agent that asks a surface for a kind it would drop does not compile. `POST /api/agents/validate` reports it
with the code `hosted_tool_unsupported`, the path of the tool name, the tool and the provider.

A fallback model link receives the same tools. A link whose surface drops a kind fails the same check.

A surface that runs a kind is not a promise. A model can still refuse the tool, and the refusal is the provider's
own error. Check your model and plan with a real call.

A provider you write opts in with `IHostedToolSupport`. A provider that does not state its support runs no kind.

## What the run record shows

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    accTitle: A hosted tool call in a run
    accDescr: The model call carries the hosted tool. The provider runs it and returns the call content. A cost ring reports the price to the run total and the budget. The recorder writes a tool event pair under the registered name.
    A["Model call<br/>carries the tool"] --> B["Provider runs it<br/>inside the call"]
    B --> C["Response holds<br/>the call content"]
    C --> D["Cost ring<br/>price · budget"]
    C --> E["Recorder<br/>ToolInvoking · ToolInvoked"]
    D --> F["Run non-token cost<br/>quota · webhook"]
    E --> G["Tool invocation record<br/>with the measurement"]
```

A call of a registered tool is a `ToolInvoking` and a `ToolInvoked` event with the registered name and the
provider's call identifier. The result of the call is part of the same call and adds no event. The event has no
payload: a search query is the user's text.

The tool invocation record holds one measurement for the call: unit `calls`, quantity `1`, the price when one
is configured, and the provider's name.

A hosted call that no registered tool owns keeps the content event `tracon.content`. The harness's own web
search is one such call. Both kinds of call are priced.

A provider can show one call in several pieces while it streams. Tracon writes the call once.

## Cost

Set a price for each provider and kind:

```text
Tracon:Pricing:HostedTools:{provider}:{kind}:PerCall
```

```json
{
  "Tracon": {
    "Pricing": {
      "Currency": "USD",
      "HostedTools": {
        "openai-responses": {
          "WebSearch": { "PerCall": 0.01 },
          "CodeInterpreter": { "PerCall": 0.03 }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Tracon has no built-in prices. Check your provider's price page. The values above are examples.

The price of a call joins the run's non-token cost. The run total, the tree's cost budget, the tenant's quota and
the `run.completed` webhook all count it once. Cost reaches the budget when the call arrives, so a budget that the
call used up stops the next model turn.

- **A kind with no price is not priced at zero.** The call is listed on the run, the run says one item is not
  added, and the host logs one warning. Set the price to add it.
- **A code interpreter price is an estimate.** The provider bills a container session, and the response names no
  container. The record marks the measurement as estimated.
- **Anthropic states how many searches it billed.** When that number is higher than the calls in the response,
  Tracon adds the difference. When it is lower, the calls already counted stay and Tracon logs the difference.
- **A cached response is not billed again.** A response cache hit spends nothing.

## Limits

- **The data goes to the provider.** A web search sends the query. A code interpreter sends the data it works on.
  A file search reads the vector store of the account behind the key. The provider is the one the model call
  already uses, and the tenant's [egress policy](/concepts/governance/) already applies to it.
- **A hosted tool runs when the model chooses it.** `ToolMode` `required:<name>` cannot name a hosted tool.
- **A harness agent that turns on `EnableWebSearch` cannot also select a hosted web search.** The model would
  receive two. Turn one off.
- **A replay never runs a hosted tool.** `ReplayTools` and `NoTools` remove it, so a replay does not search and
  bill again. `LiveTools` keeps it.
- **A code interpreter file output is not collected.** Tracon does not store files that the interpreter makes.
- **The response cache keys a hosted tool by what it puts on the wire.** Two file searches over different vector
  stores do not share an answer. A hit replays the stored response, so a hosted call in it is a content event and
  costs nothing: the run did not search.
- **Automatic run continuation does not stop for a hosted call.** The provider ran it inside a model turn that already
  answered, and a continuation runs no hosted call again.

## Test an agent that uses a hosted tool

`FakeModelProvider` from `Tracon.Testing` runs every kind. Its `Requests` list shows the tool objects that reached
the model, so a test can check the selection without a network call.

## Read next

- [Tools, skills, and MCP](/concepts/tools/) - where each kind of tool runs
- [Model providers](/guides/model-providers/) - the API surfaces and what each one sends
- [Observability](/guides/observability/) - runs, tool events and cost
